title: Part 1, Chapter 23
paragraphs: About what befell Don Quixote in the Sierra Morena, which was one of the rarest adventures related in this veracious history

Seeing himself treated this way, Don Quixote said to his squire, "I've always heard it said, Sancho, that doing good to boors is throwing water into the sea. If I'd believed your words, I'd have avoided this trouble; but it's done now — there's nothing for it but to have patience and take it as a warning for the future."

"Your worship will take warning about as much as I am a Turk," returned Sancho. "But, as you say this mischief might have been avoided if you'd believed me, believe me now, and a still greater one will be avoided. I tell you, chivalry is of no account with the Holy Brotherhood, and they don't care two maravedís for all the knights-errant in the world; and I can tell you I think I hear their arrows whistling past my ears this very minute."

"You're a coward by nature, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "but so you won't say I'm stubborn and never do as you advise, this once I'll take your advice and withdraw out of reach of that fury you dread so much. But on one condition: that never, in life or in death, are you to tell anyone that I retired or withdrew from this danger out of fear, but only in compliance with your entreaties. If you say otherwise you'll be lying; and from this time to that, and from that to this, I give you the lie and say you lie and will lie every time you think it or say it. Don't answer me back; for at the mere thought that I'm withdrawing or retiring from any danger — above all from this one, which does seem to carry some little shadow of fear with it — I'm ready to take my stand here and await alone, not only that Holy Brotherhood you talk of and dread, but the brothers of the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Seven Maccabees, and Castor and Pollux, and all the brothers and brotherhoods in the world."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "to retire is not to flee, and there's no wisdom in waiting when danger outweighs hope. It's the part of wise men to preserve themselves today for tomorrow, and not risk everything in a single day. And let me tell you, though I'm a clown and a boor, I have some notion of what they call safe conduct. So don't repent of having taken my advice; mount Rocinante if you can, and if not, I'll help you; and follow me, for my mother-wit tells me we have more need of legs than hands just now."

Don Quixote mounted without replying, and Sancho, leading the way on his ass, headed for the side of the Sierra Morena, which was close by; Sancho's plan was to cross it entirely and come out at El Viso or Almodóvar del Campo, and hide for some days among its crags to escape the search of the Brotherhood should they come looking. He was encouraged in this by noticing that the stock of provisions carried by the ass had come safe out of the brawl with the galley slaves — something he regarded as a miracle, considering how they pillaged and ransacked everything else.

That night they reached the very heart of the Sierra Morena, where Sancho thought it prudent to spend the night and even some days — at least as many as the supplies he carried might last — and so they encamped between two rocks and among some cork trees. But fatal destiny, which, according to the opinion of those who don't have the light of the true faith, directs, arranges, and settles everything in its own way, so ordered it that Gines de Pasamonte, the famous knave and thief who by Don Quixote's virtue and madness had been released from the chain, driven by fear of the Holy Brotherhood (which he had good reason to dread), resolved to take hiding in the mountains. His fate and fear led him to the same spot to which Don Quixote and Sancho Panza had been led by theirs, just in time to recognise them and leave them to fall asleep. And since the wicked are always ungrateful, and necessity leads to evildoing, and immediate advantage overcomes all considerations of the future, Gines, who was neither grateful nor well-principled, made up his mind to steal Sancho Panza's ass — not bothering about Rocinante, since the horse was a prize good neither to pledge nor sell. While Sancho slept, he stole the ass, and before day dawned he was far out of reach.

Aurora made her appearance, bringing gladness to the earth but sadness to Sancho Panza, for he found that his Dapple was missing; and seeing himself bereft of him, he began the saddest and most doleful lament in the world, so loud that Don Quixote awoke at his cries and heard him saying, "Oh son of my bowels, born in my very house, my children's plaything, my wife's joy, the envy of my neighbours, relief of my burdens, and finally, half-supporter of myself! For with the twenty-six maravedís you earned me daily I met half my charges."

Don Quixote, when he heard the lament and learned the cause, consoled Sancho with the best arguments he could, begging him to be patient and promising to give him a letter of exchange ordering three of the five ass-colts that he had at home to be given to him. Sancho took comfort at this, dried his tears, choked back his sobs, and thanked Don Quixote for the kindness shown him. Don Quixote, for his part, was overjoyed at entering the mountains, since they seemed to him just the place for the adventures he was looking for. They brought back to his memory the marvellous adventures that had befallen knights-errant in similar solitudes and wilds, and he went along reflecting on these things, so absorbed and carried away by them that he had no thought for anything else.

Nor did Sancho have any other care (now that he thought he was travelling in a safe quarter) than to satisfy his appetite with what was left of the clerical spoils; so he marched behind his master loaded with what Dapple used to carry, emptying the sack and packing his paunch — and as long as he could go that way, he wouldn't have given a farthing to meet with another adventure.

While so engaged he raised his eyes and saw that his master had halted and was trying with the tip of his pike to lift some bulky object that lay on the ground. He hurried over to join him and help him if needed, and reached him just as Don Quixote was raising on his pike a saddle-pad with a valise attached to it, half or rather wholly rotten and torn; but they were so heavy that Sancho had to help carry them, and his master directed him to see what the valise contained. Sancho did so with great alacrity; and though the valise was secured by a chain and padlock, from its torn and rotten state he was able to see its contents, which were four shirts of fine holland, and other linen items no less elegant than clean. And in a handkerchief he found a good handful of gold crowns, and as soon as he saw them he exclaimed:
"Blessed be all Heaven for sending us an adventure that's good for something!"

Searching further he found a richly bound little notebook; this Don Quixote asked of him, telling him to take the money and keep it for himself. Sancho kissed his hands for the favour, and cleared the valise of its linen, which he stowed away in the provision sack. Considering the whole matter, Don Quixote remarked:

"It seems to me, Sancho — and it can't possibly be otherwise — that some lost traveller must have crossed this sierra and been attacked and killed by footpads, who brought him to this remote spot to bury him."
"That can't be," answered Sancho, "because if they'd been robbers they wouldn't have left this money."

"You're right," said Don Quixote, "and I can't guess or explain what this may mean; but wait — let's see if there's anything written in this notebook by which we can trace out or discover what we want to know."
He opened it, and the first thing he found in it, written roughly but in a very fine hand, was a sonnet; and reading it aloud so Sancho could hear it, he found it ran as follows:
SONNET

Or Love is lacking in intelligence, Or to the height of cruelty attains, Or else it is my doom to suffer pains Beyond the measure due to my offence. But if Love be a God, it follows thence That he knows all, and certain it remains No God loves cruelty; then who ordains This penance that enthrals while it torments? It were a falsehood, Chloe, thee to name; Such evil with such goodness cannot live; And against Heaven I dare not charge the blame, I only know it is my fate to die. To him who knows not whence his malady A miracle alone a cure can give.
"There's nothing to be learned from that rhyme," said Sancho, "unless by that clew there's in it, one may draw out the ball of the whole matter."
"What clew is there?" said Don Quixote.
"I thought your worship spoke of a clew in it," said Sancho.

"I only said Chloe," replied Don Quixote, "and that no doubt is the name of the lady the author of the sonnet is complaining about; and honestly, he must be a passable poet, or I know little of the craft."
"Then your worship understands rhyming too?"

"And better than you think," replied Don Quixote, "as you'll see when you carry a letter written in verse from beginning to end to my lady Dulcinea del Toboso — for I would have you know, Sancho, that all, or most, of the knights-errant of old were great troubadours and great musicians, both these accomplishments, or rather gifts, being the particular property of lovers-errant. True it is that the verses of the knights of old have more spirit than polish in them."
"Read more, your worship," said Sancho, "and you'll find something that will enlighten us."
Don Quixote turned the page and said, "This is prose, and it seems to be a letter."
"A correspondence letter, señor?"
"From the beginning it seems to be a love letter," replied Don Quixote.
"Then let your worship read it aloud," said Sancho, "because I'm very fond of love matters."
"With all my heart," said Don Quixote, and reading it aloud as Sancho had asked, he found it ran thus:

Your false promise and my sure misfortune are carrying me to a place from which the news of my death will reach your ears before the words of my complaint. You ungrateful one, you've rejected me for one more wealthy, but not more worthy; but if virtue were esteemed wealth, I would neither envy the fortunes of others nor weep for misfortunes of my own. What your beauty raised up, your deeds have laid low; by your beauty I believed you to be an angel, by your deeds I know you are a woman. Peace be with you, who have sent war to me; and Heaven grant that the deceit of your husband be ever hidden from you, so that you don't repent of what you've done, and I don't reap a revenge I would not have.

When he'd finished the letter, Don Quixote said, "There's even less to be gathered from this than from the verses, except that whoever wrote it is some rejected lover." Turning over nearly all the pages of the book, he found more verses and letters, some of which he could read while others he could not; but they were all made up of complaints, laments, misgivings, desires and aversions, favours and rejections, some rapturous, some doleful. While Don Quixote examined the book, Sancho examined the valise, not leaving a corner of it or of the pad that he didn't search, peer into, and explore; not a seam he didn't rip, not a tuft of wool he didn't pick to pieces, lest anything escape for want of care and trouble — so keen was the greed stirred in him by the discovery of the crowns, which came to nearly a hundred. And though he found no more booty, he considered the blanket-tossings, balsam vomitings, stake-blessings, carriers' fisticuffs, missing saddlebags, stolen coat, and all the hunger, thirst, and weariness he had endured in the service of his good master, cheap at the price — since he considered himself more than fully indemnified for it all by the payment he had received in the gift of the treasure-trove.

The Knight of the Rueful Countenance was still very anxious to find out who the owner of the valise could be, gathering from the sonnet and letter, from the gold money and the fineness of the shirts, that he must be some lover of distinction whom the scorn and cruelty of his lady had driven to some desperate course. But in that uninhabited and rugged spot there was no one to be seen of whom he could enquire, so he saw nothing for it but to push on, taking whatever road Rocinante chose — which was wherever he could make his way — firmly persuaded that among these wilds he could not fail to meet some rare adventure. As he went along, occupied with these thoughts, he spotted on the summit of a height that rose before his eyes a man who went springing from rock to rock and from tussock to tussock with marvellous agility. As well as he could make out, the man was nearly unclothed, with a thick black beard, long tangled hair, and bare legs and feet; his thighs were covered by breeches apparently of tawny velvet but so ragged that they showed his skin in several places.

He was bareheaded, and despite the swiftness with which he passed by, as has been described, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance observed and noted all these trifles; though he made the attempt, he was unable to follow him, since it wasn't granted to Rocinante's feebleness to make way over such rough ground, the horse being moreover slow-paced and sluggish by nature. Don Quixote at once concluded that this was the owner of the saddle-pad and of the valise, and made up his mind to go in search of him, even if he had to wander a year in those mountains before finding him. So he directed Sancho to take a shortcut over one side of the mountain, while he himself went by the other, and perhaps by this means they might come across this man who had passed so quickly out of their sight.

"I couldn't do that," said Sancho, "because the moment I separate from your worship fear takes hold of me and assails me with all kinds of panics and fancies. And let what I now say be notice that from this time forward I'm not going to stir a finger's width from your side."

"So be it," said he of the Rueful Countenance, "and I'm very glad you're willing to rely on my courage, which will never fail you, even though the soul in your body fail you. So come on behind me slowly as best you can, and make lanterns of your eyes. Let's make the circuit of this ridge; perhaps we'll come upon this man we saw, who's no doubt the owner of what we found."

To which Sancho answered, "It would be far better not to look for him, because if we find him and he happens to be the owner of the money, it's plain I have to give it back. It would be better, therefore, to take no such needless trouble and instead keep possession of it until in some other less meddlesome and officious way the real owner may be discovered — and perhaps that will be after I've spent it, and then the king will hold me harmless."

"You're wrong there, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because now that we have a suspicion who the owner is, and have him almost in front of us, we're bound to seek him out and make restitution. And if we don't see him, the strong suspicion we have as to his being the owner makes us as guilty as if he were. So, friend Sancho, don't let our search for him trouble you — for if we find him, it will relieve my mind."

So saying he gave Rocinante the spur, and Sancho followed him on foot and loaded; and after they'd partly made the circuit of the mountain, they found lying in a ravine, dead and half devoured by dogs and pecked by jackdaws, a mule saddled and bridled, all of which further strengthened their suspicion that the man who'd fled was the owner of both the mule and the saddle-pad.

As they stood looking at it they heard a whistle like that of a shepherd watching his flock, and suddenly on their left there appeared a great number of goats, and behind them on the summit of the mountain the goatherd in charge of them, a man advanced in years. Don Quixote called out to him and begged him to come down to where they stood. The goatherd shouted back, asking what had brought them to that spot, seldom or never trodden except by goats or by the wolves and other wild beasts that roamed around. Sancho in return called for him to come down, and they'd explain everything to him.

The goatherd descended, and reaching the place where Don Quixote stood, said, "I'll wager you're looking at that hack mule lying dead in the hollow there, and, faith, it's been lying there now these six months. Tell me, have you come across its master anywhere around here?"
"We've come across nobody," answered Don Quixote, "nor on anything except a saddle-pad and a little valise we found not far from here."

"I found it too," said the goatherd, "but I wouldn't lift it or go near it for fear of some ill-luck or being charged with theft, because the devil is crafty, and things rise up under one's feet to make one fall without knowing why or wherefore."
"That's exactly what I say," said Sancho. "I found it too, and I wouldn't go within a stone's throw of it. I left it there, and there it lies just as it was, for I don't want a dog with a bell."
"Tell me, good man," said Don Quixote, "do you know who the owner of this property is?"

"All I can tell you," said the goatherd, "is that about six months ago, more or less, there arrived at a shepherd's hut some three leagues from here a youth of well-bred appearance and manners, mounted on that same mule lying dead here, and with the same saddle-pad and valise you say you found and didn't touch. He asked us what part of this sierra was the most rugged and remote; we told him it was where we are now, and so in truth it is — for if you push on half a league farther, perhaps you'll not be able to find your way out, and I'm wondering how you've managed to come here, since there's neither road nor path that leads to this spot. Well, on hearing our answer the youth turned about and made for the place we'd pointed out, leaving us all charmed by his good looks and wondering at his question and at the haste with which we saw him depart towards the sierra. After that we saw him no more, until some days later he crossed the path of one of our shepherds, and without saying a word came up to him and gave him several cuffs and kicks, and then turned to the ass with our provisions and took all the bread and cheese it carried; and having done this made off back into the sierra with extraordinary swiftness. When some of us goatherds learned of this, we went in search of him for about two days through the most remote part of this sierra, at the end of which we found him lodged in the hollow of a large, thick cork tree. He came out to meet us very gently, with his clothes now torn and his face so disfigured and burned by the sun that we hardly recognised him; but his clothes, though torn, convinced us, from the recollection we had of them, that he was the person we were looking for. He greeted us courteously, and in a few well-spoken words told us not to wonder at seeing him going about in this guise, since it was binding on him in order to work out a penance imposed on him for his many sins. We asked him to tell us who he was, but we were never able to find out from him; we begged him too, when he was in want of food (which he couldn't do without), to tell us where we could find him, since we would bring it to him with all good will and readiness, and if this wasn't to his taste, at least to come and ask it of us and not take it by force from the shepherds. He thanked us for the offer, begged pardon for the recent assault, and promised in the future to ask for it in God's name without offering violence to anyone. As for a fixed abode, he said he had no other than wherever night might overtake him. His words ended in an outburst of weeping so bitter that we who listened to him must have been stones not to join him in it, comparing what we saw of him the first time with what we saw now. For, as I said, he was a graceful and gracious youth, and his courteous and polished language showed him to be of good birth and courtly breeding; and rustics as we listeners were, even to our rusticity his gentle bearing was enough to make it plain.

"But in the middle of his conversation he stopped and became silent, keeping his eyes fixed on the ground for some time, during which we stood still, waiting anxiously to see what would come of this abstraction; and with no little pity, for from his behaviour — now staring at the ground with fixed gaze and eyes wide open without moving an eyelid, now closing them, compressing his lips and raising his eyebrows — we could see plainly that a fit of madness of some kind had come over him. Before long he showed that what we'd imagined was true, for he arose in a fury from the ground where he'd thrown himself and attacked the first man he found near him with such rage and ferocity that if we hadn't dragged him off, he would have beaten or bitten him to death, all the while crying, 'Oh faithless Fernando, here, here you will pay the penalty for the wrong you've done me; these hands will tear out that heart of yours, the abode and dwelling of all iniquity, but of deceit and fraud above all!' And he added other words, all in effect upbraiding this Fernando and charging him with treachery and faithlessness.

"We forced him to release his hold with no little difficulty, and without another word he left us and rushed off, plunging into these brakes and brambles in such a way that it was impossible for us to follow him. From this we suppose that madness comes upon him from time to time, and that someone called Fernando must have done him a wrong of so grievous a nature that the condition to which it has reduced him bears it out. All this has been since then confirmed on the many occasions on which he has crossed our path — at one time to beg the shepherds to give him some of the food they carry, at another to take it from them by force; for when there's a fit of madness on him, even though the shepherds offer it freely he'll not accept it but snatches it from them with blows; but when he's in his senses he begs it for the love of God, courteously and civilly, and receives it with many thanks and not a few tears. And to tell you the truth, sirs," continued the goatherd, "it was yesterday that we resolved — I and four of the lads, two of them our servants and the other two friends of mine — to go in search of him until we find him; and when we do, to take him, whether by force or with his consent, to the town of Almodóvar, which is eight leagues from here, and there try to cure him (if indeed his malady admits of a cure), or learn when he's in his senses who he is and whether he has relatives we may notify of his misfortune. This, sirs, is all I can say in answer to what you've asked me; and be sure that the owner of the things you found is the man you saw pass by with such nimbleness and so nearly naked."

For Don Quixote had already described how he'd seen the man go bounding along the mountainside, and he was now filled with amazement at what he heard from the goatherd, and more eager than ever to discover who the unhappy madman was. In his heart he resolved, as he'd done before, to search for him all over the mountain, not leaving a corner or cave unexamined until he'd found him. But chance arranged matters better than he expected or hoped, for at that very moment, in a gorge in the mountain that opened where they stood, the youth he wished to find made his appearance, coming along talking to himself in a way that would have been unintelligible up close, much more at a distance. His garb was as described, except that as he drew near, Don Quixote noticed that a tattered doublet he wore was amber-tanned, from which he concluded that one who wore such garments couldn't be of very low rank.

Approaching them, the youth greeted them in a harsh and hoarse voice but with great courtesy. Don Quixote returned his greeting with equal politeness, and dismounting from Rocinante advanced with well-bred bearing and grace to embrace him, and held him for some time close in his arms as if he'd known him for a long time. The other, whom we may call the Ragged One of the Sorry Countenance, as Don Quixote was of the Rueful, after submitting to the embrace pushed him back a little and, placing his hands on Don Quixote's shoulders, stood gazing at him as if trying to see whether he knew him — no less amazed, perhaps, at the sight of the face, figure, and armour of Don Quixote than Don Quixote was at the sight of him. To be brief, the first to speak after the embrace was the Ragged One, and what he said will be told further on.

title: Part 1, Chapter 24
paragraphs: In which the adventure of the Sierra Morena continues
The history tells us that Don Quixote listened with the closest attention to the ragged knight of the Sierra, who began by saying:

“Whoever you are, señor — for I don’t know you — I sincerely thank you for the kindness and courtesy you have shown me, and I wish I were in a position to repay you with something more than goodwill for the warm welcome you have given me; but my fate leaves me no other way of returning the favors done to me except a heartfelt desire to repay them.”

“Mine,” Don Quixote replied, “is to be of service to you — so much so that I had made up my mind not to leave these mountains until I had found you and learned from you whether any kind of relief exists for the sorrow that, judging by the strangeness of your life, you seem to suffer from; and I meant to search for you with all possible diligence, if searching had been necessary. And if your misfortune turned out to be the kind that refuses any sort of consolation, I intended to join you in grieving and mourning over it as far as I could, for it is still some comfort in misfortune to find someone who can feel it with you. And if my good intentions deserve to be acknowledged with any kind of courtesy, I beg you, señor, by the courtesy I can see you possess in such abundance — and I likewise implore you by whatever you love or have loved most in this life — to tell me who you are, and what cause has brought you to live or die in these wild solitudes like a brute animal, dwelling among them in a way so foreign to your station, as your clothing and appearance make plain. And I swear,” Don Quixote added, “by the order of knighthood I have received and by my vocation as a knight-errant, that if you grant me this, I will serve you with all the dedication my calling demands of me — either by relieving your misfortune, if it admits of relief, or by joining you in lamenting it, as I promised to do.”

When the Knight of the Thicket heard the Knight of the Rueful Countenance talk in this way, he did nothing but stare at him, then stare at him again, and look him over from head to foot; and when he had examined him thoroughly, he said to him:
“If you have anything to give me to eat, then for God’s sake give it to me. Once I have eaten, I will do everything you ask, in gratitude for the goodwill you have shown me.”

Sancho dug into his sack and the goatherd into his pouch, and between them they gave the Ragged One the means of satisfying his hunger. He ate what they offered like a man out of his mind, so fast that he left no pause between mouthfuls — gulping his food down rather than swallowing it — and while he ate, neither he nor those watching him said a word. As soon as he finished, he signaled for them to follow him, which they did, and he led them to a patch of green grass a little farther on, around the corner of a rock. When they reached it, he stretched out on the grass, and the others did the same, all in silence, until the Ragged One, settling himself in his place, said:

“If you want me, gentlemen, to describe in a few words the enormous scope of my misfortunes, you must promise not to break the thread of my sad story with any question or other interruption, because the moment you do, the tale I am telling will come to an end.”

These words from the Ragged One reminded Don Quixote of the story his squire had told him, when he failed to keep count of the goats that had crossed the river and the tale was left unfinished. But to return to the Ragged One — he went on to say:

“I give you this warning because I want to pass quickly over the story of my misfortunes; calling them back to memory only adds new ones, and the less you question me, the sooner I will finish the account — though I won’t leave out anything important, so as to satisfy your curiosity in full.”
Don Quixote gave the promise on behalf of himself and the others, and with that assurance the man began as follows:

“My name is Cardenio; my birthplace is one of the finest cities of this Andalusia; my family is noble; my parents are rich; and my misfortune is so great that my parents must have wept over it and my family grieved, without all their wealth being able to lighten it — because the gifts of fortune can do little against the reverses Heaven sends. In that same region there was a heaven in which love had placed all the glory I could wish for: such was the beauty of Luscinda, a young woman as noble and as rich as I am, but luckier in her fortunes, and less constant than a love as worthy as mine deserved. I loved this Luscinda, worshipped her, adored her, from my earliest and tenderest years, and she loved me with all the innocence and sincerity of childhood. Our parents knew how we felt and were not sorry to see it, for they could tell plainly that as our feelings matured they would have to end in marriage between us — something that seemed almost arranged in advance by the equal standing of our families and our wealth. We grew up, and our love grew with us, so much so that Luscinda’s father felt obliged, for propriety’s sake, to bar me from his house — in this perhaps imitating the parents of that Thisbe the poets have made so famous. The ban only added love to love and flame to flame, because though they could force silence on our tongues, they could not impose it on our pens, which reveal the heart’s secrets to the one you love more freely than tongues can; for the presence of the person you love often shakes the firmest resolve and strikes the boldest tongue dumb. Heavens, how many letters I wrote her, and how many delicate, modest replies I received! How many songs and love poems I composed, in which my heart declared and laid bare its feelings, described its burning longings, lingered over its memories, and toyed with its desires! At last, growing impatient and feeling my heart wasting away with the longing to see her, I decided to act on what seemed to me the best way of winning the reward I desired and deserved: to ask her father for her hand as my lawful wife. And I did. His answer was that he thanked me for the honor I showed in wanting to ally myself with him and to consider myself honored by the gift of his treasure; but since my father was alive, the request was rightfully his to make — because if the match were not entirely according to his will and pleasure, Luscinda was not a woman to be taken or given in secret. I thanked him for his kindness, thinking there was sense in what he said and that my father would agree to it the moment I told him; and with that in mind, I went that very instant to let my father know what I wanted. When I entered the room where he was, I found him with an open letter in his hand, and before I could say a word he handed it to me, saying, ‘This letter will show you, Cardenio, how ready Duke Ricardo is to do you a service.’ This Duke Ricardo, as you gentlemen probably know already, is a grandee of Spain whose seat lies in the best part of this Andalusia. I took the letter and read it, and it was worded so flatteringly that even I felt it would be wrong of my father not to grant what the duke asked in it — which was that my father send me to him immediately, because he wanted me to be the companion, not the servant, of his eldest son, and would take it upon himself to place me in a position matching the esteem in which he held me. Reading the letter left me speechless, and I was struck dumber still when I heard my father say, ‘Two days from now you will set out, Cardenio, as the duke wishes; and give thanks to God, who is opening a road for you toward what I know you deserve’ — and to these words he added others of fatherly advice. The day of my departure came. I spoke to Luscinda one night and told her everything that had happened, and I told her father too, begging him to allow some delay and to put off deciding her hand until I saw what Duke Ricardo wanted of me. He gave me his promise, and she confirmed it with countless vows and fainting fits. Finally, I presented myself to the duke, who received and treated me so kindly that envy very soon got to work: the old servants grew jealous of me and took the duke’s inclination to favor me as an injury to themselves. But the person my arrival pleased most was the duke’s second son, Fernando by name — a dashing young man, noble, generous, and amorous by temperament — who very quickly made me such a close friend that everyone remarked on it. Though the elder son liked me and treated me kindly, he never carried his affection to the lengths Don Fernando did. Now, since no secret stays unshared between friends, and since the favor I enjoyed with Don Fernando had grown into real friendship, he told me all his thoughts, and in particular a love affair that was troubling him somewhat. He was deeply in love with a peasant girl, one of his father’s vassals, the daughter of wealthy parents — and herself so beautiful, modest, sensible, and virtuous that no one who knew her could decide in which of these qualities she was most gifted or most excelled. The fair peasant girl’s attractions drove Don Fernando’s passion to such a pitch that, in order to get what he wanted and overcome her virtuous resistance, he decided to pledge his word to her that he would become her husband — since trying it any other way was attempting the impossible. Bound to him as I was by friendship, I did my best, with the strongest arguments and the most forceful examples I could think of, to hold him back and talk him out of such a course; but seeing I was getting nowhere, I resolved to inform his father, Duke Ricardo, of the matter. Don Fernando, however, being sharp and shrewd, foresaw and feared exactly this, realizing that as a loyal servant I was duty-bound not to keep hidden something so damaging to the honor of my lord the duke. And so, to mislead and deceive me, he told me he could find no better way of driving from his mind the beauty that so enslaved him than to go away for a few months — and that he wanted the absence to take the form of the two of us going together to my father’s house, under the pretext, which he would give the duke, of going to see and buy some fine horses in my city, which produces the best in the world. The moment I heard him say it — even if his plan had been less sound — my own feelings would have made me hail it as one of the happiest ideas imaginable, seeing what a perfect chance and opportunity it offered me to go back and see my Luscinda. With that thought and that wish, I applauded his idea and encouraged his plan, urging him to carry it out as quickly as possible, since absence does its work, in truth, against even the most deeply rooted feelings. But, as it later turned out, when he said all this to me he had already enjoyed the peasant girl under the title of husband, and was only waiting for a chance to reveal it safely, afraid of what his father the duke would do when he learned of his folly. Now, with young men, love is for the most part nothing more than appetite, and since appetite’s final goal is pleasure, it ends the moment it obtains it, and what seemed to be love takes flight — because it cannot pass the limit nature sets, a limit nature sets nowhere for true love. What I mean is that once Don Fernando had enjoyed the peasant girl, his passion subsided and his eagerness cooled; and if at first he pretended to want to go away in order to cure his love, he was now genuinely eager to leave in order to avoid keeping his promise.

“The duke gave him permission and ordered me to go with him. We arrived at my city, and my father gave him the reception his rank deserved. I saw Luscinda without delay, and my love — though it had never been dead or even dulled — gained fresh life. To my sorrow, I told the whole story of it to Don Fernando, because it seemed to me that under the law of the great friendship he showed me, I was bound to hide nothing from him. I praised her beauty, her liveliness, her wit, so warmly that my praises stirred in him a desire to see a young woman graced with such attractions. To my misfortune, I gave in to it, and showed her to him one night by the light of a candle, at a window where she and I used to talk. He saw her in her dressing gown, and she drove every beauty he had seen until then out of his memory. He was struck speechless; his head spun; he was spellbound; and in the end he was lovesick, as you will see as the story of my misfortune unfolds. And to inflame his passion further — a passion he hid from me and confessed only to Heaven — it happened that one day he found a note of hers begging me to ask her father for her hand in marriage, a note so delicate, so modest, and so tender that on reading it he told me that in Luscinda alone were gathered all the charms of beauty and intelligence that were scattered among all the other women in the world. It is true — and I admit it now — that although I knew how much reason Don Fernando had to praise Luscinda, it unsettled me to hear those praises from his mouth, and I began to fear him, and with good reason to distrust him, because there was no moment when he wasn’t ready to talk about Luscinda; he would bring up the subject himself, even dragging it in where it didn’t belong — which woke a certain jealousy in me. Not that I feared any change in Luscinda’s constancy or faithfulness; but even so, my fate made me dread the very thing she kept assuring me against. Don Fernando always contrived to read the letters I sent Luscinda and her replies to me, on the pretext that he enjoyed the wit and intelligence of us both. So it happened that Luscinda, having asked me for a book of chivalry to read — one she was very fond of, Amadis of Gaul—”
The moment Don Quixote heard a book of chivalry mentioned, he said:

“If your worship had told me at the start of your story that the Lady Luscinda was fond of books of chivalry, no other praise would have been needed to convince me of the superiority of her mind — for it could not have been as excellent as you describe if she had lacked a taste for such delightful reading. So as far as I am concerned, you need not waste another word describing her beauty, worth, and intelligence: just from hearing what her taste is, I declare her the most beautiful and the most intelligent woman in the world. And I wish your worship had sent her, along with Amadis of Gaul, the worthy Don Rugel of Greece, because I know the Lady Luscinda would thoroughly enjoy Daraida and Garaya, and the shrewd sayings of the shepherd Darinel, and the wonderful verses of his pastoral songs, which he sang and delivered with such liveliness, wit, and ease. But a time may come when that omission can be put right, and to fix it nothing more is needed than for your worship to be kind enough to come with me to my village, where I can give you more than three hundred books that are the delight of my soul and the entertainment of my life — though now that I think of it, I do not have a single one of them left, thanks to the spite of wicked and envious enchanters. But forgive me for breaking the promise we made not to interrupt your account; when I hear chivalry or knights-errant mentioned, I can no more help talking about them than the sun’s rays can help giving heat, or the moon’s giving moisture. So forgive me, and go on — that is what matters most now.”

While Don Quixote was saying this, Cardenio let his head drop onto his chest and seemed sunk in deep thought; and though Don Quixote twice urged him to go on with his story, he neither looked up nor answered a word. But after a while he raised his head and said, “I cannot get the idea out of my head — and no one in the world will remove it or make me think otherwise, and anyone who holds or believes anything else is a blockhead — that that utter scoundrel Master Elisabad was carrying on with Queen Madasima.”

“That is not true, by all that’s good,” said Don Quixote in a fury, rounding on him angrily, as his way was. “It is an outrageous slander — or rather, a villainy. Queen Madasima was a most illustrious lady, and it is unthinkable that so exalted a princess would have carried on with a quack; and whoever claims the contrary lies like a complete scoundrel, and I will make him know it, on foot or on horseback, armed or unarmed, by night or by day, or however he likes best.”

Cardenio was staring at him fixedly. His mad fit had now come over him, and he had no inclination to go on with his story — nor would Don Quixote have listened to it, so thoroughly had what he heard about Madasima disgusted him. Strangely enough, he defended her as if she were truly and literally his own born lady; that is the state his unholy books had brought him to. Cardenio, then, being mad as I said, heard himself called a liar and a scoundrel and other insulting names, and did not take the joke well: he snatched up a stone he found near him and struck Don Quixote such a blow on the chest with it that he knocked him flat on his back. Sancho Panza, seeing his master treated this way, went at the madman with his fists clenched; but the Ragged One met him with a punch that stretched him out at his feet, and then climbed on top of him and crushed his ribs to his own satisfaction. The goatherd, who came to the rescue, got the same treatment; and once he had beaten and pounded them all, he left them and calmly withdrew to his hiding place in the mountains. Sancho got up, and in his rage at being thrashed so badly without deserving it, ran to take his revenge on the goatherd, accusing him of failing to warn them that this man was sometimes seized by fits of madness — because if they had known, they would have been on their guard to protect themselves. The goatherd replied that he had said so, and that if Sancho had not heard him, that was no fault of his. Sancho shot back, the goatherd answered him, and the argument ended with the two of them grabbing each other by the beard and trading such punches that if Don Quixote had not made peace between them, they would have beaten each other to pieces.

“Leave me alone, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance,” said Sancho, grappling with the goatherd. “This fellow is a commoner like me, not a dubbed knight, so I can safely take satisfaction for the insult he has done me, fighting him hand to hand like an honest man.”
“True enough,” said Don Quixote, “but I know that he is not to blame for what has happened here.”

With that he calmed them down, and again asked the goatherd whether it would be possible to find Cardenio, because he felt the keenest anxiety to learn how his story ended. The goatherd told him, as he had told him before, that there was no knowing for certain where his lair was; but that if he roamed around that neighborhood long enough, he could not fail to come across him, in or out of his senses.

title: Part 1, Chapter 25
paragraphs: Which treats of the strange things that happened to the stout knight of La Mancha in the Sierra Morena, and of his imitation of the penance of Beltenebros

Don Quixote took leave of the goatherd, and once more mounting Rocinante, bade Sancho follow him, which he, having no ass, did very reluctantly. They proceeded slowly, making their way into the most rugged part of the mountain, Sancho all the while dying to have a talk with his master and longing for him to begin, so that there would be no breach of the injunction laid upon him; but unable to keep silence so long, he said:

"Señor Don Quixote, give me your worship's blessing and dismissal, for I'd like to go home at once to my wife and children, with whom I can at least talk and converse as much as I like. Wanting me to go through these solitudes day and night and not speak to you when I have a mind to is burying me alive. If luck would have it that animals spoke as they did in the days of Guisopete, it wouldn't be so bad, because I could talk to Rocinante about whatever came into my head, and so put up with my ill fortune; but it's a hard case, and not to be borne with patience, to go seeking adventures all one's life and get nothing but kicks and blanketings, brickbats and punches, and with all this to have to sew up one's mouth without daring to say what's in one's heart, just as if one were dumb."
"I understand you, Sancho," replied Don Quixote. "You're dying to have the ban I placed on your tongue removed. Consider it removed, and say what you will while we're wandering in these mountains."

"So be it," said Sancho. "Let me speak now, for God knows what will happen later. To take advantage of the permission at once, I ask: what made your worship stand up so for that Queen Majimasa, or whatever her name is, and what did it matter whether that abbot was a friend of hers or not? If your worship had let it pass — you weren't a judge in the matter — it's my belief the madman would have gone on with his story, and the blow of the stone, and the kicks, and more than half a dozen cuffs would have been avoided."

"In faith, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "if you knew as I do what an honourable and illustrious lady Queen Madasima was, I know you'd say I had great patience not to break in pieces the mouth that uttered such blasphemies — for a very great blasphemy it is to say or imagine that a queen has made free with a surgeon. The truth of the story is that that Master Elisabad whom the madman mentioned was a man of great prudence and sound judgment, and served as governor and physician to the queen; but to suppose that she was his mistress is nonsense deserving very severe punishment. And as proof that Cardenio didn't know what he was saying, remember that when he said it he was out of his wits."

"That's what I say," said Sancho. "There was no occasion for minding the words of a madman; for if good luck hadn't helped your worship, and he had aimed that stone at your head instead of at your breast, a fine state we'd be in for standing up for my lady yonder, God confound her! And then wouldn't Cardenio have gone free as a madman?"

"Against men in their senses or against madmen," said Don Quixote, "every knight-errant is bound to stand up for the honour of women, whoever they may be — much more for queens of such high degree and dignity as Queen Madasima, for whom I have a particular regard on account of her amiable qualities; for besides being extremely beautiful, she was very wise, and very patient under her misfortunes, of which she had many. And the counsel and society of Master Elisabad were a great help and support to her in enduring her afflictions with wisdom and resignation; hence the ignorant and ill-disposed common people took occasion to say and think that she was his mistress. They lie, I say it once more, and will lie two hundred times more, all who think and say so."

"I neither say nor think so," said Sancho. "Let them look to it; with their bread let them eat it. They've rendered account to God for whether they misbehaved or not. I come from my vineyard, I know nothing; I'm not fond of prying into other men's lives; he who buys and lies feels it in his purse. Besides, naked was I born, naked I find myself, I neither lose nor gain. But if they did, what's that to me? Many think there are flitches where there are no hooks; but who can put gates to the open plain? Moreover, they said of God —"

"God bless me," said Don Quixote, "what a string of absurdities you're stringing together! What's what we're talking about got to do with the proverbs you're threading one after the other? For God's sake hold your tongue, Sancho, and from now on stick to prodding your ass and don't meddle in what doesn't concern you. And understand with all your five senses that everything I've done, am doing, or shall do is well founded on reason and in conformity with the rules of chivalry, which I understand better than anyone in the world who professes them."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "is it a good rule of chivalry that we should go astray through these mountains without path or road, looking for a madman who, when he's found, will perhaps take a fancy to finish what he began — not his story, but your worship's head and my ribs — and end by breaking them altogether?"

"Peace, I say again, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because let me tell you, it isn't so much the desire of finding that madman that leads me into these regions as the desire I have of performing among them an achievement that will win me eternal name and fame throughout the known world — and it shall be such that I shall set the seal on all that can make a knight-errant perfect and famous."
"And is it very dangerous, this achievement?"
"No," replied he of the Rueful Countenance, "though it may be that the dice will throw deuce-ace instead of sixes; but it will all depend on your diligence."
"On my diligence!" said Sancho.

"Yes," said Don Quixote, "for if you return soon from the place where I mean to send you, my penance will soon be over, and my glory will soon begin. But since it's not right to keep you in suspense any longer, waiting to see what comes of my words, I would have you know, Sancho, that the famous Amadis of Gaul was one of the most perfect knights-errant — no, I'm wrong to say he was one of them; he stood alone, the first, the only one, the lord of all who were in the world in his time. A fig for Don Belianis and for all who say he equalled him in any respect, for, by my oath, they're deceiving themselves. I say, too, that when a painter wants to become famous in his art, he tries to copy the originals of the rarest painters he knows; and the same rule holds for all the most important crafts and callings that serve to adorn a state. Thus he who would be esteemed prudent and patient must imitate Ulysses, in whose person and labours Homer presents us with a lively picture of prudence and patience; as Virgil, too, shows us in the person of Æneas the virtue of a pious son and the sagacity of a brave and skilful captain — not representing or describing them as they were, but as they ought to be, so as to leave the example of their virtues to posterity. In the same way Amadis was the polestar, day-star, and sun of valiant and devoted knights, whom all we who fight under the banner of love and chivalry are bound to imitate. This being so, then, I consider, friend Sancho, that the knight-errant who imitates him most closely will come nearest to reaching the perfection of chivalry. Now one of the instances in which this knight most conspicuously showed his prudence, worth, valour, endurance, fortitude, and love was when he withdrew, rejected by the Lady Oriana, to do penance on the Peña Pobre, changing his name to that of Beltenebros — a name assuredly significant and appropriate to the life he had voluntarily adopted. So, since it's easier for me to imitate him in this than in cleaving giants asunder, cutting off serpents' heads, slaying dragons, routing armies, destroying fleets, and breaking enchantments, and since this place is so well suited for a similar purpose, I mustn't let the opportunity escape that now so conveniently offers me its forelock."
"What is it, in reality," said Sancho, "that your worship means to do in such an out-of-the-way place as this?"

"Haven't I told you," answered Don Quixote, "that I mean to imitate Amadis here, playing the victim of despair, the madman, the maniac, so as at the same time to imitate the valiant Don Roland, when at the fountain he had evidence of the fair Angelica having disgraced herself with Medoro, and through grief at it went mad, and uprooted trees, troubled the waters of clear springs, slew shepherds, destroyed flocks, burned down huts, levelled houses, dragged mares after him, and committed a hundred thousand other outrages worthy of everlasting renown and record? And though I have no intention of imitating Roland — or Orlando, or Rotolando (for he went by all these names) — step by step in all the mad things he did, said, and thought, I'll make a rough copy to the best of my ability of all that seems to me most essential. But perhaps I'll content myself with the simple imitation of Amadis, who, without giving way to any mischievous madness but merely to tears and sorrow, gained as much fame as the most famous."

"It seems to me," said Sancho, "that the knights who behaved this way had provocation and cause for those follies and penances; but what cause has your worship for going mad? What lady has rejected you, or what evidence have you found that the lady Dulcinea del Toboso has been trifling with Moor or Christian?"

"There's the point," replied Don Quixote, "and that's the beauty of this business of mine. No thanks to a knight-errant for going mad when he has a cause; the trick is to turn crazy without provocation, and let my lady know — if I do this in the dry, what I'd do in the wet. Moreover I have abundant cause in the long separation I've endured from my lady till death, Dulcinea del Toboso; for as you heard that shepherd Ambrosio say the other day, in absence all ills are felt and feared. And so, friend Sancho, don't waste time advising me against so rare, so happy, and so unheard-of an imitation. Mad I am, and mad I must be until you return with the answer to a letter I mean to send by you to my lady Dulcinea; and if it's such as my constancy deserves, my madness and penance will come to an end; and if it's to the opposite effect, I shall become mad in earnest, and, being so, I shall suffer no more. So in whatever way she may answer, I shall escape from the struggle and affliction in which you'll leave me, enjoying in my senses the boon you bring me, or as a madman not feeling the evil you bring me. But tell me, Sancho, do you have Mambrino's helmet safe? For I saw you pick it up from the ground when that ungrateful wretch tried to smash it but couldn't, which shows the fineness of its temper."

To which Sancho answered, "By the living God, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, I cannot endure or bear with patience some of the things your worship says. From them I begin to suspect that all you tell me about chivalry, and winning kingdoms and empires, and giving islands, and bestowing other rewards and dignities after the custom of knights-errant, must be all made up of wind and lies, and all pigments or figments, or whatever we want to call them. For what would anyone think who heard your worship calling a barber's basin Mambrino's helmet without ever seeing the mistake all this time, but that one who says and maintains such things must have his brains addled? I have the basin in my sack, all dented, and I'm taking it home to have it mended, to trim my beard in it, if, by God's grace, I'm allowed to see my wife and children some day or other."

"Look here, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "by him you just swore by, I swear you have the most limited understanding of any squire in the world has now or ever had. Is it possible that all this time you've been going around with me you've never figured out that all things belonging to knights-errant seem to be illusions and nonsense and ravings, and to go always by contraries? And not because it really is so, but because there's always a swarm of enchanters attending us who change and alter everything with us, and turn things as they please, according as they're disposed to aid or destroy us. Thus what seems to you a barber's basin seems to me Mambrino's helmet, and to another it will seem something else; and rare foresight it was in the sage who is on my side to make what is really and truly Mambrino's helmet seem a basin to everybody — for, being held in such high estimation, all the world would pursue me to rob me of it; but when they see it's only a barber's basin, they don't take the trouble to obtain it, as was plainly shown by the man who tried to break it and left it on the ground without taking it. For by my faith, had he known what it was, he would never have left it behind. Keep it safe, my friend, for just now I have no need of it; indeed, I'll have to take off all this armour and remain as naked as I was born, if I have a mind to follow Roland rather than Amadis in my penance."

Talking like this they reached the foot of a high mountain that stood like an isolated peak among the others surrounding it. Past its base flowed a gentle brook, and all around it spread a meadow so green and luxuriant that it was a delight to the eyes to look upon. Forest trees in abundance, and shrubs and flowers, added to the charms of the spot. Upon this place the Knight of the Rueful Countenance fixed his choice for the performance of his penance, and as he beheld it exclaimed in a loud voice as if he were out of his senses:

"This is the place, O ye heavens, that I select and choose for bewailing the misfortune in which ye yourselves have plunged me: this is the spot where the overflowing of my eyes shall swell the waters of yon little brook, and my deep and endless sighs shall ceaselessly stir the leaves of these mountain trees, in testimony and token of the pain my persecuted heart is suffering. O ye rural deities, whoever ye be that haunt this lonely spot, give ear to the complaint of a wretched lover whom long absence and brooding jealousy have driven to bewail his fate among these wilds and to complain of the hard heart of that fair and ungrateful one, the end and limit of all human beauty! O ye wood nymphs and dryads who dwell in the thickets of the forest, so may the nimble wanton satyrs by whom ye are vainly wooed never disturb your sweet repose — help me lament my hard fate, or at least weary not in listening to it! O Dulcinea del Toboso, day of my night, glory of my pain, guide of my path, star of my fortune, so may Heaven grant thee in full all thou seekest of it, bethink thee of the place and condition to which absence from thee has brought me, and make that return in kindness that is due to my fidelity! O lonely trees, that from this day forward shall bear me company in my solitude, give me some sign by the gentle movement of your boughs that my presence is not distasteful to you! O thou, my squire, pleasant companion in my prosperous and adverse fortunes, fix well in thy memory what thou shalt see me do here, that thou mayest relate and report it to the sole cause of it all!" And so saying he dismounted from Rocinante, and in an instant relieved him of saddle and bridle, and giving him a slap on the croup, said, "He gives thee freedom who is bereft of it himself, O steed as excellent in deed as thou art unfortunate in thy lot. Begone where thou wilt, for thou bearest written on thy forehead that neither Astolfo's hippogriff nor the famed Frontino that cost Bradamante so dear could equal thee in speed."

Seeing this, Sancho said, "Good luck to whoever spared us the trouble of stripping the pack-saddle off Dapple! By my faith he wouldn't have gone without a slap on the croup and something said in his praise; though if he were here I wouldn't let anyone strip him, for there'd be no occasion, since he had nothing of the lover or victim of despair about him — inasmuch as his master, which I was while it was God's pleasure, was nothing of the sort. And indeed, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, if my departure and your worship's madness are to come off in earnest, it would be just as well to saddle Rocinante again so that he may make up for the lack of Dapple, because it'll save me time in going and returning. If I go on foot, I don't know when I'll get there or when I'll get back, since, truth be told, I'm a bad walker."

"I declare, Sancho," returned Don Quixote, "let it be as you wish, for your plan doesn't seem to me a bad one; and three days from now you'll depart, since I want you to observe in the meantime what I do and say for her sake, so you'll be able to tell it."
"But what more do I have to see besides what I've already seen?" said Sancho.

"Much you know about it!" said Don Quixote. "I now have to tear up my garments, scatter my armour about, knock my head against these rocks, and more of the same sort of thing — which you must witness."

"For the love of God," said Sancho, "be careful, your worship, how you give yourself those knocks on the head, for you may come across such a rock, and in such a way, that the very first may put an end to the whole contrivance of this penance. I should think, if knocks on the head really seem necessary to you, and this business can't be done without them, you might be content — since the whole thing is feigned, and counterfeit, and a joke — you might be content, I say, with giving them to yourself in the water, or against something soft like cotton; and leave it all to me, since I'll tell my lady that your worship knocked your head against a point of rock harder than a diamond."

"I thank you for your good intentions, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "but I would have you know that all the things I am doing are not in joke but very much in earnest, since anything else would be a transgression of the ordinances of chivalry, which forbid us to tell any lie whatever under the penalties due to apostasy; and to do one thing instead of another is just the same as lying. So my knocks on the head must be real, solid, and valid, without anything sophisticated or fanciful about them — and it will be necessary to leave me some lint to dress my wounds, since fortune has compelled us to do without the balsam we lost."

"It was worse losing the ass," replied Sancho, "for with him, lint and all were lost. But I beg of your worship not to remind me again of that accursed liquor, for my soul, not to mention my stomach, turns at hearing the very name of it. And I beg of you, too, to count as past the three days you allowed me for seeing the mad things you do, for I take them as already seen and pronounced upon, and I'll tell wonderful stories to my lady. So write the letter and send me off at once, for I long to return and take your worship out of this purgatory where I'm leaving you."
"Purgatory you call it, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Rather call it hell, or even worse if there's anything worse."
"For one who is in hell," said Sancho, "_nulla est retentio_, as I've heard say."
"I don't understand what _retentio_ means," said Don Quixote.

"_Retentio_," answered Sancho, "means that whoever is in hell never comes nor can come out of it — which will be the opposite case with your worship, or my legs will be idle (that is, if I have spurs to enliven Rocinante). Let me once get to El Toboso and into the presence of my lady Dulcinea, and I'll tell her such things of the follies and madnesses (for it's all one) that your worship has done and is still doing, that I'll manage to make her softer than a glove even if I find her harder than a cork tree; and with her sweet and honeyed answer I'll come back through the air like a witch, and take your worship out of this purgatory that seems to be hell but isn't, since there's hope of getting out of it — which, as I've said, those in hell have not, and I believe your worship won't say anything to the contrary."
"That is true," said he of the Rueful Countenance, "but how shall we manage to write the letter?"
"And the ass-colt order too," added Sancho.

"All shall be included," said Don Quixote; "and since there's no paper, it would be well done to write it on the leaves of trees, as the ancients did, or on wax tablets — though that would be as hard to find just now as paper. But it has just occurred to me how it may be conveniently — and more than conveniently — written, and that's in the notebook that belonged to Cardenio. You'll take care to have it copied out on paper, in a good hand, at the first village you come to where there's a schoolmaster; or if not, any sacristan will copy it. But mind you don't give it to any notary to copy, because they write a law hand Satan himself couldn't make out."
"But what's to be done about the signature?" said Sancho.
"The letters of Amadis were never signed," said Don Quixote.
"That's all very well," said Sancho, "but the order must be signed, and if it's copied they'll say the signature is false, and I'll be left without ass-colts."

"The order shall go signed in the same book," said Don Quixote, "and on seeing it my niece will make no difficulty about obeying it. As for the love letter, you can put by way of signature, '_Yours till death, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance._' And it won't matter much if it's in some other person's hand, because, as well as I recall, Dulcinea can neither read nor write, nor has she in her whole life seen any handwriting or letter of mine; for my love and hers have always been platonic, never going beyond a modest look — and even that so seldom that I can safely swear I haven't seen her four times in all these twelve years I've been loving her more than the light of these eyes that the earth will one day devour; and perhaps even of those four times she may not once have noticed that I was looking at her — such is the retirement and seclusion in which her father Lorenzo Corchuelo and her mother Aldonza Nogales have brought her up."
"So, so!" said Sancho. "Lorenzo Corchuelo's daughter is the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, otherwise called Aldonza Lorenzo?"
"She it is," said Don Quixote, "and she it is who is worthy to be lady of the whole universe."

"I know her well," said Sancho, "and let me tell you, she can fling a crowbar as well as the lustiest lad in all the town. Giver of all good! she's a brave lass, and a right and stout one, and fit to be helpmate to any knight-errant that is or is to be who may make her his lady. The whoreson wench, what spirit she has, and what a voice! I can tell you, one day she posted herself on top of the village belfry to call some labourers of theirs who were in a ploughed field of her father's, and though they were better than half a league off they heard her as well as if they were at the foot of the tower. And the best of her is that she's not a bit prudish, for she has plenty of affability, and jokes with everybody, and has a grin and a jest for everything. So, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, I say you not only may and ought to do mad freaks for her sake, but you have a good right to give way to despair and hang yourself; and no one who knows of it but will say you did well, though the devil should take you. And I wish I were on my road already, simply to see her, for it's many a day since I saw her, and she must be changed by now, since going about the fields always, and the sun and the air, spoil women's looks greatly. But I must own the truth to your worship, Señor Don Quixote: until now I've been under a great mistake, for I truly and honestly believed the lady Dulcinea must be some princess your worship was in love with, or some person great enough to deserve the rich presents you've sent her, like the Biscayan and the galley slaves, and many more no doubt, for your worship must have won many victories in the time when I wasn't yet your squire. But, all things considered, what good can it do the lady Aldonza Lorenzo — I mean, the lady Dulcinea del Toboso — to have the vanquished your worship sends or will send coming to her and going down on their knees before her? Because maybe when they came, she'd be hackling flax or threshing on the threshing floor, and they'd be ashamed to see her, and she'd laugh, or resent the present."

"I've told you many times before, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you're a mighty great chatterer, and that with a blunt wit you're always striving at sharpness. But to show you what a fool you are and how rational I am, I'd have you listen to a short story. You must know that a certain widow, fair, young, independent, and rich, and above all free and easy, fell in love with a sturdy strapping young lay-brother. His superior came to know of it, and one day said to the worthy widow by way of brotherly remonstrance, 'I am surprised, señora, and not without good reason, that a woman of such high standing, so fair, and so rich as you should have fallen in love with such a mean, low, stupid fellow as So-and-so, when in this house there are so many masters, graduates, and divinity students from among whom you might choose as if they were a lot of pears, saying, This one I'll take, that I won't take.' But she replied to him with great liveliness and candour, 'My dear sir, you are very much mistaken, and your ideas are very old-fashioned, if you think that I've made a bad choice in So-and-so, fool as he seems; because for all I want with him, he knows as much philosophy as Aristotle, and more.' In the same way, Sancho, for all I want with Dulcinea del Toboso she is just as good as the most exalted princess on earth. It's not to be supposed that all those poets who sang the praises of ladies under the fancy names they give them had any such mistresses. Do you think the Amarillises, the Phillises, the Sylvias, the Dianas, the Galateas, the Fílidas, and all the rest of them, that the books, the ballads, the barber's shops, and the theatres are full of, were really and truly ladies of flesh and blood, and mistresses of those who glorify and have glorified them? Nothing of the kind; they only invent them for the most part to furnish a subject for their verses, and that they may pass for lovers, or for men valiant enough to be lovers. So it's enough for me to think and believe that the good Aldonza Lorenzo is fair and virtuous; and as for her pedigree, it matters very little, since no one will examine into it for the purpose of conferring any order on her, and I, for my part, reckon her the most exalted princess in the world. For you should know, Sancho, if you don't know, that two things alone above all others are incentives to love, and these are great beauty and a good name; and these two things are to be found in Dulcinea in the highest degree, for in beauty no one equals her, and in good name few approach her. To put the whole thing in a nutshell, I persuade myself that all I say is as I say, neither more nor less; and I picture her in my imagination as I would have her to be, as well in beauty as in condition. Helen approaches her not, nor does Lucretia come up to her, nor any other of the famous women of times past, Greek, Barbarian, or Latin; and let each say what he will, for if in this I'm taken to task by the ignorant, I won't be censured by the critical."

"I say that your worship is entirely right," said Sancho, "and that I'm an ass. But I don't know how the name of ass came into my mouth, for a rope is not to be mentioned in the house of him who has been hanged. But now for the letter, and then, God be with you, I'm off."

Don Quixote took out the notebook, and, retiring to one side, very deliberately began to write the letter; when he had finished it he called Sancho over, saying he wanted to read it to him, so that he might commit it to memory in case of losing it on the road — for with evil fortune like his, anything was to be feared. To which Sancho replied, "Write it two or three times there in the book and give it to me, and I'll carry it very carefully, because expecting me to keep it in my memory is all nonsense — I have such a bad one I often forget my own name. But for all that, repeat it to me, since I'll like to hear it, for surely it will run as if it were in print."
"Listen," said Don Quixote, "this is what it says:"
_Don Quixote's Letter to Dulcinea del Toboso_

"Sovereign and exalted Lady, — He who is pierced by the point of absence, the one wounded to the heart's core, sends thee, sweetest Dulcinea del Toboso, the health that he himself enjoys not. If thy beauty despises me, if thy worth is not for me, if thy scorn is my affliction, though I be sufficiently long-suffering, hardly shall I endure this anxiety, which, besides being oppressive, is protracted. My good squire Sancho will relate to thee in full, fair ingrate, dear enemy, the condition to which I am reduced on thy account: if it be thy pleasure to give me relief, I am thine; if not, do as may be pleasing to thee, for by ending my life I shall satisfy thy cruelty and my desire. Thine till death, The Knight of the Rueful Countenance."

"By the life of my father!" said Sancho when he heard the letter. "It's the loftiest thing I ever heard. Body of me! how your worship says everything as you like in it! And how well you fit in 'The Knight of the Rueful Countenance' into the signature. I declare your worship is indeed the very devil, and there's nothing you don't know."
"Everything is needed for the calling I follow," said Don Quixote.
"Now then," said Sancho, "let your worship put the order for the three ass-colts on the other side, and sign it very plainly, so they may recognise it at first sight."
"With all my heart," said Don Quixote; and having written it, he read it to this effect:

"Mistress Niece, — By this first of ass-colts, please pay to Sancho Panza, my squire, three of the five I left at home in your charge: said three ass-colts to be paid and delivered for the same number received here in hand, which upon this and upon his receipt shall be duly paid. Done in the heart of the Sierra Morena, the twenty-seventh of August of this present year."
"That will do," said Sancho. "Now let your worship sign it."
"There's no need to sign it," said Don Quixote, "but merely to put my flourish, which is the same as a signature, and enough for three asses — or even three hundred."

"I can trust your worship," returned Sancho. "Let me go and saddle Rocinante, and be ready to give me your blessing, for I mean to go at once without seeing the fooleries your worship is going to do; I'll say I saw you do so many that she'll not want any more."

"At any rate, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "I should like — and there is reason for it — I should like you, I say, to see me stripped to the skin and performing a dozen or two of insanities, which I can get done in less than half an hour; for, having seen them with your own eyes, you can then safely swear to the rest that you might add. And I promise you that you won't tell of as many as I mean to perform."

"For the love of God, master mine," said Sancho, "let me not see your worship stripped, for it'll grieve me sorely, and I shan't be able to keep from tears, and my head aches so with all I shed last night for Dapple that I'm not fit to begin any fresh weeping. But if it's your worship's pleasure that I should see some insanities, do them in your clothes, short ones, and such as come readiest to hand; for I myself want nothing of the sort, and, as I've said, it'll save time for my return, which will be with the news your worship desires and deserves. If not, let the lady Dulcinea look to it; if she doesn't answer reasonably, I swear as solemnly as I can that I'll fetch a fair answer out of her stomach with kicks and cuffs. For why should it be borne that a knight-errant as famous as your worship should go mad without rhyme or reason for a —? Her ladyship had best not drive me to say it, for by God I'll speak out and let off everything cheap, even if it doesn't sell: I'm pretty good at that! She little knows me; faith, if she knew me she'd be in awe of me."
"In faith, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "by all appearances you're no sounder in your wits than I."

"I'm not so mad," answered Sancho, "but I am more peppery. But apart from all this, what does your worship have to eat until I come back? Will you sally out on the road like Cardenio to force it from the shepherds?"

"Let that anxiety not trouble you," replied Don Quixote, "for even if I had food, I would eat nothing but the herbs and the fruits this meadow and these trees may yield me; the beauty of this business of mine lies in not eating, and in performing other mortifications."
"Do you know what I'm afraid of?" said Sancho at this. "That I shan't be able to find my way back to this spot where I'm leaving you, it's such an out-of-the-way place."

"Observe the landmarks well," said Don Quixote, "because I'll try not to go far from this neighbourhood, and I'll even take care to climb the highest of these rocks to see if I can spot you returning. However, so as not to miss me and lose yourself, the best plan will be to cut some branches of the broom that grows so abundantly around here, and as you go to lay them at intervals until you've come out onto the plain. These will serve you, in the manner of the clue in the labyrinth of Theseus, as marks and signs for finding me on your return."

"So I will," said Sancho Panza, and having cut some, he asked his master's blessing, and not without many tears on both sides took his leave; and mounting Rocinante (of whom Don Quixote charged him earnestly to take as much care as of his own person), he set out for the plain, strewing at intervals the branches of broom as his master had recommended. And so he went his way, though Don Quixote still entreated him to see him do were it only a couple of mad acts. He hadn't gone a hundred paces, however, when he returned and said:

"I must say, señor, your worship was quite right: in order to be able to swear without a weight on my conscience that I'd seen you do mad things, it would be well for me to see even just one — though in your worship's remaining here I've already seen a very great one."

"Didn't I tell you so?" said Don Quixote. "Wait, Sancho, and I'll do them in the saying of a creed." And pulling off his breeches in all haste, he stripped himself to his skin and his shirt, and then, without more ado, cut a couple of capers in the air and a couple of somersaults, heels over head, making such a display that, in order not to see it a second time, Sancho wheeled Rocinante round and felt easy and satisfied in his mind that he could swear he'd left his master mad. And so we'll leave him to follow his road until his return, which was a quick one.

title: Part 1, Chapter 26
paragraphs: In which Don Quixote continues his refinements as a lover in the Sierra Morena

Returning to what the Knight of the Rueful Countenance did once he was alone, the history says that when Don Quixote had finished the somersaults and capers — naked from the waist down, clothed from the waist up — and saw that Sancho had gone off without waiting to watch any further mad feats, he climbed to the top of a high rock and there set himself to ponder a question he had pondered several times before without ever reaching a conclusion: whether it would be better and more to his purpose to imitate the outrageous madness of Roland or the melancholy madness of Amadis. Talking it over with himself, he said:

"What's so impressive about Roland being as good and valiant a knight as everyone says he was, when after all he was enchanted, and nobody could kill him except by driving a corking pin into the sole of his foot, and he always wore shoes with seven iron soles? Though even those clever devices did him no good against Bernardo del Carpio, who knew all about them and strangled him in his arms at Roncesvalles.
