But setting aside the question of his valour, let's come to his losing his wits — for certain it is that he did lose them, in consequence of the proofs he discovered at the fountain, and of the news the shepherd gave him that Angelica had slept more than two siestas with Medoro, a little curly-headed Moor and page to Agramante. If he was persuaded this was true, and that his lady had wronged him, it's no wonder he went mad. But how am I to imitate him in his madness, when I cannot imitate him in the cause of it? For my Dulcinea, I'll venture to swear, never saw a Moor in her life, in his proper costume, and she is this day as the mother that bore her, and I would plainly be doing her a wrong if, fancying anything else, I were to go mad in the same way as Roland the Furious. On the other hand, I see that Amadis of Gaul, without losing his senses and without doing anything mad, acquired as a lover as much fame as the most famous; for, according to his history, on finding himself rejected by his lady Oriana, who had ordered him not to appear in her presence until it should be her pleasure, all he did was withdraw to the Peña Pobre in the company of a hermit, where he took his fill of weeping until Heaven sent him relief in the midst of his great grief and need. And if this is true — as it is — why should I now take the trouble to strip stark naked, or do mischief to these trees that have done me no harm, or disturb the clear water of these brooks that will give me drink whenever I want? Long live the memory of Amadis, and let him be imitated as far as possible by Don Quixote of La Mancha — of whom it will be said, as was said of the other, that if he did not achieve great things, he died in attempting them; and if I am not rebuffed or rejected by my Dulcinea, it is enough for me, as I have said, to be absent from her. So, now to work — come to my memory, you deeds of Amadis, and show me how to begin imitating you. I know already that the chief thing he did was pray and commend himself to God; but what am I to do for a rosary, since I have not got one?"

Then it occurred to him how he might make one: by tearing a long strip off the tail of his shirt, which hung down, and making eleven knots in it, one bigger than the rest, and this served him for a rosary the whole time he was there, during which he repeated countless _ave-marias_. But what distressed him greatly was not having another hermit there to confess him and offer consolation; so he consoled himself instead by pacing up and down the little meadow, writing and carving on the bark of the trees and in the fine sand a multitude of verses all in keeping with his sadness, some in praise of Dulcinea. When he was later found there, the only ones completely legible that could be made out were these:

You that grow on the mountainside, you green things — trees, shrubs, and bushes — are you weary of the woe that crushes this poor aching breast? If it disturbs you, and I owe you some reparation, let it be a defence for me to let you know that Don Quixote's tears are flowing, and all for distant Dulcinea del Toboso.

The most loyal lover time can show, doomed to languish for his lady, wanders among these solitudes, prey to every kind of anguish. Why Love should treat him like a spiteful foe, he has no idea — but he knows this much: hogsheads full. Don Quixote's tears are flowing, and all for distant Dulcinea del Toboso.

Adventure-seeking he goes, up rugged heights, down rocky valleys; but hill or dale, high or low, mishap attends all his sallies. Love still pursues him to and fro, plying its cruel scourge — ah, me, a relentless fate, an endless woe. Don Quixote's tears are flowing, and all for distant Dulcinea del Toboso.

The addition of "del Toboso" to Dulcinea's name gave rise to no little laughter among those who found these lines, for they suspected Don Quixote must have thought that unless he tacked on "del Toboso" whenever he introduced Dulcinea's name, the verse would be unintelligible — which was indeed the case, as he himself afterwards admitted. He wrote many more, but, as has been said, these three were all that could be plainly and perfectly deciphered. In this way — and in sighing, and calling on the fauns and satyrs of the woods and the nymphs of the streams, and Echo, moist and mournful, to answer, console, and hear him, and in looking for herbs to sustain him — he passed his time until Sancho's return. Had that been delayed three weeks, as it was three days, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance would have worn so altered a countenance that the mother who bore him would not have known him. Here it will be well to leave him, wrapped up in sighs and verses, to relate how Sancho Panza fared on his mission.

As for Sancho, once he came out onto the high road he made for El Toboso, and the next day reached the inn where the blanket-tossing mishap had befallen him. As soon as he recognised it, he felt as if he were once more living through the air, and he could not bring himself to enter, though it was an hour when he might well have done so — it was dinner time, and he longed to taste something hot, since for many days past it had all been cold fare. This craving drew him toward the inn, still undecided whether to go in or not, and as he was hesitating, two men came out who at once recognised him and said to each other:
"Señor licentiate, isn't that Sancho Panza on the horse — the one our adventurer's housekeeper told us went off with her master as squire?"

"So it is," said the licentiate, "and that is our friend Don Quixote's horse." They knew him so well because they were the curate and the barber of his own village — the same two who had carried out the scrutiny and sentence on the books. As soon as they had recognised Sancho Panza and Rocinante, eager to hear about Don Quixote, they came up, and calling him by name the curate said, "Friend Sancho Panza, where is your master?"

Sancho recognised them at once and resolved to keep secret the place and circumstances where and under which he had left his master, so he replied that his master was engaged in a certain quarter on a certain matter of great importance to him, which he could not disclose for the eyes in his head.

"No, no," said the barber, "if you don't tell us where he is, Sancho Panza, we'll suspect — as we already suspect — that you've murdered and robbed him, for here you are mounted on his horse. You must produce the owner of the hack, or take the consequences."

"There's no need to threaten me," said Sancho, "for I'm not a man to rob or murder anybody; let each man's own fate, or God who made him, kill him. My master is engaged very much to his taste, doing penance in the middle of these mountains." And then, offhand and without stopping, he told them how he had left him, what adventures had befallen him, and how he was carrying a letter to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, daughter of Lorenzo Corchuelo, with whom his master was head over heels in love. They were both amazed at what Sancho Panza told them, for though they were aware of Don Quixote's madness and the nature of it, each time they heard about it they were filled with fresh wonder. They then asked Sancho Panza to show them the letter he was carrying to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso. He said it was written in a notebook, and that his master's directions were that he should have it copied onto paper at the first village he came to. At this the curate said if he showed it to him, he himself would make a fair copy. Sancho put his hand into his shirt in search of the notebook but could not find it; nor, if he had been searching until now, could he have found it, for Don Quixote had kept it and had never given it to him, nor had Sancho himself thought of asking for it. When Sancho realised he could not find the book, his face went deadly pale, and in great haste he felt his body all over again, and seeing plainly it was nowhere to be found, without more ado he seized his beard with both hands and plucked out half of it; and then, as fast as he could and without stopping, gave himself half a dozen cuffs on the face and nose till they were bathed in blood.
Seeing this, the curate and the barber asked him what had happened to make him treat himself so roughly.
"What should happen to me," replied Sancho, "but to lose, from one hand to the other in a moment, three ass-colts, each one of them like a castle?"
"How is that?" said the barber.

"I've lost the notebook," said Sancho, "that had the letter to Dulcinea in it, and an order signed by my master telling his niece to give me three ass-colts out of four or five he had at home." And he then told them about the loss of Dapple.

The curate consoled him, telling him that when his master was found he would get him to renew the order, and make out a fresh draft on paper, as was usual and customary, for those made in notebooks were never accepted or honoured.

Sancho comforted himself with this, and said if that were so, the loss of Dulcinea's letter did not trouble him much, for he had it almost by heart, and it could be taken down from him wherever and whenever they liked.
"Recite it, then, Sancho," said the barber, "and we'll write it down afterwards."

Sancho Panza stopped to scratch his head to bring the letter back to his memory, and balanced himself now on one foot, now the other, one moment staring at the ground, the next at the sky; and after having half gnawed off the end of a finger and kept them in suspense waiting for him to begin, he said, after a long pause, "By God, señor licentiate, devil a thing can I recall of the letter; but it began, 'Exalted and scrubbing Lady.'"
"It can't have said 'scrubbing,'" said the barber, "but 'superhuman' or 'sovereign.'"

"That's it," said Sancho. "Then, as well as I remember, it went on, 'The wounded, and wanting of sleep, and the pierced, kisses your worship's hands, ungrateful and very unrecognised fair one'; and it said something or other about health and sickness he was sending her; and from that it went tailing off until it ended with 'Yours till death, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.'"

It gave them no little amusement, both of them, to see what a good memory Sancho had, and they complimented him greatly on it, and begged him to repeat the letter a couple more times so that they too might learn it by heart and write it out later. Sancho repeated it three times, and each time uttered three thousand more absurdities; then he told them more about his master, but he never said a word about the blanket-tossing he himself had suffered at that inn — which was why he refused to enter it. He told them, moreover, how his lord, if he brought back a favourable answer from the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, was to set about becoming an emperor, or at least a monarch; for it had been so settled between them, and with his personal worth and the might of his arm it was an easy matter to come to be one. And how on becoming one, his lord was to make a marriage for him (since he would by that time be a widower, as a matter of course) and was to give him as a wife one of the empress's damsels, heiress to some rich and grand state on the mainland — having nothing to do with islands of any sort, since he no longer cared for those. All this Sancho delivered with so much composure — wiping his nose from time to time — and with so little common sense, that his two hearers were once again filled with wonder at the force of Don Quixote's madness, which could run away with this poor man's reason. They didn't care to take the trouble of disabusing him of his error, since they considered that as it did not in any way hurt his conscience, it would be better to leave him in it, and they would get more amusement out of hearing his simplicities. So they bade him pray to God for his master's health, since it was a very likely and feasible thing for him in course of time to come to be an emperor, as he said, or at least an archbishop, or some other dignitary of equal rank.

To which Sancho answered, "If fortune, sirs, should bring things about in such a way that my master had a mind, instead of being an emperor, to be an archbishop, I should like to know what archbishops-errant commonly give their squires?"

"They commonly give them," said the curate, "some simple benefice or cure, or some place as sacristan, which brings in a good fixed income, not counting the altar fees, which may be reckoned at as much again."

"But for that," said Sancho, "the squire must be unmarried, and must know, at any rate, how to help at mass; and if so, woe is me, for I am married already and I don't know the first letter of the A B C. What will become of me if my master takes a fancy to be an archbishop and not an emperor, as is the usual and customary thing for knights-errant?"

"Don't worry, friend Sancho," said the barber, "for we'll plead with your master, and advise him — urging it upon him even as a matter of conscience — to become an emperor and not an archbishop, since that will be easier for him, as he is more valiant than learned."

"That's what I've thought," said Sancho; "though I can tell you he's fit for anything. What I mean to do for my part is pray to our Lord to place him where it may be best for him, and where he may be able to bestow most favours upon me."

"You speak like a man of sense," said the curate, "and you'll be acting like a good Christian. But what must now be done is to take steps to coax your master out of that useless penance you say he is performing; and we had best turn into this inn to consider what plan to adopt, and also to dine, for it's now time."

Sancho said they could go in, but that he would wait outside, and would tell them afterwards the reason he was unwilling and why it didn't suit him to enter; but he begged them to bring him out something to eat, and to let it be hot, and also to bring barley for Rocinante. They left him and went in, and shortly afterwards the barber brought him out something to eat. By and by, after they had between them carefully thought over what they should do to carry out their object, the curate hit upon an idea very well suited to humouring Don Quixote and achieving their purpose. His notion, which he explained to the barber, was that he himself would put on the disguise of a wandering damsel, while the other would try as best he could to pass for a squire, and that they would then proceed to where Don Quixote was; and the curate, pretending to be an aggrieved and distressed damsel, would ask a favour of him, which as a valiant knight-errant he could not refuse to grant. The favour he meant to ask was that the knight should accompany her wherever she would lead him, in order to redress a wrong a wicked knight had done her; and at the same time she would beg him not to require her to remove her mask, nor ask any question about her circumstances until he had set things right with that wicked knight. The curate had no doubt that Don Quixote would comply with any request made in these terms, and that in this way they could remove him and take him back to his own village, where they would try to find out if there was any kind of remedy for his extraordinary madness.

title: Part 1, Chapter 27
paragraphs: How the curate and the barber carried out their plan, together with other matters that deserve a place in this great history

The barber thought the curate’s plan was not just acceptable but so good that they set about putting it into action immediately. They borrowed a petticoat and hood from the innkeeper’s wife, leaving one of the curate’s new cassocks with her as security; and the barber made himself a beard out of a grey-brown — or perhaps reddish — ox-tail, the one the landlord used to keep his comb stuck in. The landlady asked them what they wanted all these things for, and the curate gave her a brief account of Don Quixote’s madness, explaining that the disguise was meant to draw him away from the mountains where he was currently hiding. The landlord and his wife immediately realized that this madman must be their former guest — the man with the balsam, master of the squire who got tossed in the blanket — and they told the curate everything that had happened between him and them, including the part Sancho had kept so quiet about. In the end the landlady dressed the curate up so well that nothing more could be asked: she put him in a cloth petticoat with black velvet stripes a hand’s-width broad, all slashed in the old style, and a bodice of green velvet trimmed with a white satin binding — both the bodice and the petticoat looked as if they dated from the days of King Wamba. The curate refused to let them put the hood on him; instead he wore on his head a little quilted linen cap he normally used as a nightcap, tied a strip of black silk across his forehead, and with another strip made a mask that hid his beard and face very effectively. Then he put on his hat, which was broad enough to double as an umbrella, wrapped himself in his cloak, and seated himself sideways on his mule like a woman, while the barber mounted his own mule wearing a beard that reached down to his waist, a mix of red and white — for it was, as has been said, the tail of a clay-red ox.

They said goodbye to everyone, including the good Maritornes, who — sinner that she was — promised to pray a full rosary so that God would grant them success in the difficult and Christian undertaking they had in hand. But the curate had barely left the inn when it struck him that he was doing something wrong by rigging himself out this way: it was unseemly for a priest to dress like that, even with a great deal at stake. He said as much to the barber and asked him to swap costumes — it was more fitting that the barber play the damsel in distress, while he himself would take the squire’s part, which would be less damaging to his dignity. If the barber refused, he was determined to drop the whole business and let the devil take Don Quixote. Just at that moment Sancho came up, and at the sight of the two of them in such an outfit he could not hold back his laughter. The barber, however, agreed to do what the curate wanted, and with the plan rearranged, the curate began coaching him on how to play his part and what to say to Don Quixote to push and persuade him to come with them and give up his attachment to the spot he had chosen for his pointless penance. The barber said he could manage it perfectly well without any coaching. Since he didn’t care to put the costume on until they were close to where Don Quixote was, he folded up the clothes, the curate adjusted his beard, and they set off with Sancho Panza as their guide. As they went, Sancho told them about their encounter with the madman they had met in the Sierra — though he said nothing about finding the valise and what was inside it; for all his simplicity, the fellow had a streak of greed in him.

The next day they reached the spot where Sancho had laid down broom branches as markers to help him find the place where he had left his master. Recognizing it, he told them this was the way in, and that they had better get into their costumes if that was what it took to rescue his master — for they had already explained to him that going in this disguise and dressing this way was of the highest importance for pulling his master out of the destructive life he had chosen. They gave him strict instructions not to tell his master who they were or admit that he knew them; and if Don Quixote asked — as he certainly would — whether he had delivered the letter to Dulcinea, he was to say yes, and that since she could not read, she had answered by word of mouth, commanding him on pain of her displeasure to come and see her at once. This mattered greatly for Don Quixote himself, they said, because with this story and what they planned to say to him, they were confident of bringing him back to a better way of life and getting him to take immediate steps toward becoming an emperor or a monarch — there was no danger of his becoming an archbishop. Sancho listened to all of it, fixed it firmly in his memory, and thanked them warmly for planning to recommend his master for emperor rather than archbishop, since he felt sure that when it came to handing out rewards to their squires, emperors could do far more than archbishops-errant. He added that it might be a good idea for him to go ahead of them to find his master and deliver his lady’s answer; that alone might be enough to bring him out of the place without putting them to all this trouble. They liked Sancho’s suggestion and decided to wait for him until he came back with word that he had found his master.

Sancho pushed on into the ravines of the Sierra, leaving the two of them in one where a small, gentle stream flowed and where the rocks and trees offered a cool, welcome shade. It was an August day with all the heat of one — and the heat in those parts is intense — and the hour was three in the afternoon, all of which made the spot more inviting and tempted them to wait there for Sancho’s return, which is what they did. They were resting in the shade, then, when a voice reached their ears — unaccompanied by any instrument, but sweet and pleasing in its tone — and it astonished them more than a little, since the place hardly seemed the sort where anyone would sing so well. People often say that woods and fields are home to shepherds with wonderful voices, but that is more poetic fancy than truth. They were even more surprised when they realized that what they were hearing was not the verse of rustic shepherds but the work of polished city wits. And so it proved, for these were the verses they heard:

What makes my search for happiness seem vain? Disdain. What tells me to abandon hope of ease? Jealousies. What holds my heart in an agony of suspense? Absence. If that is so, then for my grief where can I turn to find relief, when hope on every side lies slain by Absence, Jealousies, Disdain?

What proves to be the prime cause of all my woe? Love. What looks with envy on my every chance at glory? Chance. Who gave permission for me to be afflicted so? Heaven. If that is so, I only wait for the blow of an unstoppable fate, since, working for my ruin, these three — Love, Chance, and Heaven — stand in league, I see.

What must I do to find a remedy? Die. What is the cure for love grown cold and strange? Change. What, if all else fails, will heal the heart of sadness? Madness. If that is so, it is pure folly to seek a cure for melancholy: ask where the cure lies, and the answer says in Change, in Madness, or in Death.

The hour, the summer season, the lonely spot, the voice and skill of the singer — everything combined to fill the two listeners with wonder and delight, and they stayed quiet, waiting to hear something more. When the silence stretched on for a while, though, they decided to go looking for the musician who sang with such a fine voice. But just as they were about to move, the same voice stopped them in their tracks; it reached their ears once more, this time singing a
A SONNET

Holy Friendship — when you rose to heaven, soaring up to seek your home beyond the sky and take your seat among the saints on high, you chose to leave behind on earth below your likeness, and on it you bestowed your veil, behind which hypocrisy, parading in your shape, at times deceives the eye and makes its vileness shine as bright as virtue. Friendship, come back to us — or force the fraud who wears your livery now to give it back, since by its help sincerity is being murdered. If you will not unmask your counterfeit, this earth will fall prey to strife once more, as it did when primeval discord held its reign.

The song ended with a deep sigh, and again the two listeners waited attentively for the singer to go on. But when they realized that the music had given way to sobs and heartbroken moaning, they decided to find out who this unhappy person could be — someone whose voice was as remarkable as his sighs were pitiful. They had not gone far when, rounding the corner of a rock, they came upon a man whose look and bearing matched exactly the description Sancho had given them when he told the story of Cardenio. The man showed no surprise at seeing them; he stood still with his head sunk on his chest like someone deep in thought, and after one first glance when they suddenly appeared, he did not raise his eyes to look at them again. The curate, who knew of his misfortune and recognized him from the description, was a man with a good way with words; he went up to him and in a few sensible sentences begged and urged him to give up such a miserable existence, before he lost his life out there — which would be the worst misfortune of all. Cardenio at that moment was in his right mind, free of the fits of madness that so often swept him away, and seeing the two of them dressed in a style so unusual among the people who frequented those wilds, he could not help showing some surprise — all the more when he heard them speak of his situation as if it were common knowledge, which is what the curate’s words implied. So he answered them like this:

“I can see plainly, gentlemen, whoever you may be, that Heaven — which takes care to rescue the good, and quite often the wicked too — has sent me, here in this remote place cut off from all human contact, people I do not deserve: people who want to draw me away from this life to somewhere better, and who use many forceful arguments to show me how unreasonably I am behaving by living the way I do. But since they don’t know what I know — that if I escape this misery I will only fall into one still greater — they will probably write me off as weak-minded, or worse, as a man with no reason left at all. And that would be no surprise, because I myself can tell that the memory of my misfortunes hits me with such force, and works so powerfully toward my ruin, that despite myself I sometimes turn into a kind of stone, without feeling or awareness. I know it is true, because people tell me and show me proof of the things I have done while the terrible fit has hold of me; and all I can do then is grieve uselessly over my lot, curse my fate to no purpose, and offer an excuse for my madness by explaining its cause to anyone who cares to hear it — for no reasonable person who learns the cause will wonder at the effects. And if they cannot help me, at least they will not blame me, and the disgust they feel at my wild behavior will turn into pity for my suffering. So, gentlemen, if you have come here with the same purpose that has brought others, then before you go any further with your wise arguments, I beg you to hear the story of my countless misfortunes. Perhaps once you have heard it, you will spare yourselves the trouble of offering consolation for a grief that is beyond all consolation’s reach.”

Since the two of them wanted nothing more than to hear from his own lips the cause of his suffering, they begged him to tell it, promising to do nothing for his relief or comfort that he himself did not want. With that, the unhappy gentleman began his sad story in nearly the same words and the same manner he had used a few days earlier when telling it to Don Quixote and the goatherd — the time when, thanks to Master Elisabad and Don Quixote’s scrupulous insistence on the proprieties of chivalry, the tale was left unfinished, as this history has already recorded. But now, fortunately, the fit of madness held off and let him tell it through to the end. And so, coming to the incident of the note that Don Fernando had found in the volume of “Amadis of Gaul,” Cardenio said he remembered it perfectly, and that it ran like this:
“From Luscinda to Cardenio.”

“Every day I discover qualities in you that oblige and compel me to value you more highly. So if you want to release me from this debt without any cost to my honor, you can easily do it. I have a father who knows you and who loves me dearly; he will never force my inclination, and he will grant whatever it is reasonable for you to ask — if you really value me as you say you do, and as I believe you do.”

“That letter was what moved me, as I told you, to ask for Luscinda as my wife; that letter was what fixed Luscinda in Don Fernando’s mind as one of the most discreet and prudent women of the day; and that letter was what first planted in him the plan to destroy me before my own plan could be carried out. I told Don Fernando that all Luscinda’s father was waiting for was for my father to ask him for her hand — something I didn’t dare suggest to my father, for fear he would refuse. Not because he failed to recognize Luscinda’s rank, goodness, virtue, and beauty — she had qualities that would do honor to any family in Spain — but because I understood that he didn’t want me to marry so soon, not before we saw what the Duke Ricardo would do for me. In short, I told Don Fernando that I couldn’t bring myself to mention it to my father, partly because of that obstacle and partly because of many other vague discouragements I couldn’t quite name — only that I had a feeling that what I longed for was never going to happen. To all this Don Fernando answered that he would take it on himself to speak to my father and persuade him to speak to Luscinda’s. Oh, ambitious Marius! Oh, cruel Catiline! Oh, wicked Sylla! Oh, perfidious Ganelon! Oh, treacherous Vellido! Oh, vindictive Julian! Oh, covetous Judas! Traitor — cruel, vindictive, and perfidious — how had this poor wretch failed in his loyalty to you, when he so openly showed you the secrets and joys of his heart? What offense did I commit? What words did I say, what advice did I give, that wasn’t aimed entirely at advancing your honor and your welfare? But what am I complaining about, miserable as I am? When misfortunes come down from the stars, they descend from such a height and fall on us with such fury and violence that no power on earth can check their course and no human scheme can hold off their coming. Who would have thought that Don Fernando — a highborn gentleman, intelligent, bound to me by gratitude for my services, a man who could win the object of his love wherever he chose to set his affections — would harden himself, as the saying goes, to the point of robbing me of my one ewe lamb, which wasn’t even yet in my possession? But let me set aside these useless, unavailing reflections and pick up the broken thread of my unhappy story.

“To go on, then: Don Fernando found that my presence stood in the way of carrying out his treacherous and wicked design, so he decided to send me to his elder brother on the pretext of asking him for money to pay for six horses. He had bought them deliberately, with the sole aim of getting me out of the way so he could carry out his infernal scheme more easily — he bought them the very day he offered to speak to my father — and now he wanted me to go and fetch the payment. Could I have anticipated this betrayal? Could I possibly have suspected it? Of course not — far from it, I offered with the greatest pleasure to leave at once, delighted at the good bargain that had been struck. That night I spoke with Luscinda and told her what had been agreed with Don Fernando, and how I had strong hopes that our fair and reasonable wishes would come true. She, as unsuspecting of Don Fernando’s treachery as I was, urged me to come back quickly, since she believed the fulfillment of our desires would be delayed only as long as my father put off speaking to hers. I don’t know why, but as she said this her eyes filled with tears and a lump rose in her throat, stopping her from saying a single word of the many more it seemed to me she was trying to say. I was astonished at this strange mood, which I had never seen in her before; whenever luck and my ingenuity gave us the chance, we had always talked with the greatest gaiety and cheerfulness, never mixing tears, sighs, jealousies, doubts, or fears into our words. On my side it was all celebration of my good fortune that Heaven had given her to me as my lady: I glorified her beauty, I extolled her worth and her understanding; and she paid me back by praising in me whatever, loving me as she did, she thought worth praising. Beyond that we had a hundred thousand small things to talk about — the doings of our neighbors and acquaintances — and the boldest thing I ever did was to take, almost by force, one of her lovely white hands and press it to my lips, as far as the narrowness of the low grating between us allowed. But the night before the miserable day of my departure, she wept, she moaned, she sighed, and then she withdrew, leaving me bewildered and shaken, overwhelmed by these strange and painful signs of grief and sorrow in Luscinda. Not wanting to crush my own hopes, I put it all down to the depth of her love for me and the pain that separation causes those who love tenderly. In the end I set off, sad and dejected, my heart full of imaginings and suspicions, without knowing exactly what it was I suspected or imagined — plain omens, pointing to the sad event and the misfortune that lay waiting for me.

“I reached the place I had been sent to and gave the letter to Don Fernando’s brother. I was received kindly, but not dispatched quickly: to my great frustration, he told me to wait eight days, somewhere the duke his father would not be likely to see me, because his brother had written that the money was to be sent without their father’s knowledge. All of this was a scheme of the treacherous Don Fernando, since his brother had no shortage of money and could have sent me off at once.

“It was an order that sorely tempted me to disobey, because it seemed impossible to endure life for so many days separated from Luscinda — especially after leaving her in the sorrowful state I have described to you. Even so, like a dutiful servant, I obeyed, though I felt it would come at the cost of my well-being. But four days later a man arrived looking for me, carrying a letter; from the address I could see it came from Luscinda, for the handwriting was hers. I opened it in fear and trembling, convinced that only something serious would have driven her to write to me at a distance, since she rarely did so even when I was near. Before reading it, I asked the man who had given it to him and how long he had been on the road. He told me that he happened to be passing through one of the city’s streets around noon when a very beautiful lady called to him from a window. With tears in her eyes, she said to him hurriedly, ‘Brother, if you are a Christian, as you seem to be, I beg you for the love of God to have this letter sent without a moment’s delay to the place and the person named on the address — both are well known — and in doing this you will do a great service to our Lord. And so that you are at no inconvenience in doing it, take what is in this handkerchief.’ ‘And with that,’ he said, ‘she threw a handkerchief out of the window with a hundred reals tied up in it, along with this gold ring I have brought here together with the letter I have given you. Then, without waiting for any answer, she left the window — though not before she saw me take the letter and the handkerchief and signal to her that I would do what she asked. Seeing myself so well paid for the trouble of bringing it to you, and knowing from the address that it was meant for you — because, señor, I know you very well — and unable, besides, to resist that beautiful lady’s tears, I decided to trust no one else but to come and deliver it to you myself. And in the sixteen hours since it was handed to me, I have made the journey, which, as you know, is eighteen leagues.’

“The whole time this kind-hearted improvised courier was telling me this, I hung on his words, my legs trembling beneath me so badly I could barely stand. At last I opened the letter and read these words:

Don Fernando has kept the promise he gave you to urge your father to speak to mine — but he has kept it in a way that serves him far more than it helps you. I must tell you, señor, that he has asked for my hand, and my father, swayed by what he sees as Don Fernando’s superiority over you, has welcomed his suit so warmly that the betrothal is set to take place two days from now, in such secrecy and so privately that the only witnesses will be the Heavens above and a few members of the household. Imagine the state I am in; decide for yourself whether it is urgent for you to come; whether I love you or not, the outcome of this affair will show you. God grant that this reaches your hand before mine is forced to join itself with the hand of a man who keeps his pledged word so badly.

“Those, in brief, were the words of the letter — words that made me set out at once without waiting any longer for the reply or the money, for I now saw clearly that it was not the purchase of horses but the pursuit of his own pleasure that had made Don Fernando send me to his brother. My fury at Don Fernando, combined with the fear of losing the prize I had won through so many years of love and devotion, gave me wings: almost flying, I reached home that same day, at the hour that served for speaking with Luscinda. I arrived unseen, left the mule I had ridden at the house of the good man who had brought me the letter, and fortune was kind enough, for once, that I found Luscinda at the grating that had been the witness of our love. She recognized me at once, and I her — but not as she should have recognized me, nor I her. But who in this world can claim to have fathomed or understood the wavering mind and unstable nature of a woman? No one, truly. To continue: the moment Luscinda saw me, she said, ‘Cardenio, I am in my wedding dress. The treacherous Don Fernando and my greedy father are waiting for me in the hall, with the other witnesses — who will witness my death before they witness my betrothal. Don’t be distressed, my friend, but find a way to be present at this sacrifice. If my words cannot prevent it, I have a dagger hidden on me that can prevent more deliberate violence, by ending my life and giving you a first proof of the love I have borne you and bear you still.’ I answered her distractedly and in haste, terrified I would not have time to answer at all: ‘May your deeds make good your words, my lady. If you carry a dagger to save your honor, I carry a sword to defend you — or to kill myself, if fortune turns against us.’

“I don’t think she could have heard all of those words, because I saw them calling her away in a hurry — the bridegroom was waiting. Then the night of my sorrow closed in; the sun of my happiness set; my eyes were left without sight, my mind without reason. I could not bring myself to enter the house; I was incapable of any movement at all. But reflecting on how important it was that I be present for whatever might happen, I steadied myself as best I could and went in — I knew all the entrances and exits well, and besides, with the secret commotion running through the house, no one noticed me. Without being seen, I managed to station myself in the recess formed by a window of the hall itself, hidden by the ends and borders of two tapestries, from between which I could watch everything that happened in the room without being observed. Who could describe the agitation of heart I suffered as I stood there — the thoughts that came to me, the reflections that ran through my mind? They were such as cannot be told, and perhaps should not be. Let it be enough to say that the bridegroom entered the hall in his everyday clothes, without ornament of any kind. As groomsman he had with him a cousin of Luscinda’s, and apart from the household servants there was no one else in the room. A little later, Luscinda came out from an antechamber, accompanied by her mother and two of her maids, dressed and adorned as suited her rank and beauty, in full festival and ceremonial attire. My anxiety and distraction didn’t let me observe or note the details of what she wore; I could only take in the colors — crimson and white — and the glitter of the gems and jewels on her headdress and clothing, all of it outshone by the rare beauty of her lovely auburn hair, which rivaled the precious stones and the light of the four torches standing in the hall, and gleamed brighter than them all. Oh memory, mortal enemy of my peace! Why set before me now the incomparable beauty of that adored enemy of mine? Wouldn’t it be better, cruel memory, to remind me and replay what she did then, so that, stirred by so glaring a wrong, I might seek — if not vengeance now — at least an end to my own life? Don’t grow tired, gentlemen, of listening to these digressions. My sorrow is not the kind that can or should be told tersely and briefly; to me, every part of it seems to demand many words.”

To this the curate replied that far from being tired of listening to him, they found the details he mentioned deeply interesting — they were the kind of thing that should by no means be left out, and they deserved the same attention as the main story.

“To continue, then,” Cardenio went on: “when everyone was assembled in the hall, the parish priest came in, and as he took the couple by the hand to perform the required ceremony, he spoke the words, ‘Will you, Señora Luscinda, take Señor Don Fernando, here present, as your lawful husband, as holy Mother Church ordains?’ At that I thrust my head and neck out from between the tapestries and, with straining ears and a pounding heart, set myself to listen for Luscinda’s answer — waiting on her reply for my death sentence or the granting of my life. Oh, if only I had dared at that moment to rush forward and shout, ‘Luscinda, Luscinda! Watch what you are doing; remember what you owe me; remember that you are mine and cannot belong to another; understand that the instant you say “Yes” is the instant my life ends! Oh, treacherous Don Fernando — thief of my glory, death of my life! What do you want? Realize that as a Christian you cannot achieve what you desire, for Luscinda is my bride, and I am her husband!’ Fool that I am — now that I am far away and out of danger, I say I should have done what I did not do; now that I have let my precious treasure be stolen from me, I curse the thief, on whom I might have taken vengeance if I had as much heart for that as I have for lamenting my fate. In short, since I was a coward and a fool then, it is no great wonder that I am dying now — ashamed, remorseful, and mad.

“The priest stood waiting for Luscinda’s answer, and for a long while she withheld it. Just when I thought she was about to draw the dagger to save her honor, or to find the words for some declaration of the truth that would speak on my behalf, I heard her say in a faint, feeble voice, ‘I will.’ Don Fernando said the same; he gave her the ring, and they stood bound by a knot that could never be undone. The bridegroom then stepped forward to embrace his bride, and she, pressing her hand against her heart, fell fainting into her mother’s arms. It only remains now to tell you the state I was in when, in that consent I had just heard, I saw all my hopes mocked, Luscinda’s words and promises exposed as lies, and the recovery of the prize I had lost in that instant made impossible forever. I stood there stunned, abandoned — it seemed — by Heaven itself, declared an enemy by the very earth that bore me, the air refusing me breath for my sighs, the water refusing moisture for my tears; only fire gathered strength, until my whole body burned with rage and jealousy. The whole company was thrown into confusion by Luscinda’s fainting, and as her mother loosened her dress to give her air, a sealed paper was discovered in her bosom. Don Fernando seized it at once and began to read it by the light of one of the torches; and when he had finished, he sat down in a chair, resting his cheek on his hand like a man deep in thought, taking no part in the efforts being made to revive his bride from her faint.

“Seeing the whole household in confusion, I risked coming out, indifferent to whether I was seen or not — and determined, if I was seen, to do something so frenzied that the whole world would understand the righteous indignation in my breast, through the punishment of the treacherous Don Fernando and even of that fickle, fainting traitress. But my fate, no doubt holding me in reserve for greater sorrows — if greater ones exist — arranged things so that at that moment I had an abundance, even a surplus, of the very reason that has failed me ever since. And so, instead of taking revenge on my worst enemies (which would have been easy, since no one’s thoughts were anywhere near me), I resolved to take it on myself instead — to inflict on myself the pain they deserved, perhaps with even greater severity than I would have shown them if I had killed them on the spot; for sudden pain is quickly over, but pain drawn out by torment kills continually without ever ending a life. In short, I left the house and went to the house of the man with whom I had left my mule. I had him saddle it for me, mounted without a word of farewell, and rode out of the city like another Lot, not daring to turn my head to look back at it. When I found myself alone in the open country, screened by the darkness of the night and tempted by the stillness to pour out my grief without worry or fear of being heard or seen, I broke my silence and raised my voice in curses against Luscinda and Don Fernando, as if cursing could avenge the wrong they had done me. I called her cruel, ungrateful, false, and thankless — but above all greedy, since my enemy’s wealth had blinded the eyes of her love and turned it away from me, handing it over to a man on whom fortune had been more generous and openhanded. And yet, in the middle of this storm of curses and reproaches, I found excuses for her. It was no wonder, I said, that a young girl, sheltered in her parents’ house, raised and trained to obey them always, should have been ready to bow to their wishes when they offered her as a husband a gentleman of such distinction, wealth, and noble birth; if she had refused him, people would have thought she was out of her mind, or that her affections were set elsewhere — a suspicion damaging to her good name and reputation. But then again, I said, if she had declared that I was her husband, they would have seen that in choosing me she had not chosen so badly that they couldn’t forgive her; for before Don Fernando made his offer, her parents themselves — if their wishes had been governed by reason — could not have wanted a more suitable husband for their daughter than I was. And she, before taking the final, fatal step of giving her hand, could easily have said that I had already given her mine, and I would have come forward to back up any such claim she made. In the end I concluded that weak love, too little reflection, great ambition, and a craving for rank had made her forget the words with which she had deceived me — words I had trusted, sustained by my firm hopes and my honorable passion.

“Talking to myself this way, in turmoil, I traveled on through the rest of the night, and at daybreak I reached one of the passes into these mountains. I wandered through them for three more days, following no path or road, until I came to some meadows lying on I don’t know which side of the range, and there I asked some herdsmen where the most rugged part of these mountains lay. They told me it was in this direction, and I headed here at once, intending to end my life in this place. But as I was picking my way among these crags, my mule dropped dead from exhaustion and hunger — or, as I think more likely, simply to be rid of the worthless burden it carried in me. I was left on foot, worn out and starving, with no one to help me and no thought of looking for help. I lay stretched out on the ground for I don’t know how long, and when I got up my hunger was gone, and I found some goatherds beside me — no doubt the people who had relieved my need, because they told me how they had found me, and how I had been raving in a way that made it plain I had lost my reason. Since then, I have been aware that I am not always in full possession of it: at times I am so deranged and crazed that I do a thousand mad things — tearing my clothes, crying aloud through these solitudes, cursing my fate, and calling pointlessly on the dear name of the woman who is my enemy, with no aim in those moments but to end my life in lamentation. And when I come back to my senses, I find myself so drained and weary that I can barely move. Most often my dwelling is the hollow of a cork tree, big enough to shelter this miserable body. The herdsmen and goatherds who pass through these mountains, moved by compassion, supply me with food, leaving it by the wayside or on the rocks where they think I might pass by and find it; and so, even when I am out of my senses, the needs of nature teach me what is required to keep me alive, and make me crave it and reach for it. At other times — so they tell me, when they find me in a rational state — I come out onto the road and snatch food by force from the shepherds carrying it from the village to their huts, even though they would gladly give it to me. This is how I pass the wretched remainder of my life, until Heaven wills it to end, or wills my memory so reordered that I no longer remember Luscinda’s beauty and treachery or the wrong Don Fernando did me. If Heaven will do that without taking my life, I will turn my thoughts to some better course; if not, I can only pray it to have full mercy on my soul, for I feel no power or strength in myself to free my body from this hardship into which I have chosen, of my own accord, to place it.

“That, gentlemen, is the bitter story of my misfortune. Tell me whether it could be told with less emotion than you have seen in me — and don’t trouble yourselves with urging or pressing on me whatever reason suggests might serve for my relief, for it will do me as much good as a wise physician’s prescription does the sick man who refuses to take it. I want no health without Luscinda; and since it is her pleasure to belong to another, when she is mine — or should be — let it be my pleasure to belong to misery when I might have enjoyed happiness. By her fickleness she tried to make my ruin permanent; I will try to satisfy her wishes by pursuing my own destruction. And future generations will see that I alone lacked the thing every other unfortunate has in abundance: for them, the impossibility of consolation is itself a consolation, while for me it is the cause of greater griefs and sufferings, because I believe they will not end even in death.”

Here Cardenio brought his long discourse and story to a close — a tale as full of misfortune as it was of love. But just as the curate was about to offer him some words of comfort, he was stopped by a voice that reached his ear, saying in mournful tones what will be told in the Fourth Part of this narrative; for at this point the wise and shrewd historian, Cid Hamete Benengeli, brought the Third Part to its conclusion.

title: Part 1, Chapter 28
paragraphs: Which describes the strange and delightful adventure that happened to the curate and the barber in the same sierra

How happy and fortunate were the times when that boldest of knights, Don Quixote of La Mancha, was sent into the world. Because he formed a resolution so honorable — to revive and restore to the world the long-lost and nearly extinct order of knight-errantry — we now enjoy, in this age of ours so starved for light entertainment, not only the pleasure of his truthful history but also the tales and episodes woven into it, which are in their way no less delightful, clever, and true than the history itself. And that history, picking up its thread again — carded, spun, and wound — relates that just as the curate was about to offer Cardenio some consolation, he was interrupted by a voice that reached his ear, saying in mournful tones:

“Oh God! Is it possible that I have found a place that can serve as a secret grave for the weary burden of this body I carry so unwillingly? If the solitude these mountains promise is not deceiving me, then I have. Ah, how wretched I am! How much more welcome to my mind will be the company of these rocks and thickets, which let me complain of my misfortune to Heaven, than the company of any human being — for there is no one on earth to turn to for advice in doubt, comfort in sorrow, or relief in distress!”

The curate and his companions heard all this distinctly, and since the voice seemed to come from close by — as in fact it did — they got up to look for the speaker. They had not gone twenty paces before they discovered, behind a rock, a youth in peasant clothing sitting at the foot of an ash tree. They could not see his face at that moment, because he was leaning forward, bathing his feet in the brook that ran past. They approached so quietly that he did not notice them; he was completely absorbed in washing his feet, which were so fair that they looked like two pieces of gleaming crystal lying among the other stones of the brook. The whiteness and beauty of those feet astonished them, since they hardly seemed made for crushing clods of earth or trudging behind a plow and oxen, as their owner's clothes suggested. So, finding they had not been noticed, the curate, who was in front, signaled to the other two to hide behind some fragments of rock that lay nearby; they did, watching closely to see what the youth would do. He wore a loose, double-skirted, dark brown jacket cinched tight to his body with a white cloth; he also had on breeches and gaiters of brown cloth, and on his head a brown montera cap. He had the gaiters rolled up to mid-calf, and his legs truly looked as if they were made of pure alabaster.

As soon as he had finished bathing his beautiful feet, he dried them with a towel he pulled from under the montera, and when he took the cap off he raised his face — and the watchers got a view of beauty so exquisite that Cardenio whispered to the curate:
“Since this is not Luscinda, this is no human creature; it's a divine being.”

Then the youth removed the montera, and as he shook his head from side to side, a mass of hair broke loose and tumbled out — hair the beams of the sun themselves might have envied. By this they realized that the apparent peasant was actually a lovely woman; indeed, the most beautiful that two of them had ever laid eyes on, and even the most beautiful Cardenio had ever seen, had he not seen and known Luscinda — for he later declared that only Luscinda's beauty could rival hers. Her long auburn tresses not only covered her shoulders; they were so long and so abundant that they hid her entire body beneath their masses, so that nothing of her figure was visible except her feet. She now used her hands as a comb, and if her feet had looked like pieces of crystal in the water, her hands among her locks looked like handfuls of driven snow — all of which increased not only the admiration of the three watchers but also their eagerness to learn who she was. With that aim they decided to show themselves, and at the noise they made getting to their feet, the lovely girl raised her head, parted the hair from her eyes with both hands, and looked to see who had made the sound. The moment she saw them she sprang up, and without pausing to put on her shoes or gather her hair, she hastily snatched up a bundle, apparently of clothes, that lay beside her and, frightened and alarmed, tried to run. But before she had gone six paces she fell to the ground, her delicate feet unable to bear the roughness of the stones. Seeing this, the three hurried toward her, and the curate spoke to her first:

“Stop, señora, whoever you may be. The men you see here want only to be of service to you. There is no need for such a reckless attempt to flee — your feet cannot endure it, and we will not allow it.”
Caught off guard and bewildered, she made no reply to these words. They came toward her anyway, and the curate, taking her hand, went on to say:

“What your clothes would conceal, señora, your hair reveals to us — clear proof that it can be no small matter that has disguised your beauty in a costume so unworthy of it and sent it into a wilderness like this, where we have had the good luck to find you, if not to relieve your distress, then at least to offer you comfort. For no distress, while life lasts, can be so crushing, or reach such an extreme, that the sufferer should refuse to listen to comfort offered with good intentions. And so, señora — or señor, or whatever you prefer to be — set aside the fear our appearance has caused you and tell us about your fortunes, good or bad; from all of us together, or from each of us alone, you will find sympathy in your trouble.”

While the curate spoke, the disguised young woman stood as if spellbound, staring at them without opening her lips or saying a word — exactly like a village rustic who has suddenly been shown some strange thing he has never seen before. But when the curate addressed a few more words to the same effect to her, she sighed deeply, broke her silence, and said:

“Since the solitude of these mountains has failed to hide me, and since my loosened, disheveled hair will not let my tongue tell lies, it would be pointless for me to keep up any further pretense now — anything you believed of it, you would believe out of courtesy rather than for any other reason. That being so, I say that I thank you, sirs, for the offer you have made me, which obliges me to comply with what you have asked; though I fear the account I give of my misfortunes will stir in you as much concern as compassion, since you will be unable to suggest anything to remedy them, or any consolation to ease them. Even so — so that my honor will not be left in doubt in your minds, now that you have discovered I am a woman and can see that I am young, alone, and dressed like this, circumstances that together or separately would be enough to destroy any good reputation — I feel bound to tell you what I would gladly keep secret if I could.”

She who was now revealed to be a lovely woman delivered all this without any hesitation, so fluently and in so sweet a voice that they were as charmed by her intelligence as by her beauty. And when they repeated their offers and their pleas that she keep her promise, she needed no further urging. First modestly covering her feet and gathering up her hair, she seated herself on a stone with the three men placed around her, and after an effort to hold back some tears that came to her eyes, she began her story in a clear, steady voice:

“Here in Andalusia there is a town from which a duke takes his title, making him one of those they call Grandees of Spain. This nobleman has two sons: the elder, heir to his rank and apparently to his good qualities; the younger, heir to I don't know what, unless it is the treachery of Vellido and the deceit of Ganelon. My parents are vassals of this lord — humble in origin, but so wealthy that if their birth had given them as much as their fortune did, they would have had nothing left to wish for, and I would have had no reason to fear a misfortune like the one I am in now; for it may well be that my bad luck springs from theirs, in not having been nobly born. It is true they are not so lowly that they have any reason to be ashamed of their station, but neither are they so high as to rid my mind of the suspicion that my disaster comes from their humble birth. They are, in short, farmers, plain ordinary people, with no strain of disreputable blood in them — old rusty Christians, as the saying goes — but so rich that their wealth and open-handed way of living are gradually earning them the standing of gentlefolk by birth, and even by position. Yet the wealth and nobility they prized most was having me as their daughter; and since they have no other child to make their heir, and are devoted parents, I was one of the most pampered daughters that parents ever pampered.

“I was the mirror in which they saw themselves, the staff of their old age, and — with all submission to Heaven — the single object of all their wishes; and mine never strayed from theirs, because I knew their worth. And just as I was mistress of their hearts, so I was also mistress of their property. Through me they hired and dismissed their servants; the accounts and records of everything sown and harvested passed through my hands; the oil mills, the wine presses, the tally of the flocks and herds, the beehives — everything, in short, that a rich farmer like my father owns or could own, I had in my care, and I served as steward and mistress with a diligence on my part, and a satisfaction on theirs, that I cannot adequately describe to you. The leisure hours left to me, after giving the necessary orders to the head shepherds, the overseers, and the other laborers, I spent on pursuits that are not only permissible but necessary for young girls — the ones the needle, the embroidery cushion, and the spinning wheel usually provide — and if I set them aside for a while to refresh my mind, I found recreation in reading some devotional book or playing the harp, for experience had taught me that music calms a troubled mind and relieves weariness of spirit. That was the life I led in my parents' house, and if I have painted it in such detail, it is not out of vanity, or to let you know that I am rich, but so that you can see how, through no fault of my own, I have fallen from the happy condition I have described into the misery I am in now. The truth is that while I was leading this busy life, in a seclusion that could rival a convent's, unseen — as I believed — by anyone except the household servants (for when I went to Mass it was so early in the morning, and I was so closely escorted by my mother and the women of the house, and so heavily veiled and so shy, that my eyes scarcely saw more ground than my feet stepped on), despite all this, the eyes of love — or more accurately, of idleness — eyes a lynx cannot match, found me out, aided by the persistence of Don Fernando; for that is the name of the duke's younger son I told you about.”

The moment the speaker mentioned the name Don Fernando, Cardenio's color changed and he broke into a sweat, with such visible signs of distress that the curate and the barber, who noticed it, feared that one of the mad fits they had heard came over him from time to time was about to strike. But Cardenio showed no further agitation and stayed quiet, studying the peasant girl with fixed attention, because he was beginning to suspect who she was. She, without noticing his agitation, continued her story, and went on to say:

“And his eyes had hardly found me when — as he admitted afterwards — he was struck with a violent passion for me, as the way it displayed itself made perfectly plain. But to shorten the long account of my sorrows, I will pass over in silence all the schemes Don Fernando used to declare his feelings for me. He bribed the entire household; he gave and offered gifts and presents to my parents; every day in our street was like a holiday or a festival; at night nobody could sleep for the music; the love letters that reached my hand — no one knew how — were beyond counting, crammed with tender pleadings and pledges, containing more promises and oaths than they had letters in them. None of it softened me; instead it hardened my heart against him, as though he were my mortal enemy and everything he did to make me yield had been done with the opposite intention. Not that Don Fernando's aristocratic bearing displeased me, or that I found his attentions tiresome; it gave me a certain kind of satisfaction to find myself so pursued and prized by such a distinguished gentleman, and I was not sorry to read my own praises in his letters — for however plain we women may be, it seems to me we are always pleased to hear ourselves called beautiful. What stood against all this was my own sense of what was right, along with the repeated advice of my parents, who by now saw Don Fernando's purpose very clearly, since he hardly cared whether the whole world knew it. They told me they were entrusting their honor and good name to my virtue and integrity alone, and asked me to consider the gap in rank between Don Fernando and myself — from which I could conclude that his intentions, whatever he might claim to the contrary, aimed at his own pleasure rather than my good. And they said that if I wanted to put any obstacle in the way of his unreasonable pursuit, they were ready to marry me at once to anyone I preferred, whether among the leading families of our own town or any of the neighboring ones; with their wealth and my good reputation, a match could be looked for anywhere. This offer, and their sound advice, strengthened my resolve, and I never gave Don Fernando a single word in reply that could offer him even the remotest hope of success.

“All this caution of mine, which he must have taken for disdain, apparently only sharpened his lustful appetite — for that is the name I give to his passion for me; if it had been what he claimed it was, you would never have heard of it, because there would have been no occasion to tell you about it. Eventually he learned that my parents were arranging a marriage for me, to put an end to his hopes of possessing me, or at least to give me additional protectors to watch over me; and that news, or suspicion, drove him to do what you are about to hear. One night I was in my room with no other company than the maid who attended me, the doors carefully locked so that no carelessness could endanger my honor — and I do not know, I cannot imagine, how it happened, but despite all this seclusion and all these precautions, in the solitude and silence of my retreat, I found him standing in front of me. The sight so stunned me that it robbed my eyes of sight and my tongue of speech. I had no strength to cry out, and I do not think he would have given me time to anyway, because he came straight to me, took me in his arms (since, overwhelmed as I was, I had, as I say, no power to defend myself), and began making such declarations to me that I still do not understand how lies could have the skill to dress themselves up to look so much like truth. And the traitor arranged for his tears to vouch for his words, and his sighs for his sincerity.

“I was a poor young thing, alone, untrained by my upbringing in matters like this; and somehow, I do not know how, I began to believe all those lying declarations were true — though his sighs and tears moved me to nothing more than simple compassion. And so, as the first shock of bewilderment wore off and I began to recover myself a little, I said to him, with more courage than I thought I possessed: 'Señor, if instead of being in your arms I were in the claws of a savage lion, and I could win my freedom by doing or saying anything that damaged my honor, I could no more do it or say it than the past could be made never to have happened. So if you hold my body clasped in your arms, I hold my soul secured by virtuous intentions, very different from yours, as you will see if you try to force them through. I am your vassal, but I am not your slave; your noble blood has no right — and should have none — to dishonor or degrade my humble birth; and low-born peasant though I am, I have my self-respect as much as you, a lord and a gentleman. Your violence will get you nowhere with me, your wealth will carry no weight, your words will have no power to deceive me, and your sighs and tears no power to soften me. If I saw any of the things I am describing in the man my parents gave me as a husband, my will would bend to his and never stray beyond it; and with my honor preserved, even if my desires were not, I would willingly give him what you, señor, are now trying to obtain by force. I say all this so you will not imagine that anyone but my lawful husband will ever win anything from me.' 'If that,' said this disloyal gentleman, 'is the only scruple holding you back, loveliest Dorothea' (for that is the name of this unhappy creature), 'look — here and now I give you my hand to be yours, and let Heaven, from which nothing is hidden, and this image of Our Lady that you have here, be witnesses to my pledge.'”

When Cardenio heard her say her name was Dorothea, he showed fresh agitation, now convinced that his earlier suspicion was correct; but he did not want to interrupt the story, wishing to hear the end of what he already nearly knew, so he said only:

“What — your name is Dorothea, señora? I have heard of another woman of the same name whose misfortunes may perhaps match yours. But go on; in due course I may tell you something that will astonish you as much as it will move you to pity.”

Dorothea was struck by Cardenio's words, and by his strange, wretched clothing, and she begged him, if he knew anything about her situation, to tell her at once; for if fortune had left her one blessing, it was the courage to bear whatever calamity might fall on her, since she felt certain that none could come that would add in the slightest degree to what she suffered already.

“I would not let the moment pass, señora,” Cardenio replied, “without telling you what I think — if what I suspect were certain. But so far the right opportunity has not come, and it is not of any importance to you to know it yet.”

“Be that as it may,” Dorothea replied, “what happened next in my story was that Don Fernando took an image that stood in the room and set it up as a witness to our betrothal, and with the most binding words and the most extravagant oaths he gave me his promise to become my husband — though before he had even finished pledging himself, I told him to consider carefully what he was doing, and to think of the anger his father would feel at seeing him married to a peasant girl, one of his own vassals. I told him not to let my beauty, such as it was, blind him, since it was not enough to provide an excuse for his offense; and that if the love he bore me made him want to do me any kindness, it would be to leave my lot to run its course at the level my station required, because marriages so unequal never bring happiness, and the pleasure they begin with never lasts for long.

“All this that I have just repeated I said to him, and much more that I cannot remember; but none of it persuaded him to abandon his purpose — a man who has no intention of paying does not worry himself about the difficulties when he is striking the bargain. Meanwhile I argued the matter over briefly in my own mind, telling myself: 'I will not be the first woman who has risen through marriage from a humble station to a high one, nor will Don Fernando be the first man whom beauty — or more likely, blind infatuation — has led to take a partner beneath his rank. Since I am starting no new custom or practice, I might as well accept the honor that chance is offering me; for even if his feelings for me last no longer than the satisfaction of his desires, I will still, after all, be his wife before God. And if I try to drive him off with scorn, I can see that, when fair means fail, he is in a mood to use force, and I will be left dishonored and with no way of proving my innocence to those who cannot know how innocently I came to be in this situation. What arguments could ever convince my parents that this gentleman entered my room without my consent?'

“All these questions and answers ran through my mind in an instant; but what swayed me most, and began to drag me unawares toward my ruin, were Don Fernando's oaths, the witnesses he called on, the tears he shed, and finally his graceful person and aristocratic charm, which, accompanied by so many signs of genuine love, might well have conquered a heart even freer and more guarded than mine. I called my waiting maid to me, so that there would be a witness on earth besides those in Heaven; and Don Fernando renewed and repeated his oaths once again, invoked new saints as witnesses on top of the earlier ones, called down a thousand future curses on himself if he failed to keep his promise, summoned more tears, redoubled his sighs, and pressed me tighter in his arms, from which he had never once let me escape. And so, when my maid left the room, I stopped being one, and he became a traitor and a perjurer.

“The day that followed the night of my misfortune did not arrive, I imagine, as quickly as Don Fernando wished, for once desire has obtained what it wanted, the greatest pleasure is to get away from the scene of the pleasure. I say this because Don Fernando was in a great hurry to leave me, and through the cunning of my maid — who was in fact the one who had let him in — he was out in the street before daybreak. On taking leave of me he told me, though not with the same earnestness and passion as when he arrived, that I could rest assured of his faithfulness and of the sanctity and sincerity of his oaths; and to seal his words he drew a rich ring from his finger and placed it on mine. Then he left, and I was left behind — whether sad or happy, I cannot say; all I can tell you is that I was left agitated and troubled in mind and almost dazed by what had happened, and I either lacked the spirit, or it simply did not occur to me, to scold my maid for the treachery she had committed in hiding Don Fernando in my room; for I still could not make up my mind whether what had befallen me was good or bad. I told Don Fernando as he left that, since I was now his, he could see me on other nights in the same way, until he chose to let the matter become public. But except for the following night, he never came again, and for more than a month I could not catch a glimpse of him in the street or at church, though I exhausted myself watching for one; I knew he was in town, and that nearly every day he went out hunting, a pastime he was very fond of. I remember well how sad and dreary those days and hours were for me; I remember well how, as they passed, I began to doubt, and even to lose confidence in Don Fernando's word; and I remember, too, how my maid then heard the words rebuking her insolence that she had not heard before, and how I had to force a restraint on my tears and on the expression of my face, so as not to give my parents reason to ask why I was so unhappy and drive me to invent lies in answer. But all of this came to a sudden end, when the moment arrived in which all such considerations were swept aside, all thought of honor was abandoned, my patience gave out, and the secret of my heart became known abroad. The reason was that a few days later a report spread through the town that in a nearby city Don Fernando had married a young woman of extraordinary beauty, the daughter of parents of distinguished position, though not so rich that her dowry would have entitled her to expect so brilliant a match. It was said her name was Luscinda, and that at the betrothal some strange things had happened.”

Cardenio heard the name Luscinda, but he did nothing except shrug his shoulders, bite his lips, and knit his brows — and before long two streams of tears spilled from his eyes. Dorothea, however, did not break off her story, but continued in these words:

“When this grim news reached my ears, instead of freezing my heart it set it blazing with such rage and fury that I could barely stop myself from running out into the streets, shouting aloud and openly proclaiming the betrayal and treachery I had suffered. But that surge of rage was checked, for the moment, by a plan I formed to carry out that very night: to put on these clothes, which I got from one of my father's servants — one of the zagals, as they are called on farms — to whom I confided the whole of my misfortune and whom I begged to go with me to the city where I had heard my enemy was. He scolded me for my recklessness and condemned my decision, but when he saw that I was set on my purpose, he offered to keep me company, as he put it, to the end of the world. I immediately packed a woman's dress into a linen pillowcase, along with some jewels and money for emergencies, and in the silence of the night, without alerting my treacherous maid, I left the house, accompanied by my servant and a crowd of anxieties, and set out on foot for the city — though my eagerness to reach it practically carried me on wings, if not to prevent what I assumed was already done, then at least to demand of Don Fernando with what conscience he had done it. I reached my destination in two and a half days, and on entering the city I asked the way to the house of Luscinda's parents. The first person I asked gave me more in answer than I had wanted to know. He pointed out the house and told me everything that had happened at the betrothal of the family's daughter — an affair so notorious in the city that it was the gossip of every cluster of idlers in the street. He said that on the night Don Fernando was betrothed to Luscinda, the moment she had consented to be his bride by saying 'Yes,' she was overcome by a sudden fainting fit; and that when the bridegroom came to unlace the bosom of her dress to give her air, he found a paper in her own handwriting, in which she stated and declared that she could not be Don Fernando's bride because she was already Cardenio's — who, by this man's account, was a gentleman of distinction in the same city — and that if she had accepted Don Fernando, it was only out of obedience to her parents. In short, he said, the words of the paper made it clear that she had meant to kill herself when the betrothal was completed, and gave her reasons for ending her life — all of which, it was said, was confirmed by a dagger they found somewhere in her clothing. On seeing this, Don Fernando, convinced that Luscinda had fooled, slighted, and toyed with him, attacked her before she had recovered from her faint and tried to stab her with the very dagger that had been found — and he would have succeeded if her parents and the others present had not stopped him. It was said, moreover, that Don Fernando left at once, and that Luscinda did not come out of her collapse until the next day, when she told her parents that she was truly the bride of that Cardenio I mentioned. I learned besides that Cardenio, according to report, had been present at the betrothal, and that on seeing her promised to another — something he had never expected — he had left the city in despair, leaving behind a letter declaring the wrong Luscinda had done him and announcing his intention of going where no one would ever see him again. All this was common knowledge throughout the city, and everyone was talking about it — all the more when it became known that Luscinda had disappeared from her father's house and from the city, for she was nowhere to be found, leaving her parents beside themselves, not knowing what steps to take to recover her. What I learned revived my hopes, and I was happier not to have found Don Fernando at all than to have found him married, because it seemed to me that the door to relief in my case was not yet completely shut. I told myself that Heaven might have placed this obstacle in the way of the second marriage to bring him to recognize his obligations under the first, and to reflect that as a Christian he was bound to put his soul above all human concerns. All this turned over in my mind, and I tried to comfort myself though there was no comfort, indulging in faint, far-off hopes of clinging to this life that I now despise.
