“But while I was in the city, unsure what to do since I could not find Don Fernando, I heard a public crier announce a large reward for anyone who found me, giving the details of my age and a description of the very clothes I was wearing; and I heard it said that the boy who had come with me had taken me away from my father's house — a thing that cut me to the heart, showing how far my good name had fallen: it was not enough that I should lose it by running away; they had to add who I had supposedly fled with — someone so far beneath me and so unworthy of my regard. The instant I heard the announcement I left the city with my servant, who was already beginning to show signs that his loyalty to me was wavering, and that same night, fearing discovery, we entered the most thickly wooded part of these mountains. But, as the saying goes, one evil summons another, and the end of one misfortune tends to be the beginning of a greater one — and so it proved in my case. My good servant, until then so faithful and reliable, once he found me in that lonely place, was moved more by his own villainy than by my beauty, and decided to seize the opportunity these solitudes seemed to offer him; with little shame, less fear of God, and no respect for me, he began making advances to me. And when he found that I answered the impudence of his propositions with the justly harsh language it deserved, he set aside the pleading he had tried at first and began to use force.

“But just Heaven, which rarely fails to watch over and assist good intentions, assisted mine, so that with my slight strength, and without much effort, I pushed him over a precipice, where I left him — whether dead or alive, I do not know. Then, faster than seemed possible given my terror and exhaustion, I made my way into these mountains, with no other thought or plan than to hide myself in them and escape my father and the men he had sent out searching for me on his orders. I do not know how many months it has been since I came here with that aim. I met a herdsman who took me on as his servant at a place deep in the heart of this Sierra, and all this time I have been working for him as a herder, trying to stay always out in the fields to hide this hair that has now betrayed me when I least expected it. But all my care and effort came to nothing, because my master discovered that I was not a man, and conceived the same vile designs as my servant had; and since fortune does not always provide a remedy for every difficulty, and I had no cliff or ravine at hand down which to throw the master and cure his passion, as I had in the servant's case, I judged it the lesser evil to leave him and hide once more among these crags rather than test my strength or my arguments against him. So, as I say, I went into hiding again, looking for some place where, with sighs and tears, I might beg Heaven to take pity on my misery and grant me the help and strength to escape it — or else let me die in these solitudes, leaving no trace of an unhappy woman who, through no fault of her own, has given people material for gossip and scandal at home and abroad.”

title: Part 1, Chapter 29
paragraphs: Which describes the comical trick and strategy used to rescue our lovesick knight from the harsh penance he had imposed on himself

“That, gentlemen, is the true story of my sad misfortunes. Judge for yourselves now whether the sighs and laments you heard, and the tears that ran from my eyes, didn’t have cause enough — even if I had given way to them far more freely. And once you consider the nature of my disaster, you will see that consolation is pointless, because there is no possible cure for it. All I ask of you — and it is something you can do easily and reasonably — is to show me a place where I can spend my life without being hounded by the fear and dread of being found by the people searching for me. I know the great love my parents have for me would guarantee me a kind welcome from them, but the shame I feel at the mere thought that I cannot stand before them as the person they expect is so overwhelming that I would rather banish myself from their sight forever than look them in the face knowing they were seeing mine stripped of the purity they had every right to expect from me.”

With those words she fell silent, and the color flooding her face showed plainly the pain and shame she was suffering inside. The listeners felt as much pity as amazement at her misfortunes, and the curate was just about to offer her some comfort and advice when Cardenio got there first. “So then, señora,” he said, “you are the beautiful Dorothea, the only daughter of the wealthy Clenardo?” Dorothea was astonished to hear her father’s name, and astonished at the miserable appearance of the man who spoke it — it has already been described how wretchedly Cardenio was dressed. So she said to him:
“And who might you be, brother, that you seem to know my father’s name so well? Because as far as I can remember, I haven’t mentioned it once in the whole story of my misfortunes.”

“I am that unhappy man, señora,” Cardenio replied, “the one who, as you said, Luscinda declared to be her husband. I am the unfortunate Cardenio, and the wrongdoing of the same man who brought you to your present condition has reduced me to the state you see: bare, ragged, deprived of all human comfort and — worse still — of my reason, since I only have it during the brief stretches when Heaven chooses to give it back to me. I, Dorothea, am the man who witnessed the wrong Don Fernando committed, who stood there waiting to hear the ‘Yes’ by which Luscinda declared herself his betrothed. I am the man who didn’t have the courage to see how her fainting fit ended, or what came of the paper found in her bodice, because my heart didn’t have the strength to endure so many blows of bad fortune at once. So I lost all patience and left the house, and after leaving a letter with my host, begging him to put it into Luscinda’s hands, I made my way to these wild solitudes, determined to end here a life I hated as though it were my mortal enemy. But fate refused to take that life from me, and settled for taking my reason instead — perhaps to preserve me for the good luck I have just had in meeting you. Because if what you have told us is true, and I believe it is, it may be that Heaven still has a happier ending in store for both our misfortunes than we expect. Since Luscinda cannot marry Don Fernando — she is mine, as she herself declared so openly — and Don Fernando cannot marry her because he is yours, we can reasonably hope that Heaven will give back to each of us what belongs to us, since it still exists and has not yet been signed away or destroyed. And since we have this consolation, born of no far-fetched hope or wild fantasy, I beg you, señora, to make new resolutions in your better judgment, as I intend to make in mine, and to prepare yourself to look forward to better fortune. I swear to you, on my faith as a gentleman and a Christian, not to desert you until I see you in possession of Don Fernando. And if I cannot persuade him with words to acknowledge what he owes you, I will then use the right my rank as a gentleman gives me and challenge him with just cause for the injury he has done you — setting aside my own wrongs, which I will leave to Heaven to avenge, while here on earth I devote myself to yours.”

Cardenio’s words completed Dorothea’s astonishment. Not knowing how to give thanks for such an offer, she tried to kiss his feet, but Cardenio wouldn’t allow it, and the licentiate answered for them both. He praised Cardenio’s sound reasoning, and then begged, advised, and urged them to come with him to his village, where they could supply themselves with whatever they needed and work out how to find Don Fernando, or return Dorothea to her parents, or do whatever seemed best to them. Cardenio and Dorothea thanked him and accepted his kind offer. The barber, who had been listening to everything attentively and in silence, added some kind words of his own, and with as much goodwill as the curate he offered his services in any way that might be useful to them. He also explained to them briefly the purpose that had brought the two of them there, along with the strange nature of Don Quixote’s madness, and that they were waiting for his squire, who had gone off to look for him. Like the memory of a dream, the quarrel he had had with Don Quixote came back to Cardenio, and he described it to the others — though he couldn’t say what the argument had been about.

At that moment they heard a shout and recognized it as Sancho Panza, who was calling out loudly because he hadn’t found them where he’d left them. They went to meet him, and when they asked about Don Quixote, he told them how he had found him stripped to his shirt, gaunt, yellow, half dead with hunger, and sighing for his lady Dulcinea. Sancho had told him that she ordered him to leave that place and come to El Toboso, where she was waiting for him, but he had answered that he was determined not to appear before her beauty until he had done deeds that made him worthy of her favor. If this kept up, Sancho said, his master ran the risk of never becoming an emperor, as he was duty-bound to do, or even an archbishop, which was the least he could be — so they really needed to think about how to get him away from there. The licentiate told him in reply not to worry: they would get him out of there whether he liked it or not. He then told Cardenio and Dorothea what they had planned for curing Don Quixote, or at least getting him home. At that, Dorothea said she could play the damsel in distress better than the barber could — especially since she had with her the very dress to do it convincingly — and that they could trust her to act the part exactly as the scheme required in every detail, because she had read a great many books of chivalry and knew precisely the style in which afflicted damsels begged favors from knights-errant.

“In that case,” said the curate, “there’s nothing left to do but get started right away. Fortune is clearly declaring itself in our favor, since it has so unexpectedly opened a door for your relief and smoothed the road toward our goal.”

Dorothea then pulled out of her pillowcase a full petticoat of some rich fabric and a green mantle of another fine material, along with a necklace and other jewelry from a little box, and in an instant she had dressed herself up so that she looked like a great and wealthy lady. All this, and more, she said, she had taken from home in case she needed it, though until now she’d had no occasion to use it. They were all delighted by her grace, her bearing, and her beauty, and they declared Don Fernando a man of very poor taste for rejecting such charms. But the one who admired her most was Sancho Panza, because it seemed to him — and it was true — that in all the days of his life he had never seen so lovely a creature. He eagerly asked the curate who this beautiful lady was and what she was doing in this out-of-the-way place.

“This fair lady, brother Sancho,” the curate replied, “is no less a person than the heiress in the direct male line of the great kingdom of Micomicon. She has come in search of your master to beg a favor of him — namely, that he right a wrong, an injury that a wicked giant has done her. And because of the fame as a good knight that your master has won far and wide, this princess has come all the way from Guinea to find him.”

“A lucky search and a lucky find!” said Sancho Panza at this. “Especially if my master has the good luck to right that injury and fix that wrong by killing that son of a bitch of a giant your worship mentions — and kill him he will if he meets him, unless the giant turns out to be a phantom, because my master has no power at all against phantoms. But there’s one thing among others I’d beg of you, señor licentiate: to stop my master from taking a fancy to becoming an archbishop, which is what I’m afraid of, your worship should advise him to marry this princess right away. That way he’ll be disqualified from taking archbishop’s orders, he’ll come into his empire easily, and I’ll get to the end of what I’ve been wanting. I’ve thought the matter over carefully, and as far as I can work out, it won’t do for me if my master becomes an archbishop, because I’m no use to the Church — I’m married. And for a man like me, with a wife and children, to start chasing dispensations so I could hold a paying position in the Church would be endless work. So, señor, it all comes down to my master marrying this lady right away — though I don’t yet know her grace, so I can’t call her by her name.”
“She is called Princess Micomicona,” said the curate, “for since her kingdom is Micomicon, it’s obvious that must be her name.”

“No doubt about that,” Sancho replied. “I’ve known plenty of people who take their name and title from the place they were born, calling themselves Pedro of Alcalá, Juan of Úbeda, or Diego of Valladolid. Maybe over there in Guinea the queens do the same thing and take the names of their kingdoms.”

“That may well be,” said the curate, “and as for your master’s marriage, I’ll do everything in my power to help it along.” Sancho was as pleased by this as the curate was amazed at his simplicity, and at seeing how thoroughly his master’s absurdities had taken hold of his imagination — for Sancho had clearly convinced himself that Don Quixote was going to become an emperor.

By now Dorothea had seated herself on the curate’s mule and the barber had fitted the ox-tail beard to his face, and they told Sancho to lead them to where Don Quixote was, warning him not to let on that he knew either the licentiate or the barber, since his master’s becoming an emperor depended entirely on his not recognizing them. Neither the curate nor Cardenio thought it wise to go along, though — Cardenio in case he reminded Don Quixote of the quarrel they had had, and the curate because his presence wasn’t needed just yet. So they let the others ride on ahead while they followed slowly on foot. The curate didn’t forget to coach Dorothea on how to act, but she told them not to worry: everything would be done exactly as the books of chivalry required and described.

They had gone about three-quarters of a league when they spotted Don Quixote in a wilderness of rocks, dressed by now, though not in his armor. The moment Dorothea saw him and was told by Sancho that this was Don Quixote, she whipped her palfrey forward, with the well-bearded barber following. When they reached him, her squire leapt down from his mule and came forward to lift her down in his arms, and she, dismounting with great ease of manner, went and knelt at Don Quixote’s feet. Although he tried to raise her up, she stayed kneeling and addressed him like this:

“I will not rise from this spot, brave and mighty knight, until your goodness and courtesy grant me a favor — one that will add to the honor and renown of your person, and serve the most desolate and afflicted damsel the sun has ever looked upon. And if the strength of your powerful arm matches the reputation of your immortal fame, then you are bound to help a helpless woman who, drawn by the scent of your famous name, has come from far-off lands to seek your aid in her misfortunes.”
“I will not answer a single word, beautiful lady,” Don Quixote replied, “nor will I hear anything more about your situation, until you rise from the ground.”
“I will not rise, señor,” answered the afflicted damsel, “unless, of your courtesy, the favor I ask is granted to me first.”
“I grant it and accord it,” said Don Quixote, “provided it can be carried out without damage or harm to my king, my country, or the lady who holds the key to my heart and my freedom.”

“It will bring no damage or harm to any of them, my good lord,” said the afflicted damsel — and at this point Sancho Panza sidled up close to his master’s ear and whispered very softly, “Your worship can grant the favor she’s asking with complete safety. It’s nothing at all — just killing one big giant — and the lady asking is the exalted Princess Micomicona, queen of the great kingdom of Micomicon in Ethiopia.”

“Let her be whoever she may,” Don Quixote replied. “I will do what my duty demands and what my conscience tells me, in keeping with the vows of my profession.” Then, turning to the damsel, he said, “Let your great beauty rise, for I grant the favor you would ask of me.”

“Then what I ask,” said the damsel, “is that your magnanimous person come with me at once, wherever I lead you, and that you promise not to take on any other adventure or quest until you have avenged me on a traitor who, against every human and divine law, has usurped my kingdom.”

“I repeat that I grant it,” Don Quixote replied. “And so, lady, from this day forward you can set aside the sadness that weighs on you and let your failing hopes take on new life and strength. With the help of God and of my arm, you will soon see yourself restored to your kingdom and seated on the throne of your ancient and mighty realm, in defiance of every villain who would deny it. And now, hands to the work — for in delay, they say, lies danger.”

The distressed damsel made a stubborn effort to kiss his hands, but Don Quixote, who was in all things a polished and courteous knight, would not allow it on any account. Instead he made her rise and embraced her with great courtesy and politeness, then ordered Sancho to check Rocinante’s girths and to arm him without a moment’s delay. Sancho took down the armor, which was hanging from a tree like a trophy, and after seeing to the girths he had his master armed in an instant. As soon as Don Quixote found himself in his armor, he exclaimed:
“Let us go, in God’s name, to bring help to this great lady.”

The barber was on his knees all this while, taking great pains to hide his laughter and keep his beard from falling off — because if it had fallen, their whole fine scheme might have collapsed. But now, seeing the favor granted and the speed with which Don Quixote was preparing to set out and fulfill it, he stood up and took his lady’s hand, and between the two of them they lifted her onto the mule. Don Quixote then mounted Rocinante, and the barber settled onto his own animal, leaving Sancho to travel on foot — which made him feel the loss of his Dapple all over again, missing him badly now. But he bore it all cheerfully, convinced that his master was now well and truly launched and on the very point of becoming an emperor; he had no doubt at all that Don Quixote would marry this princess and end up at least king of Micomicon. The only thing that troubled him was the thought that this kingdom was in the land of the blacks, and that the people they would give him as vassals would all be black. But his imagination soon found a remedy for that, and he said to himself, “What does it matter to me if my vassals are black? What do I have to do but load them up as cargo and carry them to Spain, where I can sell them and get paid in cash, and use the money to buy some title or some office and live at my ease for the rest of my days? Yes — unless you fall asleep and don’t have the wit or skill to turn things to your advantage and sell three, six, or ten thousand vassals while you’re still talking about it! By God, I’ll move them all, big and small, however I can, and however black they are, I’ll turn them into white or yellow coin. Come on, come on — what a fool I am!” And so he trudged along, so wrapped up in his thoughts and so easy in his mind that he forgot all about the hardship of traveling on foot.

Cardenio and the curate were watching all this from behind some bushes, unsure how to join the group. But the curate, who was quick with schemes, soon hit on a way to manage it: with a pair of scissors he carried in a case, he swiftly cut off Cardenio’s beard, dressed him in a gray jerkin of his own, and gave him a black cloak, leaving himself in his breeches and doublet. Cardenio looked so different from before that he wouldn’t have recognized himself in a mirror. Once this was done — and although the others had ridden on ahead while they were disguising themselves — they easily got out onto the high road before them, because the brambles and rough ground didn’t let the riders move as fast as those on foot. They then stationed themselves on the level ground at the mouth of the Sierra, and the moment Don Quixote and his companions emerged, the curate began studying him very deliberately, as if straining to recognize him. After staring at him a good while, he rushed toward him with open arms, exclaiming, “A happy meeting with the mirror of chivalry, my worthy countryman Don Quixote of La Mancha, the flower and cream of fine breeding, the protector and relief of the distressed, the quintessence of knights-errant!” And as he said it, he clasped the knee of Don Quixote’s left leg in his arms. Don Quixote, astonished by the stranger’s words and behavior, looked at him closely and finally recognized him. Amazed to see him there, he made strenuous efforts to dismount, but the curate wouldn’t allow it, at which Don Quixote said, “Permit me, señor licentiate — it isn’t fitting that I should be on horseback while so reverend a person as your worship goes on foot.”

“I won’t allow it under any circumstances,” said the curate. “Your mightiness must stay on horseback, because it is on horseback that you achieve the greatest deeds and adventures our age has ever seen. As for me, an unworthy priest, it will be quite enough to ride on the haunches of one of the mules belonging to these gentlefolk traveling with your worship, if they have no objection. And I’ll imagine I’m mounted on the steed Pegasus, or on the zebra or charger that carried the famous Moor, Muzaraque, who to this day lies enchanted in the great hill of Zulema, a short distance from the great Complutum.”

“I won’t consent even to that, señor licentiate,” Don Quixote answered. “And I know it will please my lady the princess, out of love for me, to order her squire to give up his mule’s saddle to your worship — he can sit behind, if the animal will carry them both.”

“It will, I’m certain,” said the princess, “and I’m just as certain that I won’t need to give my squire any orders. He is far too courteous and considerate to let a churchman travel on foot when he could ride.”

“So he is,” said the barber, and dismounting at once, he offered his saddle to the curate, who accepted it without needing much persuasion. But unluckily, as the barber was climbing up behind, the mule — a hired one, which is just another way of saying bad-tempered — lifted its hind hooves and let fly a couple of kicks in the air that would have made Master Nicholas wish his whole expedition in search of Don Quixote to the devil if they had caught him in the chest or the head. As it was, they startled him so badly that he tumbled to the ground, paying so little attention to his beard that it fell off, and when he found himself without it, all he could think to do was clap both hands over his face and groan that his teeth had been knocked out. When Don Quixote saw that whole bundle of beard lying detached, with no jaws and no blood, away from the face of the fallen squire, he exclaimed:
“By the living God, this is a great miracle! It has knocked the beard clean off his face and plucked it away, as neatly as if it had been shaved off on purpose.”

The curate, seeing the danger of his scheme being exposed, immediately snatched up the beard and hurried with it over to where Master Nicholas lay, still groaning. Pulling the barber’s head against his chest, he had the beard back on in an instant, murmuring some words over him that, he said, were a special charm for sticking on beards, as they would soon see. As soon as it was fixed, he stepped back, and the squire was as well-bearded and as whole as before. Don Quixote was astonished beyond measure, and he begged the curate to teach him that charm when there was a chance. He was convinced its power must extend beyond the sticking-on of beards — for clearly, where the beard had been torn away, the flesh must have been left mangled and lacerated, and anything that could heal all that had to be good for more than beards.

“And so it is,” said the curate, and he promised to teach it to him at the first opportunity. They then agreed that for the moment the curate should ride, and that the three of them would take turns on the mules until they reached the inn, which was perhaps six leagues from where they were.
So with three mounted — that is, Don Quixote, the princess, and the curate — and three on foot — Cardenio, the barber, and Sancho Panza — Don Quixote said to the damsel:
“Let your highness, my lady, lead the way, wherever pleases you best.” But before she could answer, the licentiate said:
“Toward which kingdom does your ladyship mean to direct our route? Toward Micomicon, perhaps? It must be — either that, or I know very little about kingdoms.”
She, primed on every point, understood that she was supposed to answer “Yes,” so she said, “Yes, señor, my road lies toward that very kingdom.”

“In that case,” said the curate, “we’ll have to pass straight through my village, and from there your worship will take the road to Cartagena, where, with luck, you’ll be able to board a ship. And if the wind is fair and the sea smooth and calm, in somewhat less than nine years you may come within sight of the great lake Meona — I mean Meotides — which lies little more than a hundred days’ journey this side of your highness’s kingdom.”

“Your worship is mistaken, señor,” she said, “because it isn’t even two years since I set out from there, and although I never once had good weather, here I am nonetheless, having come to see the one thing I longed for: my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose fame reached my ears the moment I set foot in Spain and drove me to go in search of him, so I could commend myself to his courtesy and entrust the justice of my cause to the strength of his invincible arm.”

“Enough — no more praise,” Don Quixote broke in, “for I hate flattery of every kind, and even if this isn’t flattery, talk like that still offends my chaste ears. All I will say, señora, is that whatever strength my arm has or doesn’t have, every bit of what it may or may not have shall be devoted to your service until death. But leaving all that to its proper time, I would ask the señor licentiate to tell me what has brought him to these parts — alone, unattended, and so lightly dressed that it fills me with amazement.”

“I’ll answer that briefly,” the curate replied. “You should know, Señor Don Quixote, that Master Nicholas, our friend and barber, and I were on our way to Seville to collect some money that a relative of mine, who went off to the Indies many years ago, had sent me — and no small sum either, for it came to more than sixty thousand pieces of eight, full weight, which is no trifle. As we passed through this area yesterday, we were attacked by four highwaymen, who stripped us of everything, right down to our beards — and they took those off too, so completely that the barber found it necessary to put on a false one. Even this young man here” — and he pointed at Cardenio — “they transformed completely. But the best part is that the story going around the neighborhood says the men who attacked us belong to a band of galley slaves who, people say, were set free almost on this very spot by a man of such valor that, in defiance of the commissary and the guards, he released the whole lot of them. Beyond any doubt, the man must have been out of his mind, or else he is as great a scoundrel as they are — some man without heart or conscience, willing to turn the wolf loose among the sheep, the fox among the hens, the fly into the honey. He has cheated justice and defied his king and lawful master, since he defied his just commands. He has, I say, robbed the galleys of their feet, and stirred up the Holy Brotherhood, which has been quiet for many years; and in the end, he has done a deed that may cost him his soul without bringing his body any gain.” Sancho had told the curate and the barber about the adventure of the galley slaves, which his master had carried off with such glory, and so the curate, in bringing it up, laid it on thick to see what Don Quixote would say or do. The knight changed color at every word, not daring to admit that he himself had been the liberator of those fine people. “These, then,” said the curate, “were the men who robbed us — and may God in His mercy pardon the one who kept them from going to the punishment they deserved.”

title: Part 1, Chapter 30
paragraphs: About the cleverness shown by the fair Dorothea, with other pleasant and entertaining matters

The curate had hardly finished speaking when Sancho said, "On my faith, then, señor licentiate, the one who did that deed was my master; and it wasn't for lack of my warning him beforehand and telling him to be careful, that it was a sin to set them free, since they were all on the march there because they were special scoundrels."

"Blockhead!" said Don Quixote at this. "It is no business or concern of knights-errant to inquire whether the persons in distress, chained, or oppressed whom they meet on the high roads go that way and suffer in that condition because of their faults or because of their misfortunes. The only thing that concerns us is to help them as people in need, with regard to their suffering and not to their crimes. I came across a chaplet — a string of miserable, unfortunate people — and did for them what my sense of duty demands, and as for the rest, let it be as it may. Whoever objects to it — saving the sacred dignity of the señor licentiate and his honoured person — I say he knows little about chivalry and lies like a whoreson villain, and I will make him understand this to the fullest extent with my sword." And with that he settled himself in his stirrups and pressed down his morion — for the barber's basin, which to him was Mambrino's helmet, he carried hanging at the saddle-bow until he could repair the damage the galley slaves had done to it.

Dorothea, who was shrewd and quick-witted, by now thoroughly understood Don Quixote's crazy turn and that everyone except Sancho Panza was playing along; so as not to be outdone, when she saw his irritation she said to him, "Sir Knight, remember the favour you have promised me, and that under its terms you must not engage in any other adventure, however urgent. Calm yourself; if the licentiate had known that the galley slaves had been set free by that unconquered arm, he would have sewed up his mouth three times over, or even bitten his tongue three times before he said a word that smacked of disrespect to your worship."
"That I swear heartily," said the curate, "and I would even have plucked out a whisker of my moustache."

"I will hold my peace, señora," said Don Quixote, "and curb the natural anger that had risen in my chest, and I will proceed in peace and quiet until I have fulfilled my promise. But in return for this restraint I entreat you to tell me — if you have no objection — what is the nature of your trouble, and how many, who, and what kind of persons they are from whom I am to demand satisfaction and on whom I am to take vengeance on your behalf."
"I'll do that with all my heart," replied Dorothea, "if it doesn't tire you to listen to miseries and misfortunes."

"It will not tire me, señora," said Don Quixote. To which Dorothea replied, "Well, if that's so, give me your attention." As soon as she said this, Cardenio and the barber drew close to her side, eager to hear what kind of story the quick-witted Dorothea would invent for herself; and Sancho did the same, for he was as much taken in by her as his master. She settled herself comfortably in the saddle, and with the help of a few coughs and other preliminaries to give herself time to think, she began with great spirit in this fashion.

"First of all, sirs, I would have you know that my name is —" and here she stopped for a moment, because she'd forgotten the name the curate had given her. But he came to her rescue, seeing her difficulty, and said, "It's no wonder, señora, that your highness should be confused and embarrassed when telling the tale of your misfortunes; such afflictions often have the effect of depriving the sufferers of memory, so that they cannot even remember their own names, as is the case now with your ladyship, who has forgotten that she is called the Princess Micomicona, lawful heiress of the great kingdom of Micomicon. With this cue your highness may now recall to your sorrowful memory everything you wish to tell us."

"That is the truth," said the damsel, "but I think from here on I shall need no further prompting, and I shall bring my true story safely into port. Here it is. The king my father, who was called Tinacrio the Sapient, was very learned in what they call the magic arts, and by his craft he became aware that my mother, who was called Queen Jaramilla, was to die before he did, and that soon after he too was to depart this life, and I would be left an orphan without father or mother. But all this, he declared, did not grieve or distress him as much as the certain knowledge that a prodigious giant — the lord of a great island close to our kingdom, Pandafilando of the Scowl by name (for it's said that, although his eyes are properly placed and straight, he always looks sideways as if he squinted, and he does it out of malice, to strike fear and terror into those he looks at) — that he knew, I say, that this giant, on becoming aware of my orphaned condition, would overrun my kingdom with a mighty force and strip me of everything, not leaving me even a small village to shelter in; but that I could avoid all this ruin and misfortune if I were willing to marry him. However, as far as he could see, he never expected me to consent to such an unequal marriage; and he spoke no more than the truth in this, since it has never entered my mind to marry that giant, or any other, however great or enormous he may be. My father said, too, that when he was dead and I saw Pandafilando about to invade my kingdom, I was not to wait and try to defend myself, for that would be the ruin of me; instead I should leave the kingdom entirely open to him if I wished to avoid the death and total destruction of my good and loyal vassals, since there would be no way of defending myself against the giant's devilish power. He told me I should at once set out with some of my followers for Spain, where I would find relief in my distress on finding a certain knight-errant whose fame by then would extend over the whole kingdom, and who would be called, if I remember rightly, Don Azote or Don Gigote."
"He must have said 'Don Quixote,' señora," Sancho put in at this, "otherwise known as the Knight of the Rueful Countenance."

"That's it," said Dorothea. "He said, moreover, that the knight would be tall of stature and lank of feature; and that on his right side under the left shoulder, or thereabouts, he would have a grey mole with hairs like bristles."
On hearing this, Don Quixote said to his squire, "Here, Sancho my son, lend a hand and help me strip, because I want to see if I'm the knight that sage king foretold."
"What does your worship want to strip for?" said Dorothea.
"To see if I have the mole your father spoke of," answered Don Quixote.
"There's no need to strip," said Sancho. "I know your worship has just such a mole in the middle of your backbone, which is the mark of a strong man."

"That's enough," said Dorothea. "With friends we must not look too closely into trifles, and whether it's on the shoulder or on the backbone matters little; what counts is that there's a mole, wherever it may be, since it's all the same flesh. No doubt my good father hit the truth in every particular, and I have made a lucky hit in commending myself to Don Quixote — for he is the one my father spoke of, since the features of his face correspond with those given to this knight by that wide fame he has earned not only in Spain but in all La Mancha. I had hardly landed at Osuna when I heard such accounts of his exploits that at once my heart told me he was the very one I had come in search of."
"But how did you land at Osuna, señora," asked Don Quixote, "when it's not a seaport?"
Before Dorothea could reply, the curate cut in and said, "The princess means that after she had landed at Málaga, the first place where she heard of your worship was Osuna."
"That is what I meant to say," said Dorothea.
"And that would be only natural," said the curate. "Will your majesty please go on?"

"There's nothing more to add," said Dorothea, "except that in finding Don Quixote I have had such good fortune that I already count and consider myself queen and mistress of all my domains, since out of his courtesy and magnanimity he has granted me the favour of accompanying me wherever I may lead him — which will be only to bring him face to face with Pandafilando of the Scowl, so that he may kill him and restore to me what has been unjustly taken from me. All this must come about satisfactorily, since my good father Tinacrio the Sapient foretold it; he also left it stated in writing, in Chaldee or Greek characters (for I cannot read them), that if this predicted knight, after cutting the giant's throat, should be willing to marry me, I was to offer myself at once without protest as his lawful wife, and yield him possession of my kingdom together with my person."
"What do you think now, friend Sancho?" said Don Quixote at this. "Do you hear that? Didn't I tell you so? Look — we already have a kingdom to govern and a queen to marry!"

"On my oath that's so," said Sancho, "and bad luck to anyone who won't marry after slitting Señor Pandahilado's windpipe! And then, how ill-favoured the queen is! I wish the fleas in my bed were that kind!"

And with that he cut a couple of capers in the air with every sign of extreme satisfaction, then ran to seize the bridle of Dorothea's mule, and pulling it up he fell on his knees before her, begging her to give him her hand to kiss in acknowledgement that he accepted her as his queen and mistress. Which of the bystanders could have helped laughing to see the madness of the master and the simplicity of the servant? Dorothea therefore gave him her hand and promised to make him a great lord in her kingdom, when Heaven should be good enough to allow her to recover and enjoy it; for which Sancho returned his thanks in words that set them all laughing again.

"This, sirs," Dorothea continued, "is my story. It only remains to tell you that of all the attendants I took with me from my kingdom, I have none left except this well-bearded squire, for all the others were drowned in a great tempest we encountered when in sight of port. He and I came to land on a couple of planks as if by a miracle; and indeed the whole course of my life is a miracle and a mystery, as you may have noticed. If I have been over-detailed about any of it, or not as precise as I should have been, blame it on what the licentiate said at the beginning of my tale — that constant and excessive troubles deprive the sufferers of their memory."

"They shall not deprive me of mine, exalted and worthy princess," said Don Quixote, "however great and unparalleled those I endure in your service may be. Here I confirm anew the favour I have promised you, and I swear to go with you to the ends of the earth until I find myself in the presence of your fierce enemy, whose haughty head I trust by the strength of my arm to cut off with the edge of this — I will not say good sword, thanks to Ginés de Pasamonte who carried off mine" — (this he muttered between his teeth, and then went on) — "and when it has been cut off and you have been put in peaceful possession of your realm, it shall be left to your own decision to dispose of your person as may please you most; for so long as my memory is occupied, my will enslaved, and my understanding enthralled by her — I say no more — it's impossible for me even for a moment to contemplate marriage, even with a Phoenix."
His master's last words about not wanting to marry were so disagreeable to Sancho that, raising his voice, he exclaimed with great irritation:

"By my oath, Señor Don Quixote, you are not in your right senses; how can your worship possibly refuse to marry such an exalted princess as this? Do you think Fortune will offer you behind every stone a piece of luck like this one? Is my lady Dulcinea more beautiful, perhaps? Not she; not half as beautiful; I'll even go so far as to say she doesn't come up to the shoe of this one here. A poor chance I have of getting that county I'm waiting for, if your worship goes hunting for delicacies at the bottom of the sea. In the devil's name, marry, marry, and take this kingdom that comes to hand without any trouble; and when you're king, make me a marquis or governor of a province, and the rest can go to the devil."

When Don Quixote heard such blasphemies uttered against his lady Dulcinea, he could not bear it, and lifting his pike, without saying anything to Sancho or uttering a word, he gave him two such whacks that he knocked him to the ground; and if Dorothea hadn't shouted at him to spare him, he would no doubt have taken his life on the spot.

"Do you think," he said to him after a pause, "you scurvy clown, that you are always to be interfering with me, and that you are always to be giving offence and I always to be pardoning? Don't get any such idea, you impious scoundrel — for that's beyond all doubt what you are, since you've set your tongue going against the peerless Dulcinea. Don't you know, you lout, vagabond, beggar, that were it not for the strength she pours into my arm I wouldn't have the power to kill a flea? Tell me, scoffer with a viper's tongue, what do you think has won this kingdom and cut off this giant's head and made you a marquis (for I count all this as already done and decided) but the might of Dulcinea, using my arm as the instrument of her achievements? She fights in me and conquers in me, and I live and breathe in her, and owe my life and being to her. O whoreson scoundrel, how ungrateful you are! You see yourself raised from the dust of the earth to be a titled lord, and the return you make for so great a benefit is to speak ill of her who has conferred it on you!"
Sancho was not so stunned that he didn't hear everything his master said, and getting up with some quickness he ran to place himself behind Dorothea's palfrey, and from there he said to his master:

"Tell me, señor — if your worship is resolved not to marry this great princess, it's plain the kingdom won't be yours; and if it's not, how can you bestow favours on me? That's what I complain of. Let your worship at any rate marry this queen, now that we have her here as if showered down from heaven, and afterwards you can go back to my lady Dulcinea; there must have been kings in the world who kept mistresses. As to beauty, I have nothing to do with that; to tell the truth, I like them both, though I have never seen the lady Dulcinea."
"What? Never seen her, you blasphemous traitor!" exclaimed Don Quixote. "Didn't you just now bring me a message from her?"
"I mean," said Sancho, "that I did not see her at such leisure that I could take particular notice of her beauty, or of her charms piece by piece; but taken in the lump, I like her."
"Now I forgive you," said Don Quixote, "and you forgive me the injury I have done you, for our first impulses are not in our control."
"That I see," replied Sancho, "and with me the wish to speak is always the first impulse, and I cannot help saying, at least once, whatever's on the tip of my tongue."
"All the same, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "watch what you say, because the pitcher goes so often to the well — I need say no more."
"Well, well," said Sancho, "God is in heaven, and he sees all the tricks, and will judge who does more harm — me by not speaking right, or your worship by not doing it."

"That's enough," said Dorothea. "Run, Sancho, kiss your lord's hand and beg his pardon, and from now on be more careful with your praise and abuse; and say nothing in disparagement of that lady of El Toboso, of whom I know nothing except that I am her servant. Put your trust in God, and you'll not fail to obtain some position that will let you live like a prince."

Sancho came forward hanging his head and begged his master's hand, which Don Quixote presented with dignity, giving him his blessing as soon as he had kissed it. He then told him to come on ahead a little, as he had questions to ask and matters of great importance to discuss with him. Sancho obeyed, and when the two had gone some distance ahead, Don Quixote said to him, "Since your return I have had no opportunity or time to ask you many particulars concerning your mission and the answer you brought back; now that chance has granted us the time and opportunity, don't deny me the happiness you can give me with such good news."
"Let your worship ask whatever you want," answered Sancho, "and I'll find a way out of all of it, as I found a way in; but I beg you, señor, not to be so vengeful in future."
"Why do you say that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"I say it," he returned, "because those blows just now were more for the quarrel the devil stirred up between us the other night than for what I said against my lady Dulcinea, whom I love and revere as I would a relic — though there's nothing relic-like about her — merely as something belonging to your worship."
"Say no more on that subject, for your life, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for it displeases me. I have already pardoned you for it, and you know the common saying, 'for a fresh sin a fresh penance.'"

While this was going on they saw, coming along the road they were following, a man mounted on an ass. When he came close he seemed to be a gypsy; but Sancho Panza, whose eyes and heart were wherever he saw asses, had no sooner laid eyes on the man than he knew him for Ginés de Pasamonte; and by the thread of the gypsy he got at the ball — his ass. For it was, in fact, Dapple who was carrying Pasamonte, who to escape recognition and sell the ass had disguised himself as a gypsy, being able to speak the gypsy language, and many others, as well as if they were his own. Sancho saw him and recognised him, and the instant he did so he shouted at him, "Ginesillo, you thief, give up my treasure, release my life, don't trouble yourself with my repose, leave my ass, leave my delight, get out, scoundrel, get gone, thief, and give back what isn't yours!"

There was no need for so many words or curses, for at the first one Ginés jumped down, and at a sprinter's pace made off and got clear of them all. Sancho hurried to his Dapple, and embracing him said, "How have you been, my treasure, Dapple of my eyes, my comrade?" — all the while kissing him and caressing him as if he were a human being. The ass held his peace, and let himself be kissed and caressed by Sancho without answering a single word. The others all came up and congratulated him on having found Dapple, Don Quixote especially, who told him that despite this he would not cancel the order for the three ass-colts; for which Sancho thanked him.

While the two had been going along talking like this, the curate remarked to Dorothea that she had shown great cleverness, both in the story itself and in its conciseness, and in how closely it resembled the kind found in the books of chivalry. She said she had often amused herself reading them, but that she didn't know the location of the provinces or seaports, and so she had said at random that she had landed at Osuna.

"So I saw," said the curate, "and that's why I made haste to say what I did, by which it was all set right. But isn't it a strange thing to see how readily this unhappy gentleman believes all these fictions and lies, simply because they're in the style and manner of the absurdities in his books?"
"It is," said Cardenio, "and so uncommon and unparalleled that if anyone tried to invent and concoct it as fiction, I doubt there's any wit keen enough to imagine it."

"But another strange thing about it," said the curate, "is that, apart from the silly things this worthy gentleman says in connection with his obsession, on any other subject he can discuss things in a perfectly rational way, showing that his mind is quite clear and composed. So provided his chivalry is not touched on, no one would take him for anything but a man of thoroughly sound understanding."
While they were having this conversation, Don Quixote continued his with Sancho, saying:

"Friend Panza, let's forgive and forget our quarrels, and now tell me, putting aside any anger or irritation, where, how, and when did you find Dulcinea? What was she doing? What did you say to her? What did she answer? How did she look when she was reading my letter? Who copied it out for you? — and everything in the matter that seems to you worth knowing, asking, and learning. Neither add to it nor falsify to please me, nor cut it short and deprive me of any of it."
"Señor," replied Sancho, "if the truth is to be told, nobody copied out the letter for me, because I carried no letter at all."

"It's as you say," said Don Quixote, "for the notebook in which I wrote it I found in my own possession two days after you left, which gave me very great vexation, since I had no idea what you would do on finding yourself without any letter; I felt sure you would come back from the spot where you first noticed it was missing."

"I should have done that," said Sancho, "if I hadn't got it by heart when your worship read it to me — so that I repeated it to a sacristan, who copied it out from hearing it, so exactly that he said in all the days of his life, though he had read many a letter of excommunication, he had never seen or read so pretty a letter as that one."
"And have you got it still in your memory, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"No, señor," replied Sancho, "because as soon as I had repeated it, seeing there was no further use for it, I set about forgetting it; and if I recall any of it, it's that bit about 'Scrubbing' — I mean to say 'Sovereign Lady' — and the end, 'Yours till death, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance;' and between those two I put more than three hundred 'my souls' and 'my life's' and 'my eyes.'"

title: Part 1, Chapter 31
paragraphs: About the delightful conversation between Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, his squire, together with other incidents

"None of that is unsatisfactory to me," said Don Quixote. "Go on; you reached her — and what was that queen of beauty doing? Surely you found her stringing pearls, or embroidering some device in gold thread for this her enslaved knight."
"I didn't," said Sancho. "I found her winnowing two bushels of wheat in the yard of her house."
"Then depend on it," said Don Quixote, "the grains of that wheat were pearls when touched by her hands. And did you look, friend? Was it white wheat or brown?"
"It was neither — it was red," said Sancho.

"Then I promise you," said Don Quixote, "that, winnowed by her hands, beyond a doubt the bread it made was of the whitest. But go on; when you gave her my letter, did she kiss it? Did she place it on her head? Did she perform any ceremony worthy of it, or what did she do?"

"When I went to give it to her," replied Sancho, "she was hard at it, swaying from side to side with a lot of wheat she had in the sieve, and she said to me, 'Lay the letter, friend, on top of that sack, for I can't read it until I've finished sifting all this.'"

"Discreet lady!" said Don Quixote. "That was so she could read it at her leisure and enjoy it. Go on, Sancho — while she was busy with her work, what conversation did she hold with you? What did she ask about me, and what did you answer? Hurry up; tell me everything, and let not an atom be left in the ink-bottle."

"She asked me nothing," said Sancho. "But I told her how your worship was left doing penance in her service, naked from the waist up, in among these mountains like a savage, sleeping on the ground, not eating bread off a tablecloth nor combing your beard, weeping and cursing your fortune."

"In saying I cursed my fortune you said wrong," said Don Quixote. "Rather, I bless it, and shall bless it all the days of my life for having made me worthy of aspiring to love so lofty a lady as Dulcinea del Toboso."
"And so lofty she is," said Sancho, "that she stands more than a hand's-breadth taller than I am."
"What? Sancho," said Don Quixote, "did you measure yourself against her?"
"I measured this way," said Sancho. "Going to help her put a sack of wheat on the back of an ass, we came so close together that I could see she stood more than a good palm over me."

"Well!" said Don Quixote. "And does she not in truth accompany and adorn this stature with a thousand million charms of mind? But one thing you will not deny, Sancho — when you came close to her, did you not catch a Sabaean fragrance, an aromatic scent, a — I know not what — something delicious that I cannot name; a redolence, an exhalation, as if you were in the shop of some fine glover?"
"All I can say," said Sancho, "is that I did catch a little odour, something goatish — it must have been that she was all in a sweat with hard work."

"It cannot be that," said Don Quixote. "You must have had a cold in the head, or smelled yourself; for I know well what would be the scent of that rose among thorns, that lily of the field, that dissolved amber."
"Maybe so," replied Sancho. "There often comes from me that same odour which then seemed to me to come from her grace the lady Dulcinea; but that's no wonder — one devil is like another."
"Well then," Don Quixote continued, "now she has finished sifting the corn and sent it to the mill — what did she do when she read the letter?"

"As for the letter," said Sancho, "she didn't read it, because she said she could neither read nor write. Instead she tore it up into small pieces, saying she didn't want to let anyone read it for fear her secrets might be known in the village, and that what I had told her by word of mouth about the love your worship bore her, and the extraordinary penance you were doing for her sake, was enough; and, to make an end of it, she told me to tell your worship that she kissed your hands, and that she had a greater desire to see you than to write to you; and that therefore she begged and commanded you, on sight of this present message, to come out of these thickets and have done with carrying on absurdities, and to set out at once for El Toboso — unless something more important came up — for she had a great longing to see your worship. She laughed a great deal when I told her how your worship was called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance. I asked her if that Biscayan from the other day had been there, and she told me he had, and that he was an honest fellow; I asked her too about the galley slaves, but she said she had not seen any as yet."

"So far so good," said Don Quixote. "But tell me, what jewel did she give you on taking your leave, in return for your news of me? It's a customary and ancient practice with knights and ladies errant to give the squires, damsels, or dwarfs who bring tidings of their ladies to the knights, or of their knights to the ladies, some rich jewel as a reward for good news and acknowledgement of the message."

"That sounds very likely," said Sancho, "and a good custom too, to my mind; but that must have been in days gone by, because nowadays it seems the custom is to give only a piece of bread and cheese — which is what my lady Dulcinea gave me over the top of the yard-wall when I took leave of her. And, for added proof, it was sheep's-milk cheese."

"She is generous in the extreme," said Don Quixote, "and if she didn't give you a jewel of gold, no doubt it was because she didn't have one to hand to give you; but sleeves are good after Easter — I shall see her and all will be put right. But do you know what amazes me, Sancho? It seems to me you must have gone and come through the air, since you took little more than three days to go to El Toboso and return, even though it's more than thirty leagues from here to there. From which I'm inclined to think that the sage magician who is my friend, and watches over my interests (for there must necessarily be such a one, or else I wouldn't be a true knight-errant) — that this same magician, I say, must have helped you travel without your knowing it. Because some of these sages will catch up a knight-errant sleeping in his bed, and without his knowing how or in what way it happened, he wakes up the next day more than a thousand leagues from where he went to sleep. If it weren't for this, knights-errant could not come to one another's aid in peril, as they do at every turn. A knight, say, is fighting in the mountains of Armenia with some dragon, or fierce serpent, or another knight, and gets the worst of the battle, and is at the point of death; but when he least expects it, there appears across from him on a cloud, or chariot of fire, another knight, a friend of his, who just before had been in England, who takes his side and saves him from death; and at night he finds himself in his own quarters, supping very much to his satisfaction; and yet from one place to the other will have been two or three thousand leagues. All this is done by the craft and skill of the sage enchanters who take care of those valiant knights; so, friend Sancho, I have no difficulty in believing that you may have gone from this place to El Toboso and returned in such a short time, since, as I have said, some friendly sage must have carried you through the air without your noticing."
"That must have been it," said Sancho, "because Rocinante really did go like a gypsy's ass with quicksilver in his ears."

"Quicksilver!" said Don Quixote. "Yes, and what is more, a legion of devils — folk that can travel and make others travel without weariness, exactly as the whim takes them. But setting this aside, what do you think I should do about my lady's command to go and see her? Because, while I feel I am bound to obey her order, I feel too that I'm prevented by the boon I have granted to the princess accompanying us, and the law of chivalry compels me to honour my word in preference to my inclination. On the one hand, the desire to see my lady pursues and harasses me; on the other, my solemn promise and the glory I'll win in this enterprise urge and call to me. But what I think I'll do is travel with all speed and reach the place where this giant is as soon as possible, and on my arrival I'll cut off his head and settle the princess peacefully in her realm, and then immediately return to behold the light that illuminates my senses, to whom I will make such excuses that she'll be led to approve of my delay, since she will see that it entirely tends to increase her glory and fame — for all that I have won, am winning, or shall win by arms in this life, comes to me by the favour she extends to me, and because I am hers."

"Oh, what a sad state your worship's brains are in!" said Sancho. "Tell me, señor, do you mean to travel all that way for nothing, and to let slip and lose so rich and grand a match as this — where they give as a dowry a kingdom that in sober truth I have heard is more than twenty thousand leagues around, and abounds with everything necessary to support human life, and is bigger than Portugal and Castile put together? Peace, for the love of God! Blush for what you've said, and take my advice, and forgive me, and marry at once in the first village where there's a curate; if not, here's our licentiate, who will do the job beautifully. Remember, I'm old enough to give advice, and this advice comes pat to the purpose — for a sparrow in the hand is better than a vulture on the wing, and he who has the good in his hand and chooses the bad has no right to complain when the good doesn't come to him."

"Look here, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "If you're advising me to marry so that immediately upon killing the giant I'll become king and be able to confer favours on you and give you what I have promised — let me tell you I shall be able to satisfy your desires very easily without marrying; for before going into battle I'll make it a condition that, if I come out of it victorious, even if I don't marry, they shall give me a portion of the kingdom so I may bestow it on whomever I choose; and when they give it to me, on whom would you have me bestow it but you?"

"That's plain speaking," said Sancho. "But let your worship take care to choose it on the seacoast, so that if I don't like the life, I can ship off my black vassals and deal with them as I've said. Don't mind going to see my lady Dulcinea now — go and kill this giant and let's finish off this business; for by God it strikes me it will be a matter of great honour and great profit."

"I hold that you're right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and I'll take your advice about accompanying the princess before going to see Dulcinea. But I caution you not to say anything to anyone, including those who are with us, about what we have considered and discussed. Since Dulcinea is so discreet that she does not want her thoughts known, it is not right that I, or anyone on my behalf, should disclose them."

"Well then, if that's the case," said Sancho, "how is it that your worship makes everyone you defeat by your arm go and present themselves before my lady Dulcinea — which is the same as signing your name to it that you love her and are her lover? And since those who go must kneel before her and say they come from your worship to submit themselves to her, how can the thoughts of either of you be hidden?"

"Oh, how foolish and simple you are!" said Don Quixote. "Don't you see, Sancho, that this only adds to her greater glory? You must know that, according to our way of thinking in chivalry, it's a high honour to a lady to have many knights-errant in her service, whose thoughts go no further than serving her for her own sake, and who look for no other reward for their great and true devotion than that she should be willing to accept them as her knights."

"It's with that kind of love," said Sancho, "that I have heard preachers say we ought to love our Lord — for himself alone, without being moved by the hope of glory or the fear of punishment; though for my part, I would rather love and serve him for what he could do."
"The devil take you for a clown!" said Don Quixote. "What shrewd things you say at times! One would think you'd studied."
"In faith, then, I cannot even read."

Master Nicholas called out to them at this point to wait a while, as they wanted to stop and drink at a little spring there was nearby. Don Quixote drew up, much to the satisfaction of Sancho, who by this time was weary of telling so many lies and afraid his master would catch him tripping; for though he knew that Dulcinea was a peasant girl of El Toboso, he had never seen her in his life. Cardenio had now put on the clothes Dorothea was wearing when they found her, and though they weren't very good, they were far better than the ones he took off. They dismounted together by the side of the spring, and with what the curate had provided himself with at the inn they appeased, though not very well, the keen appetite they had all brought with them.

While they were so occupied, a youth happened to come by on his way along the road; stopping to examine the party at the spring, the next moment he ran to Don Quixote and, clasping him around the legs, began to weep freely, saying, "Oh, señor, do you not know me? Look at me well; I am that lad Andrés that your worship released from the oak-tree where I was tied."

Don Quixote recognised him, and taking his hand, he turned to those present and said: "So that your worships may see how important it is to have knights-errant in the world to redress the wrongs and injuries done by tyrannical and wicked men, I tell you that some days ago, passing through a wood, I heard cries and pitiful complaints as of a person in pain and distress; I immediately hurried, driven by my bounden duty, to the quarter from which the plaintive sounds seemed to come, and I found this lad now before you tied to an oak — which I rejoice at in my heart, for his testimony will not permit me to depart from the truth in any particular. He was, I say, tied to an oak, naked from the waist up, and a clown, whom I later found to be his master, was scoring him with lashes from the reins of his mare. As soon as I saw him I asked the reason for so cruel a flogging. The boor replied that he was flogging him because he was his servant, and because of carelessness that proceeded more from dishonesty than stupidity; at which this boy said, 'Señor, he flogs me only because I ask for my wages.' The master made I-don't-know-what speeches and explanations, which, though I listened, I didn't accept. In short, I forced the clown to unbind him and to swear he would take him with him and pay him real by real, and perfumed into the bargain. Isn't that all true, Andrés my son? Didn't you notice with what authority I commanded him, and with what humility he promised to do all I enjoined, specified, and required of him? Answer without hesitation; tell these gentlemen what took place, so they may see that it's as great an advantage as I say to have knights-errant abroad."
"All that your worship has said is quite true," answered the lad, "but the end of the business turned out just the opposite of what your worship supposes."
"What? The opposite?" said Don Quixote. "Did the clown not pay you, then?"

"Not only did he not pay me," replied the lad, "but as soon as your worship had passed out of the wood and we were alone, he tied me up again to the same oak and gave me a fresh flogging that left me like a flayed Saint Bartholomew; and every stroke he gave me he followed up with some joke or jeer about having made a fool of your worship — and but for the pain I was in, I should have laughed at the things he said. In short, he left me in such a state that I have been until now in a hospital getting cured of the injuries that rascally clown inflicted on me then — for which your worship is to blame. Because if you had gone your own way and not come where there was no call for you, nor meddled in other people's affairs, my master would have been content with giving me one or two dozen lashes and would then have untied me and paid me what he owed me. But when your worship abused him so out of all measure and gave him so many hard words, his anger was kindled; and since he couldn't take revenge on you, as soon as he saw you had left him, the storm burst on me in such a way that I feel I shall never be a man again."

"The mischief," said Don Quixote, "lay in my going away; for I should not have gone until I had seen you paid. Because I ought to have known well by long experience that there is no clown who will keep his word if he finds it doesn't suit him to keep it. But you remember, Andrés, that I swore if he didn't pay you I would go and seek him and find him, even if he hid himself in the whale's belly."
"That's true," said Andrés, "but it was no use."

"You shall see now whether it's of use or not," said Don Quixote. And so saying, he got up hastily and told Sancho to bridle Rocinante, who was grazing while they ate. Dorothea asked him what he meant to do. He replied that he meant to go in search of this clown and chastise him for such wicked conduct, and see Andrés paid to the last maravedí, in spite of all the clowns in the world. To which she replied that he must remember that, in accordance with his promise, he could not undertake any enterprise until he had finished hers; and that since he knew this better than anyone, he should restrain his ardour until his return from her kingdom.
"That's true," said Don Quixote, "and Andrés must have patience until my return, as you say, señora; but I once more swear and promise not to stop until I have seen him avenged and paid."

"I have no faith in those oaths," said Andrés. "I would rather have something now to help me get to Seville than all the revenges in the world. If you have anything to eat that I can take with me, give it to me, and God be with your worship and all knights-errant; and may their errands turn out as well for themselves as they have for me."
Sancho took a piece of bread and another of cheese out of his store and, giving them to the lad, said, "Here, take this, brother Andrés, since we all of us have a share in your misfortune."
"Why — what share have you got?"

"This share of bread and cheese I'm giving you," answered Sancho, "and God knows whether I shall feel the want of it myself or not. I'll have you know, friend, that we squires to knights-errant have to bear a great deal of hunger and hard fortune, and other things too more easily felt than told."

Andrés seized his bread and cheese, and seeing that nobody gave him anything more, bent his head and took to the road, as the saying is. Before leaving, however, he said, "For the love of God, sir knight-errant, if you ever meet me again, even if you see them cutting me to pieces, give me no aid or help, but leave me to my misfortune — which will not be so great but that a greater will come to me by being helped by your worship, on whom, and on all the knights-errant ever born, God send his curse."

Don Quixote was getting up to chastise him, but he took to his heels at such a pace that no one tried to follow him; and mightily crestfallen was Don Quixote at Andrés's story, and the others had to take great care to restrain their laughter so as not to put him entirely out of countenance.

title: Part 1, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About what befell Don Quixote's party at the inn

Their tasty meal finished, they saddled up at once, and without any adventure worth mentioning they reached the next day the inn — the object of Sancho Panza's fear and dread; but though he would rather not have gone in, there was no help for it. The landlady, the landlord, their daughter, and Maritornes, when they saw Don Quixote and Sancho coming, went out to welcome them with signs of hearty satisfaction, which Don Quixote received with dignity and gravity; and he told them to make up a better bed for him than the last time. To which the landlady replied that if he paid better than he did the last time, she would give him one fit for a prince. Don Quixote said he would, so they made up a tolerable one for him in the same garret as before; and he lay down at once, being sorely shaken and in want of sleep.
No sooner was the door shut on him than the landlady made for the barber, and seizing him by the beard, said:

"By my faith, you're not going to make a beard of my tail any longer; you must give me back my tail, for it's a shame the way that thing of my husband's is left tossing about on the floor — I mean the comb I used to stick in my good tail."

But for all she tugged at it, the barber would not give it up until the licentiate told him to let her have it, since there was no further need for that stratagem now: he could declare himself and appear in his own character and tell Don Quixote that he had fled to this inn when those thieves the galley slaves robbed him; and if he asked for the princess's squire, they could tell him that she had sent him on ahead to give notice to the people of her kingdom that she was coming, and bringing with her the deliverer of them all. At this the barber cheerfully restored the tail to the landlady, and at the same time they returned all the other items they had borrowed to bring about Don Quixote's deliverance. All the people of the inn were struck with astonishment at the beauty of Dorothea, and even at the comely figure of the shepherd Cardenio. The curate had them get ready such food as there was in the inn, and the landlord, in hope of better payment, served them up a tolerably good dinner. All this time Don Quixote was asleep, and they thought it best not to wake him, since sleeping would now do him more good than eating.

While at dinner, the company consisting of the landlord, his wife, their daughter, Maritornes, and all the travellers, they discussed the strange craze of Don Quixote and the way he had been found; and the landlady told them what had taken place between him and the carrier; and then, looking round to see if Sancho was there, when she saw he wasn't, she gave them the whole story of his blanketing, which they received with no little amusement. But when the curate observed that it was the books of chivalry Don Quixote had read that had turned his brain, the landlord said:

"I can't understand how that can be, for in truth to my mind there's no better reading in the world; I have here two or three of them, with other writings that are the very life — not only of me but of plenty of others. Because when it's harvest time, the reapers flock here on holidays, and there's always one among them who can read, and he takes up one of these books, and we gather round him, thirty or more of us, and stay listening to him with a delight that makes our grey hairs grow young again. At least I can say for myself that when I hear of what furious and terrible blows the knights deliver, the longing seizes me to do the same, and I would like to be hearing about them night and day."

"And so would I," said the landlady, "because I never have a quiet moment in my house except when you're listening to someone reading — for then you're so taken up that for the time being you forget to scold."

"That's true," said Maritornes; "and, faith, I greatly enjoy hearing these things too, for they are very pretty — especially when they describe some lady or other in the arms of her knight under the orange trees, and the duenna keeping watch for them is half dead with envy and fright; all this, I say, is as good as honey."
"And you, what do you think, young lady?" said the curate, turning to the landlord's daughter.

"I really don't know, señor," she said. "I listen too, and to tell the truth, though I don't understand it, I like hearing it. But it's not the blows that my father likes that I like — it's the laments the knights utter when they are separated from their ladies; and indeed they sometimes make me weep with the pity I feel for them."
"Then you would console them if it were for you they wept, young lady?" said Dorothea.

"I don't know what I should do," said the girl. "I only know that there are some of those ladies so cruel that they call their knights tigers and lions and a thousand other foul names; and Jesus! — I don't know what sort of folk they can be, so unfeeling and heartless that, rather than bestow a glance on a worthy man, they leave him to die or go mad. I don't know what's the good of such prudery; if it's for honour's sake, why not marry them? That's all they want."
"Hush, child," said the landlady. "It seems to me you know a great deal about these things, and it's not fitting for girls to know or talk so much."
"Since the gentleman asked me, I couldn't help answering him," said the girl.
"Well then," said the curate, "bring me those books, señor landlord, for I should like to see them."

"With all my heart," said he, and going into his own room he brought out an old valise secured with a little chain, which when opened the curate found to contain three large books and some manuscripts written in a very good hand. The first he opened he found to be _Don Cirongilio of Thrace_; the second, _Don Felixmarte of Hircania_; and the other, the _History of the Great Captain Gonzalo Hernández de Córdoba, with the Life of Diego García de Paredes_.
When the curate read the first two titles he looked over at the barber and said, "We could use my friend's housekeeper and niece here now."
"No," said the barber, "I can do just as well by carrying them out to the yard or to the hearth — and there's a very good fire there."
"What? Your worship would burn my books?" said the landlord.
"Only these two," said the curate, "_Don Cirongilio_ and _Felixmarte_."
"Are my books, then, heretics or phlegmatics, that you want to burn them?" said the landlord.
"Schismatics, you mean, friend," said the barber, "not phlegmatics."

"That's it," said the landlord; "but if you want to burn any, let it be the one about the Great Captain and that Diego García — because I'd rather have a child of mine burnt than either of the other two."

"Brother," said the curate, "those two books are made up of lies and are full of folly and nonsense; but this one about the Great Captain is true history, and contains the deeds of Gonzalo Hernández of Córdoba, who by his many and great achievements earned the title all over the world of the Great Captain — a famous and illustrious name, deserved by him alone. And this Diego García de Paredes was a distinguished knight of the city of Trujillo in Estremadura, a most gallant soldier, of such bodily strength that with one finger he stopped a mill-wheel in full motion; and posted with a two-handed sword at the foot of a bridge he kept a whole vast army from passing across it, and achieved such other exploits that if, instead of his relating them himself with the modesty of a knight and of one writing his own history, some free and impartial writer had recorded them, they would have put in the shade all the deeds of the Hectors, Achilleses, and Rolands."

"Tell that to my father!" said the landlord. "There's a thing to be astonished at — stopping a mill-wheel! By God, your worship should read what I have read of Felixmarte of Hircania, how with one single backstroke he cleft five giants asunder through the middle as if they had been made of bean-pods like the little friars the children make; and another time he attacked a very great and powerful army of more than a million six hundred thousand soldiers, all armed from head to foot, and he routed them all as if they had been flocks of sheep."

"And then, what do you say to the good Cirongilio of Thrace, who was so stout and bold? — as may be seen in the book, where it's told that as he was sailing along a river there came up out of the middle of the water against him a fiery serpent, and as soon as he saw it he flung himself on it and got astride its scaly shoulders, and squeezed its throat with both hands with such force that the serpent, finding it was being throttled, had nothing for it but to let itself sink to the bottom of the river, carrying with it the knight, who would not let go his hold; and when they got down there he found himself among palaces and gardens so beautiful it was a wonder to see; and then the serpent changed itself into an old ancient man, who told him things never heard before. Hold your peace, señor; if you were to hear this you would go mad with delight. A couple of figs for your Great Captain and your Diego García!"
Hearing this, Dorothea said in a whisper to Cardenio, "Our landlord is almost fit to play a second part to Don Quixote."

"I think so," said Cardenio, "because, as he shows, he accepts it as a certainty that everything those books relate happened exactly as it's written down; and the barefoot friars themselves could not persuade him to the contrary."

"But consider, brother," said the curate again, "there never was any Felixmarte of Hircania in the world, nor any Cirongilio of Thrace, or any of the other knights of the same sort that the books of chivalry talk about.
