The whole thing is the fabrication and invention of idle wits, devised by them for the purpose you describe — of passing the time, as your reapers do when they read. For I swear to you in all seriousness, there never were any such knights in the world, and no such exploits or nonsense ever happened anywhere."

"Try that bone on another dog!" said the landlord. "As if I didn't know how many make five, and where my shoe pinches me. Don't think to feed me with pap, for by God I'm no fool. It's a fine joke for your worship to try to convince me that everything these good books say is nonsense and lies, when they're printed by license of the Lords of the Royal Council — as if they were people who would allow such a load of lies to be printed all together, and so many battles and enchantments that they take away one's senses."

"I have told you, friend," said the curate, "that it's done to divert our idle thoughts; and just as in well-ordered states games of chess, fives, and billiards are allowed for the diversion of those who don't care to work, or aren't obliged to, or can't, so books of this kind are allowed to be printed, on the supposition — which is in fact the truth — that there can be nobody so ignorant as to take any of them for true stories. And if I were allowed now, and the present company wished it, I could say something about the qualities books of chivalry should possess to be good ones, which would be to the advantage and even to the taste of some; but I hope the time will come when I can communicate my ideas to someone who might be able to mend matters. In the meantime, señor landlord, believe what I have said, and take your books and make up your mind about their truth or falsehood; and much good may they do you — and God grant you may not fall lame of the same foot your guest Don Quixote limps on."

"No fear of that," replied the landlord. "I shall not be so mad as to make a knight-errant of myself; I see well enough that things are not now as they used to be in those days when, they say, those famous knights roamed about the world."

Sancho had appeared in the middle of this conversation, and he was very much troubled and downcast by what he heard said about knights-errant being no longer in vogue, and all books of chivalry being folly and lies. He resolved in his heart to wait and see what came of this journey of his master's, and if it didn't turn out as happily as his master expected, he determined to leave him and go back to his wife and children and his ordinary work.

The landlord was carrying away the valise and the books when the curate said to him, "Wait — I want to see what those papers are that are written in such a good hand." The landlord took them out and handed them to him to read, and he saw it was a work of about eight sheets of manuscript, with, in large letters at the beginning, the title _Novel of the Ill-Advised Curiosity_. The curate read three or four lines to himself and said, "I must say the title of this novel doesn't seem bad to me, and I feel an inclination to read it all." To which the landlord replied, "Then your reverence will do well to read it, because I can tell you that some guests who have read it here have been much pleased with it and have begged it from me very earnestly. But I wouldn't give it, meaning to return it to the person who forgot the valise, books, and papers here — since maybe he'll come back here some time or other. And though I know I shall miss the books, faith I mean to return them; for though I am an innkeeper, still I am a Christian."
"You are quite right, friend," said the curate, "but for all that, if the novel pleases me you must let me copy it."
"With all my heart," replied the host.
While they were talking, Cardenio had taken up the novel and begun to read it, and forming the same opinion of it as the curate, he begged him to read it so they might all hear it.
"I would read it," said the curate, "if the time wouldn't be better spent in sleeping."
"It will be rest enough for me," said Dorothea, "to while away the time by listening to some tale, for my spirits are not yet calm enough to let me sleep when it would be seasonable."
"Well then, in that case," said the curate, "I will read it, if only out of curiosity; perhaps it may contain something pleasant."

Master Nicholas added his entreaties to the same effect, and Sancho too; seeing which, and considering that he would give pleasure to all and receive it himself, the curate said, "Well then, everyone attend, for the novel begins like this."

title: Part 1, Chapter 33
paragraphs: In which is told the story of “The Ill-Advised Curiosity”

In Florence, a rich and famous city in the Italian province of Tuscany, there lived two wealthy, well-born gentlemen named Anselmo and Lothario. They were such close friends that everyone who knew them referred to them simply as “The Two Friends.” Both were unmarried, young, the same age, and shared the same tastes, which was reason enough to explain the mutual friendship between them. It is true that Anselmo leaned a little more toward the pleasures of love, while hunting held more attraction for Lothario; but when the occasion called for it, Anselmo would set aside his own preferences to go along with Lothario's, and Lothario would drop his to fall in with Anselmo's. In this way their inclinations stayed in step with each other so perfectly that the best-regulated clock could not have kept better time.

Anselmo was deeply in love with a beautiful, well-born young woman of the same city, the daughter of parents so respected, and so worthy of respect herself, that he decided, with the approval of his friend Lothario, without whom he did nothing, to ask her parents for her hand in marriage. And he did exactly that. Lothario carried the proposal and handled the negotiation so well on his friend's behalf that in a short time Anselmo had what he desired, and Camilla was so happy to have won Anselmo as her husband that she gave thanks endlessly to heaven, and to Lothario, since it was through him that such good fortune had come to her. During the first few days, wedding days being usually given over to celebration, Lothario visited his friend Anselmo's house as often as before, doing his best to honor him and the occasion and to please him in every way he could. But once the wedding festivities were over and the stream of visits and congratulations had slowed, Lothario began deliberately to stay away from Anselmo's house. It seemed to him, as it naturally would to any sensible man, that a friend's house should not be visited as often after his marriage as in his bachelor days: true and genuine friendship cannot and should not be suspicious in any way, but even so, a married man's honor is such a delicate thing that it is considered vulnerable even to brothers, let alone to friends. Anselmo noticed that Lothario's visits had stopped and complained to him about it. He said that if he had known marriage would cost him the pleasure of Lothario's company, he would never have married at all; and that if the perfect harmony between them in his bachelor days had earned them a name as sweet as “The Two Friends,” he was not going to let a title so rare and so delightful be lost to an unnecessary urge to look proper. So he begged him, if such a word could even be used between them, to be master of his house again and to come and go as he used to, assuring him that his wife Camilla had no wish or inclination other than whatever he wanted her to have, and that, knowing how sincerely the two of them loved each other, she was hurt to see Lothario so distant.

To all this, and to much more that Anselmo said to persuade him to visit the house as he always had, Lothario replied with such prudence, sense, and judgment that Anselmo was satisfied his friend meant well, and they agreed that Lothario would come to dine with him two days a week and on holidays. But although they made this arrangement, Lothario resolved to follow it only as far as he judged consistent with his friend's honor, since Anselmo's good name mattered more to him than his own. He said, rightly, that a married man whom heaven had blessed with a beautiful wife should think as carefully about which male friends he brought into his house as about which women his wife spent her time with, because what cannot be done or arranged in the marketplace, at church, at public festivals, or at religious stations, opportunities that husbands cannot always deny their wives, can easily be managed at the house of the female friend or relative she trusts most. Lothario also said that every married man needs a friend who will point out any carelessness in his behavior, because it sometimes happens that a husband's deep affection for his wife makes him either fail to caution her or, to avoid upsetting her, hold back from telling her to do or not do certain things, when doing or avoiding them could be a matter of honor or disgrace for him; mistakes of this kind he could easily correct if a friend warned him. But where could anyone find a friend as wise, as loyal, and as true as the one Lothario described?

Honestly, I do not know; Lothario alone was such a friend. With the utmost care and vigilance he looked after his friend's honor and worked to trim, cut down, and reduce the number of days he visited the house under their agreement, so that the visits of a young man, wealthy, well-born, and aware of his own attractive qualities, to the home of a woman as beautiful as Camilla would not be eyed with suspicion by the prying, malicious gaze of the idle public. Although his integrity and reputation might hold gossiping tongues in check, he was still unwilling to risk either his own good name or his friend's, and for that reason he spent most of the agreed-upon days on other business that he claimed was unavoidable. So a large part of each day was taken up with complaints on one side and excuses on the other. One day, however, while the two of them were walking together outside the city, Anselmo said the following to Lothario.

“You probably imagine, Lothario my friend, that I can never give enough thanks for the favors God has shown me, in making me the son of such parents as mine, in pouring out with a generous hand what people call the gifts of nature and of fortune, and above all in giving me you for a friend and Camilla for a wife: two treasures I value, if not as highly as I should, then at least as highly as I am able. And yet, with all these blessings, which are usually everything a man needs to live happily, I am the most discontented and dissatisfied man in the whole world. For some time now, I cannot say how long, a desire so strange and so far out of the ordinary has been harassing and oppressing me that I marvel at myself; when I am alone I blame and scold myself for it, and I try to smother it and hide it from my own thoughts, with no more success than if I were deliberately trying to broadcast it to the whole world. Since it must come out in the end, I want to entrust it to your safekeeping. I feel certain that by doing this, and through the effort you will make, as a true friend, to bring me relief, I will soon find myself free of the anguish it causes, and that your care will bring me as much happiness as my own foolishness has brought me misery.”

Anselmo's words left Lothario astonished, since he could not guess where such a long preamble was leading. He tried to imagine what desire could be troubling his friend this way, but his guesses all landed far from the truth. To relieve the anxiety this suspense was causing him, he told Anselmo that he was doing their great friendship a flagrant injustice by taking such a roundabout route to confide his most private thoughts, when he knew perfectly well he could count on Lothario either for advice on how to put them aside or for help in carrying them out.

“That is true,” Anselmo replied, “and trusting in it, I will tell you, friend Lothario, that the desire tormenting me is this: I want to know whether my wife Camilla is as good and as perfect as I believe her to be. And I cannot satisfy myself on this point except by testing her in a way that proves the purity of her virtue the way fire proves the purity of gold. Because I am convinced, my friend, that a woman is virtuous only to the degree that she is or is not tempted, and that the only truly strong woman is the one who does not give in to the promises, gifts, tears, and constant pleading of determined lovers. What credit does a woman deserve for being good if no one urges her to be bad? What is so remarkable about the reserve and caution of a woman who is never given an opportunity to go wrong, and who knows her husband will kill her the first time he catches her in any impropriety? So I do not hold the woman who is virtuous out of fear or lack of opportunity in the same regard as the one who emerges from temptation and trial wearing the crown of victory. For these reasons, and many others I could give you to justify and support my opinion, I want my wife Camilla to pass through this crisis, to be refined and tested in the fire of finding herself pursued, and pursued by a man worthy of setting his heart on her. If she comes out of this struggle victorious, as I know she will, I will consider my good fortune unmatched; I will be able to say that my cup of desire is full, and that the virtuous woman of whom the sage asks, 'Who shall find her?' has fallen to my lot. And if the result is the opposite of what I expect, the satisfaction of knowing my opinion was correct will let me bear without complaint the pain that such dearly bought experience will naturally cause me. And since nothing you can say against my wish will stop me from carrying it out, I want you, friend Lothario, to agree to be the instrument of this plan I am set on. I will give you the opportunities to do it, and you will lack nothing I consider necessary for the pursuit of a virtuous, honorable, modest, and high-minded woman. Among other reasons, what moves me to entrust this difficult task to you is this: if Camilla is conquered by you, the conquest will not be pushed to the final extreme, but only far enough to count as accomplished what, out of a sense of honor, will be left undone. So I will be wronged in nothing but intention, and my injury will stay buried in the integrity of your silence, which I know well will be, in anything that concerns me, as everlasting as the silence of death. So if you want me to enjoy anything that deserves to be called life, you will enter this battle of love at once, not halfheartedly or lazily, but with the energy and zeal my desire demands, and with the loyalty our friendship guarantees me.”

These were the words Anselmo spoke to Lothario, who listened so attentively that, apart from what he had already said, he did not open his lips until his friend had finished. Seeing that Anselmo had nothing more to say, Lothario looked at him for a long moment, the way one stares at something never seen before, something astonishing and bewildering, and then said to him, “I cannot convince myself, Anselmo my friend, that what you have just said is not a joke. If I had thought you were speaking seriously, I would not have let you go so far; I would have cut your long speech short simply by refusing to listen. I genuinely suspect that either you do not know me, or I do not know you. But no, I know perfectly well that you are Anselmo, and you know that I am Lothario. The trouble, it seems to me, is that you are not the Anselmo you used to be, and you must have decided I am not the Lothario I ought to be. The things you have said to me do not come from the Anselmo who was my friend, and what you are demanding of me is nothing that should be asked of the Lothario you know. True friends may test their friends and make use of them, as a poet put it, _usque ad aras;_ by which he meant that they will not call on their friendship for anything that goes against the will of God. If a pagan felt this way about friendship, how much more should a Christian, who knows that no human friendship is worth forfeiting the divine? And if a friend ever does go so far as to set aside his duty to Heaven to fulfill his duty to a friend, it should not be over trifles or small matters, but only when his friend's life and honor are at stake. So tell me, Anselmo: which of these two is in danger for you, that I should put myself at risk to gratify you and do something as detestable as what you are asking? Neither one, obviously. On the contrary, as far as I can tell, you are asking me to work hard at robbing you of your honor and your life, and at robbing myself of mine at the same time. For if I take away your honor, plainly I take away your life, since a man without honor is worse than dead; and if I become the instrument, as you insist, of so much harm to you, won't I be left without honor too, and therefore without life? Listen to me, Anselmo my friend, and do not be impatient to answer until I have said everything that occurs to me about this desire of yours. There will be time enough afterward for you to reply and for me to hear you out.”
“Fine,” said Anselmo. “Say whatever you want to say.”

Lothario went on, “It seems to me, Anselmo, that your state of mind right now is exactly like that of the Moors, who can never be brought to see the error of their creed by quotations from Holy Scripture, or by arguments that rest on rational examination or are grounded in the articles of faith. They have to have examples that are tangible, easy, intelligible, demonstrable, beyond doubt, with mathematical proofs that cannot be denied, like '_If equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal._' And if they don't understand this in words, and in fact they don't, it has to be shown to them with the hands and set right in front of their eyes; and even then no one ever succeeds in convincing them of the truth of our holy religion. I am going to have to take this same approach with you, because this desire that has sprung up in you is so absurd, so far removed from anything that even resembles reason, that I think it would be a waste of time to spend reason arguing against your simplicity, for the moment I will call it nothing worse than that. I am even tempted to leave you in your folly as punishment for this destructive desire of yours; but the friendship I feel for you, which will not let me abandon you in such obvious danger of destruction, keeps me from treating you so harshly. And so you can see this clearly, tell me, Anselmo: haven't you just told me that I must force my attentions on a modest woman, seduce one who is virtuous, make advances to one who is pure-minded, pay court to one who is prudent? Yes, that is what you told me. Well then, if you know you have a wife who is modest, virtuous, pure-minded, and prudent, what exactly are you looking for? And if you believe she will emerge victorious from every attack of mine, as she undoubtedly would, what higher titles do you think you can give her afterward than the ones she has now? How will she be any better then than she is already? Either you do not really believe she is what you say she is, or you do not know what you are demanding. If you do not believe she is what you say, why test her at all, instead of treating her as guilty and dealing with her however you see fit? But if she is as virtuous as you believe, it is pointless to put truth itself on trial, since after the trial it will hold exactly the same standing it had before. The conclusion is plain: attempting things that are more likely to harm us than to help us is the mark of reckless minds without reason, especially when they are things we are not forced or compelled to attempt, and when it is obvious from a great distance that attempting them is sheer madness.

“People attempt difficult things either for the sake of God, or for the sake of the world, or for both. Those undertaken for God's sake are what the saints attempt when they set out to live the lives of angels in human bodies. Those undertaken for the world's sake are the efforts of men who cross immense stretches of water, endure every variety of climate, and travel through so many foreign countries to acquire what people call the blessings of fortune. And those undertaken for God and the world together are the deeds of brave soldiers who, the moment they see a breach in the enemy's wall no wider than a cannonball could make, cast all fear aside and, without hesitating or weighing the obvious danger threatening them, carried forward by the desire to defend their faith, their country, and their king, hurl themselves fearlessly into the thousand waiting deaths arrayed against them. These are the kinds of things people normally attempt, and there is honor, glory, and gain in attempting them, however full of difficulty and danger they may be. But the thing you say you want to attempt and carry through will win you no glory from God, no blessings of fortune, no fame among men. Even if the outcome is exactly what you want, you will be no happier, no richer, no more honored than you are at this moment; and if it goes the other way, you will find yourself in misery greater than can be imagined, and it will do you no good then to remind yourself that no one else knows of your misfortune. It will be torture enough, enough to crush you, that you know it yourself. To confirm the truth of what I am saying, let me recite a stanza by the famous poet Luigi Tansillo, from the end of the first part of his 'Tears of Saint Peter,' which goes like this:

The anguish and the shame grew greater still in Peter's heart as morning slowly broke; no eye was there to see him, and he knew it, yet he stood ashamed before himself; exposed to every gaze or hidden from all view, a noble heart will feel the pang the same; the soul that sins is prey to shame, though none but heaven and earth can see its blame.

So keeping it secret will not spare you your sorrow; instead you will weep without ceasing, if not tears from your eyes, then tears of blood from your heart, like those wept by that simple-minded doctor our poet tells us about, who tried the test of the cup that the wiser Rinaldo, better advised, refused to attempt. That may be poetic fiction, but it contains a moral lesson worth noticing, studying, and imitating. What's more, what I am about to say will bring you to see the enormous mistake you are set on committing.

“Tell me, Anselmo: if Heaven, or good luck, had made you the owner and lawful master of a diamond of the finest quality, one whose excellence and purity satisfied every gem-cutter who examined it, with all of them declaring with one voice and in unanimous agreement that in purity, quality, and fineness it was everything a stone of its kind could possibly be, and you yourself believed the same, knowing nothing to the contrary, would it be reasonable for you to take that diamond, set it between an anvil and a hammer, and test by sheer force of blows and strength of arm whether it was as hard and as fine as everyone said? And suppose you did. If the stone survived such a stupid test, it would gain nothing in value or reputation; and if it shattered, which could happen, wouldn't everything be lost? Of course it would, and its owner would be written off as a fool in everyone's opinion. So consider, Anselmo my friend, that Camilla is a diamond of the finest quality, in your judgment and in everyone else's, and that it makes no sense to expose her to the risk of being broken; for if she stays intact, she cannot rise to any higher value than she already has, and if she gives way and cannot resist, think now about how you will be deprived of her, and how rightly you will blame yourself for having caused her ruin and your own. Remember that there is no jewel in the world as precious as a chaste and virtuous woman, and that all of a woman's honor consists in her good reputation; and since your wife's reputation stands at the supreme height you know it does, why would you want to call that truth into question? Remember, my friend, that woman is an imperfect creature, and that one should not set obstacles in her path for her to trip and fall over; rather, they should be cleared away and her road left free of every obstruction, so that, unimpeded, she can run her course swiftly toward the perfection she needs, which consists in being virtuous. Naturalists tell us that the ermine is a small animal with fur of the purest white, and that when hunters want to capture one, they use this trick: having found the places it frequents and passes through, they block those paths with mud, then flush the animal and drive it toward the spot; and when the ermine reaches the mud, it stops dead and lets itself be captured rather than pass through the muck and stain and dirty its whiteness, which it values more than freedom and life itself. The virtuous and chaste woman is an ermine, and the virtue of modesty is whiter and purer than snow; and the man who wants her not to lose it, but to keep and preserve it, must take a different approach from the one used on the ermine. He must not lay before her the mud of the gifts and attentions of persistent lovers, because perhaps, and even without the 'perhaps,' she may not have enough virtue and natural strength in herself to get through those obstacles and trample them underfoot. They must be cleared from her path, and what should be set before her instead is the brightness of virtue and the beauty that lies in a good reputation. A virtuous woman is also like a mirror of clear, shining crystal, which any breath that touches it can cloud and dim. She must be treated the way holy relics are treated: adored, but not touched. She must be guarded and prized the way one guards and prizes a beautiful garden full of roses and flowers, whose owner lets no one walk through it or pick a single blossom; it is enough for others to enjoy its fragrance and beauty from a distance, through the iron railings. Finally, let me recite some verses that have come back to me; I heard them in a modern play, and they seem to me to bear exactly on what we are discussing. A prudent old man was advising another, the father of a young girl, to shelter her, watch over her, and keep her secluded, and among his other arguments he used these:
A woman is a thing of glass; but it is best not to find out by testing whether she can break: anything at all could come to pass.
Breaking is an easy matter, and it is folly to deal blows to what cannot be repaired, to shatter what you can't make whole.
All of this, then, holds as true, and the reason is plain to see: for wherever Danaës exist, golden showers exist there too.

“Everything I have said to you so far, Anselmo, has concerned what affects you; now it is only right that I say something about what affects me. And if I run long, forgive me, because the labyrinth you have walked into, and that you want me to pull you out of, makes it necessary.

“You count me as your friend, and yet you want to strip me of my honor, something completely incompatible with friendship. And not only that: you want me to strip you of yours as well. That you would rob me of mine is clear, because when Camilla sees me courting her, as you are asking, she will certainly regard me as a man without honor or decency, since I would be attempting and doing something utterly contrary to what I owe to my own standing and to your friendship. That you want me to rob you of yours is beyond doubt, because Camilla, seeing me press my attentions on her, will assume I have spotted some looseness in her that emboldened me to reveal my shameful desire; and if she considers herself dishonored, that dishonor touches you, since she belongs to you. From this comes what happens so often: the husband of an adulterous wife, even though he knows nothing of it, has given his wife no cause to fail in her duty, and has not, through carelessness or negligence, had it in his power to prevent his disgrace, is nonetheless branded with a vile and insulting name, and the people who know of his wife's guilt look at him with contempt rather than pity, even though they can see his misfortune is not his own fault but the fault of his corrupt partner's lust. But let me tell you why, with good reason, dishonor falls on the husband of an unfaithful wife even when he does not know she is unfaithful, bears no blame, and has done nothing and given no provocation to make her so. And don't grow weary of listening to me, because all of this is for your benefit.

“When God created our first parent in the earthly paradise, Holy Scripture says that He sent sleep upon Adam, and while he slept He took a rib from his left side and from it formed our mother Eve; and when Adam awoke and looked at her, he said, 'This is flesh of my flesh, and bone of my bone.' And God said, 'For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother, and they shall be two in one flesh.' And at that moment the divine sacrament of marriage was instituted, with bonds that only death can untie. This miraculous sacrament has such force and power that it makes two different people one and the same flesh, and it does even more than that in the marriage of two virtuous people, for though they have two souls, they have only one will. It follows that, since the wife's flesh is one and the same as her husband's, any stains that fall on it, any injuries it suffers, fall on the husband's flesh too, even though, as I said, he may have done nothing to cause them. Just as pain in the foot or in any part of the body is felt by the whole body, because it is all one flesh, and just as the head feels the injury to the ankle without having caused it, so the husband, being one with his wife, shares in her dishonor. And since all worldly honor and dishonor is born of flesh and blood, and the erring wife's dishonor is exactly that kind, the husband must inevitably bear his share of it and be counted dishonored without even knowing it. See, then, Anselmo, the danger you are running by trying to disturb the peace in which your virtuous wife lives. See what an empty, ill-advised curiosity is driving you to stir up passions that now lie quiet in the breast of your chaste wife. Consider that what you are staking everything to win is little, and what you stand to lose is so much that I will leave it undescribed, since I lack the words to express it. But if everything I have said is not enough to turn you from your vile purpose, you will have to find some other instrument for your dishonor and ruin, because I refuse to be that instrument, even if it costs me your friendship, which is the greatest loss I can imagine.”

With that, the wise and virtuous Lothario fell silent, and Anselmo, troubled and deep in thought, could not say a word in reply for some time. At last he said, “You have seen, Lothario my friend, how attentively I listened to everything you chose to say to me, and in your arguments, examples, and comparisons I have recognized the great intelligence you possess and the perfection of true friendship you have attained. I also see and admit that if I ignore your opinion and follow my own, I am fleeing the good and chasing the evil. That being granted, you must consider that I am now suffering from the disease that sometimes afflicts women, when a craving seizes them to eat clay, plaster, charcoal, and even worse things, things disgusting to look at, let alone to eat. So some trick will be needed to cure me, and it could be done easily: you have only to begin, even half-heartedly and as a pretense, to pay court to Camilla, who will not be so frail that her virtue collapses at the first assault. That mere attempt will satisfy me, and you will have done what our friendship requires of you, not only in restoring my life, but in persuading me not to throw away my honor. And you are obliged to do this for one reason alone: since I am, as I am, determined to put this test into practice, you cannot allow me to reveal my weakness to some other person, which would endanger the very honor you are fighting to keep me from losing. As for your own honor, if it stands lower than it should in Camilla's estimation while you are courting her, that matters little or nothing, because before long, once we find in her the constancy we expect, you can tell her the plain truth about our trick, and your standing with her will be restored. Since you are risking so little, and since by risking it you can give me so much satisfaction, do not refuse to take this on, even if more difficulties present themselves; because, as I have said, if you will just make a start, I will consider the whole question settled.”

Seeing Anselmo's fixed determination, and not knowing what further examples to offer or arguments to make in order to talk him out of it, and seeing too that he was threatening to confide his destructive plan to someone else, Lothario decided, to avoid a greater evil, to humor him and do what he asked, intending to handle the affair in such a way that Anselmo would be satisfied without Camilla's mind being corrupted. So he answered that Anselmo should tell no one else of his plan: he would take on the task himself and begin whenever Anselmo liked. Anselmo embraced him warmly and affectionately and thanked him for the offer as though Lothario had granted him some enormous favor; and they agreed to begin the very next day. Anselmo would give Lothario the opportunity and time to speak with Camilla alone, and would supply him with money and jewels to offer her and give her as presents. He also suggested that Lothario arrange music for her and write verses in her praise, and if Lothario didn't want the trouble of composing them, Anselmo offered to write them himself. Lothario agreed to everything, with an intention very different from the one Anselmo imagined; and with this understanding they returned to Anselmo's house, where they found Camilla waiting for her husband anxiously and uneasily, because he was later coming home that day than usual. Lothario went off to his own house, and Anselmo stayed in his, as contented as Lothario was troubled, for Lothario could see no good way out of this ill-conceived business. That night, however, he thought of a plan for deceiving Anselmo without doing Camilla any harm. The next day he went to dine with his friend and was welcomed by Camilla, who received him and treated him with great warmth, knowing how fond her husband was of him. When dinner was over and the table cleared, Anselmo told Lothario to stay there with Camilla while he attended to some urgent business; he would be back in an hour and a half. Camilla begged him not to go, and Lothario offered to go with him, but nothing could persuade Anselmo. On the contrary, he insisted that Lothario stay and wait for him, because he had a matter of great importance to discuss with him; and at the same time he told Camilla not to leave Lothario alone until he came back. In short, he managed to make the reason, or the foolishness, of his absence look so plausible that no one could have guessed it was a pretense.

Anselmo left, and Camilla and Lothario remained alone at the table, since the rest of the household had gone off to eat. Lothario found himself in the arena, exactly as his friend had wished, facing an opponent whose beauty alone could conquer a squadron of armed knights; judge for yourself whether he had reason to be afraid. What he actually did was rest his elbow on the arm of the chair and his cheek on his hand, and, apologizing to Camilla for his bad manners, say that he would like to sleep a little until Anselmo came back. Camilla answered that he could rest more comfortably in the sitting room than in his chair, and urged him to go in and sleep there; but Lothario declined, and there he stayed, asleep, until Anselmo returned. Finding Camilla in her own room and Lothario asleep, Anselmo assumed that he had been gone long enough to give them time both to talk and even to nap, and he could hardly wait for Lothario to wake up so he could go out with him and ask how things had gone. Everything happened just as he wanted: Lothario woke, the two of them left the house at once, Anselmo asked what he was so eager to know, and Lothario answered that he had thought it unwise to declare himself fully the first time, so he had done nothing but praise Camilla's charms, telling her the whole city talked of nothing but her beauty and wit. This had seemed to him an excellent opening for winning her goodwill and making her inclined to listen to him gladly the next time, the same device the devil uses when he wants to deceive someone who is on guard: being the angel of darkness, he disguises himself as an angel of light, presents a pleasing appearance, and only reveals himself at the end, getting what he wants if his trick isn't discovered at the start. All this delighted Anselmo, and he said he would provide the same opportunity every day without even leaving the house, because he would keep himself busy at home in ways that would prevent Camilla from detecting the scheme.

And so several days went by, and Lothario, without saying a word to Camilla, kept reporting to Anselmo that he had talked with her and had never been able to draw from her the slightest hint of consent to anything dishonorable, not even a sign or a shadow of hope. On the contrary, he said, she was threatening to tell her husband about it.

“So far, so good,” said Anselmo. “Camilla has resisted words; now we must see how she resists deeds. Tomorrow I will give you two thousand gold crowns to offer her, or simply hand to her, and another two thousand to buy jewels to tempt her with. Women love to be becomingly dressed and to go about looking elegant, however chaste they are, and all the more so if they are beautiful. If she resists this temptation, I will be satisfied and will give you no more trouble.”

Lothario replied that since he had begun, he would see the undertaking through to the end, though he expected to come out of it exhausted and defeated. The next day he received the four thousand crowns, and with them four thousand headaches, because he had no idea what new lie to tell. In the end, though, he made up his mind to say that Camilla stood as firm against gifts and promises as she had against words, and that there was no point in taking any further trouble, since all the effort was being spent for nothing.

But chance, steering events in a different direction, arranged matters otherwise. Anselmo, after leaving Lothario and Camilla alone as on previous occasions, shut himself into a side room and stationed himself at the keyhole to watch and listen to what passed between them, and he saw that in more than half an hour Lothario said not one word to Camilla, and would not have said one if he had stood there for a century. He concluded that everything his friend had told him about Camilla's replies was pure invention and lies. To find out whether this was so, he came out, called Lothario aside, and asked what news there was and what mood Camilla was in. Lothario answered that he was not willing to carry on with the business, because she had answered him so angrily and so harshly that he didn't have the heart to say anything more to her.

“Ah, Lothario, Lothario,” said Anselmo, “how badly you are repaying what you owe me, and the boundless trust I have placed in you! I have just been watching through this keyhole, and I saw that you did not say a single word to Camilla, from which I conclude that you never spoke to her on the earlier occasions either. And if that is true, as it undoubtedly is, why are you deceiving me? Why are you scheming to take away the means I might otherwise find of getting what I want?”

Anselmo said no more, but he had said enough to leave Lothario ashamed and embarrassed. Feeling his honor wounded at having been caught in a lie, Lothario swore to Anselmo that from that moment on he would devote himself to satisfying him without any deception, as Anselmo would see for himself if he was curious enough to spy on them; though he needn't bother, because the effort Lothario would put into satisfying him would remove every suspicion from his mind. Anselmo believed him, and to give him an opportunity that was freer and less exposed to surprise, he decided to leave his house for eight days and go stay with a friend of his who lived in a village not far from the city; and to better explain the departure to Camilla, he arranged for the friend to send him a very urgent invitation.

Unhappy, shortsighted Anselmo, what are you doing? What are you plotting? What are you setting in motion? Realize that you are working against yourself, plotting your own dishonor, engineering your own ruin. Your wife Camilla is virtuous; you possess her in peace and quiet; no one threatens your happiness; her thoughts never wander beyond the walls of your house; you are her heaven on earth, the goal of her wishes, the fulfillment of her desires, the measure by which she measures her own will, conforming it in everything to yours and to Heaven's. If, then, the mine of her honor, beauty, virtue, and modesty yields you, without any labor, all the riches it holds and all that you could wish for, why insist on digging the earth for new veins, for new and unknown treasure, and risk the collapse of the whole, since in the end it rests only on the fragile props of her weak nature? Remember that from the man who seeks the impossible, even the possible may justly be withheld, as one poet expressed it better:
I go seeking life in death, and health in sickness I pursue; in prison I seek freedom's breath, in traitors, loyalty true.
And Fate, which never deigns to grant a single grace or favor to me, since I demand what cannot be, denies me even what might be.

The next day Anselmo left for the village, after telling Camilla that while he was away Lothario would come to look after the house and to dine with her, and that she should treat him exactly as she would treat Anselmo himself. Camilla was upset by her husband's instructions, as any sensible and decent woman would be, and pointed out to him that it was not proper for anyone to sit in his place at the table while he was gone; if he was doing this because he doubted she could manage his household, let him try her this once, and he would learn from experience that she was equal to far greater responsibilities. Anselmo replied that this was how he wanted it, and that her job was simply to bow her head and obey. Camilla said she would, though very much against her will.

Anselmo went, and the next day Lothario came to the house, where Camilla gave him a friendly but modest welcome. She never allowed Lothario to see her alone, however: she always kept her menservants and maidservants around her, above all a maid of her own named Leonela, of whom she was very fond (the two had been raised together since childhood in her father's house, and Camilla had kept her on after marrying Anselmo). For the first three days Lothario said nothing to her, although he could have spoken when the table was cleared and the servants went off to eat a hurried meal, for those were Camilla's orders; what's more, Leonela had instructions to eat before Camilla did and never to leave her side. But Leonela, whose mind was set on other things more to her liking, and who needed those hours and opportunities for her own pleasures, did not always follow her mistress's orders; instead she left the two of them alone, as if that were what she had been told to do. Even so, Camilla's modest bearing, the serenity of her face, the composure of her whole person were enough to hold Lothario's tongue in check. But the good that Camilla's many virtues did in silencing Lothario's tongue turned out to be the ruin of them both, because if his tongue was silent, his mind was busy, with leisure to dwell, one by one, on every perfection of Camilla's goodness and beauty: charms enough to kindle love in a marble statue, never mind a heart of flesh. Lothario gazed at her during the time he could have been speaking to her, and thought about how worthy she was of being loved; and that thought began, little by little, to undermine his loyalty to Anselmo. A thousand times he considered leaving the city and going somewhere Anselmo would never see him and he would never see Camilla, but the pleasure he found in looking at her already stood in the way and held him fast. He forced himself, he struggled to push down and drive out the delight he took in contemplating her; when he was alone, he blamed himself for his weakness, called himself a bad friend, even a bad Christian; then he reasoned the matter over, comparing himself with Anselmo, and always arrived at the same conclusion: Anselmo's folly and recklessness had been worse than his own disloyalty, and if he could excuse his intentions before God as easily as before men, he had no punishment to fear for his offense.

In short, Camilla's beauty and goodness, combined with the opportunity her blind husband had placed in his hands, overthrew Lothario's loyalty. Paying attention to nothing except where his desire was pulling him, after Anselmo had been away three days, three days of constant struggle against his own passion, Lothario began declaring his love to Camilla with such intensity, in such heated language, that she was stunned with amazement; all she could do was rise from her seat and withdraw to her room without answering him a single word. But this cold reception did nothing to weaken in Lothario the hope that is always born alongside love; on the contrary, his passion for Camilla only grew. As for Camilla, having discovered in him something she had never expected, she did not know what to do. Deciding that it was neither safe nor proper to give him another chance or opportunity to speak with her, she resolved to send one of her servants, and she sent him that very night, with a letter to Anselmo, in which she addressed the following words to him.
